#8382. On the Road Again — John Muir Trail Day 9

I admit, I was nervous about going back on the John Muir Trail.

The good news was that I did not have a big coughing fit in the night.  I woke up with a forgotten dream, I went to the bathroom, but I fell back to sleep and overall slept pretty decently.   At 4:45 a.m. I checked the time and decided, “Well the alarm is going off at five a.m., so I may as well get up.”

I could only eat half of the chorizo breakfast burrito.  It was delicious, but so big.  I mean huge!  It also seemed like my hiker hunger had been satisfied by all the barbeque I ate, so that was a factor too.

As  I packed, I kicked myself when I realized that I should have bought some more hand sanitizer – or looked for it in the free hiker boxes at the Mount Williamson Motel.  My bottle started leaking constantly on trail, to the point that I now kept it inside two nested ziplock bags.  This was an essential item for my personal hygiene.  How could I forget that?

I also practiced my play part a little bit.  I was trying to distract myself, to calm down, but I could tell I was on edge.  After two days off trail, to include a stop in the Emergency Room, this was understandable.

My driver, Mark, showed up right on time.  I was two minutes away from being ready.  Then I threw the stuff in his car and we headed off.  Good-bye to Independence, CA!

As we drove, I asked Mark about his background.  He came from the Bay Area originally where he used to be a commercial fisherman.  Then he sold his boat and bought the house next door to his brother, who lives out here and works as a geologist.  It did not sound like Mark had any regrets about the move.

The ride was 45 dollars, so I gave him an even fifty.   The sun just began peeking out above the eastern mountains when I set off on the trail.  It was 6:30 a.m.

I must admit when I first picked up my pack, having filled it with all of the food for another (probable) six-day journey, I was dismayed.  I thought, “Oh my god, I’m gonna carry THIS thing!  How??”  But once I started walking it started to feel sort of normal – well, heavy normal – and I stopped focusing on the weight.

Despite my trepidation, it felt good to be headed back into the wilderness.

Based on our descent three days earlier, I realized I would be able to see not just the Valley but the actual road and parking lot for quite a long time.  I remembered in descending it had felt very nearby, but then we had taken a long time to arrive.  So, I was prepared for a long, slow uphill.  Being mentally prepared it seemed to go steadily and, while it felt hard, it did not feel too hard.  I felt okay.

I was still coughing a little bit as I advanced, and I was still producing some mucus.  This meant I was not as much better as I had hoped, but I was definitely a whole lot better than I was before starting the antibiotics.  And I still had three days of treatment to go.

Eventually I made it to the area of the extended fall of giant boulders.  That was where I had first seen the road when descending, so I knew that I was now leaving the road behind me.   Halfway through, in the middle of this jumble of rocks, I saw a family.

This IS the boulder field I describe, but taken four days earlier during our descent. That is why Sam — who was no longer with me — is in the picture.

It was strange, they were neither ascending nor descending.  They were just hanging out in the boulders – a father, a mother, three kids about 6-12 years old, and a fluffy little brown dog, maybe a doodle or something?

They seemed a bit shook up, so I stopped to ask them what was going on.  They replied that a bear had just come into their camp site and eaten their breakfast!  I guess they figured the bear wouldn’t come after them in the rock pile.

Apparently, the dad was cooking pancakes on their grill and turned away just for a moment or two.  That was all the advantage the bear needed to move in and eat the whole batch!   The little dog barked furiously to defend their turf, but fortunately the bear did not pay it the slightest mind.  He just ate all the food and then lumbered into the forest.  They even managed to take a picture (from a distance!) of “bear eating pancakes” that they showed me.

Now I have encountered a few bears, and at this point I generally have more respect for them than fear of them.  (Though I would be terrified if I found myself between a sow and her cubs, of course!)  So, I talked to the family and reassured them, and we all walked together back to their campsite.  I urged the dad to report the incident to a ranger, telling him, “This bear is a juvenile, and it sounds like it’s making a habit of doing this around here.  When a bear gets accustomed to humans and human food, the outcome is usually bad – especially for the bear.”

Before parting, they told me something hilarious.  The little brown doodle dog?  Its name was “Bear.”

After that little episode I continued on and soon after I had a very large mammal edging closer behind me!  But it was a horse, not a bear, and it was leading a pack train of a horse and two-or-three mules.  One distinctive element on the John Muir Trail is stock animal poop.  Sometimes it is annoying, trying to avoid stepping on it when it is fresh, but other times it is helpful, in confirming that you are on the right track.   This was the first actual horse/mule train I had seen and I now found out how fast they go.  Answer:  It is not fast, but still a lot faster than I go, uphill at least!  I pulled off the trail and let them pass me.

High alpine lake en route to Kearsarge Pass.

I continued up and up at a kind of steady pace.  It felt hard, but not overwhelming, and before I knew it, I could see the Kearsarge Pass up ahead.  I was doing my usual routine of counting out 60 right-foot paces, or only 30 if it was very steep, before stopping to briefly catch my breath.  This cycle forces me to push myself a little bit and soon enough, I had reached the pass.

For some reason, both times I crossed it, Kearsarge felt like Grand Central Station.  There just always seemed to be a lot of people up there.   Still, I stopped, had my second breakfast, and chatted with the crowds.  It was only 9:30, so I made it up there in three hours.   Given my circumstances – a 69-year-old recovering from a lung infection ascending over 2,500 feet — I thought that time was quite good.

Some of the crowd at Kearsarge Pass, elevation 11,760 feet

I proceeded down the other side until I came to a fork in the trail.  Left was the route Sam and I took coming up.  Now I went right, a new route (for me) that would reconnect me with the John Muir Trail just a little further north than we left it.

From our navigation app, Sam and I guessed this other trail passed behind a ridge above us, but it turned out to be a higher altitude route within the same valley.  A few miles later the path intersected the main John Muir Trail.

This was a symbolic moment of return after my lengthy detour to resupply and get medical help.  I went a short way further to rest under a big tree and celebrate with my lunch.  Welcome back to the John Muir Trail; hooray!

I barely dared to confess to myself that my goal for the day included crossing not one but two passes.  It seemed a little crazy, but the layout of campsites and distance to my next resupply kind of dictated it.  With Kearsarge behind me, the next challenge was going to be Glen Pass.  However, I wasn’t too worried about Glen Pass.  The elevation gain would only be about 1,200 feet, or less than half of Kearsarge.

Oh, was I wrong!   It always seems to work out like that:  expect something difficult and it seems relatively easier than expected; expect something easy and it will often surprise with its difficulty.

The trail itself was rough and rocky, and several portions were very steep.  Also, I was tired from my morning exertion, and it was then the middle of the afternoon.  The sun was beating down relentlessly and there was no shade.

Finally, I tried out my umbrella in its intended role as a sunshade.  The problem was attaching it to my backpack in a way that would shade me and still be hands-free.  I had the gizmo designed for taking care of this, but it was hard to work it, especially with the splint on my finger.  When it was finally in place it worked fairly well.  I would give it a “D” for set-up and a “B” for operation.

Even shaded, Glen Pass was really hard.  There were some switchbacks, but while these are often converted into relatively smooth trails, going up to Glen Pass they were full of uneven rocks.  Getting ever more tired as I advanced, it became easy to imagine slipping or hurting myself.

Finally, I made it to the top of Glen Pass.  Hooray!  On most passes the ascent and descent meet at roughly the same point.   With Glen Pass, however, you arrive at one spot and then you have to walk along the edge of the ridgeline for about 100 yards or more before reaching the spot where you begin your descent.  On that ridge I stopped and had my second lunch.

Selfie atop the ridgeline of Glen Pass; check out my hands visible in the sunglasses…

Naturally, I was hoping the north side of the pass would be easier.  It was not.  True, I did not have to stop to catch my breath all the time, but I still had to tread very gingerly, because a twisted ankle or a fall were real possibilities on this quality of trail.

Eventually I got down lower where there were a whole series of scenic little lakes in the shadow of the mountains.  The first two were Upper Rae Lake and Middle Rae Lake and the trail traversed a narrow isthmus between the two of them that included a stream crossing.  Earlier in the season I expect you would wade through that crossing, but I was able to stay dry on stepping stones as I made my way across.

An island sat lonely in the middle of Upper Rae Lake

It was late afternoon as I entered the Rae Lakes campground on the Southeast side of Middle Rae Lake.  I was a tired puppy, because I had done two passes.  It wasn’t quite as much total elevation gain as Mount Whitney, but the difference is less than 300 feet, and I was doing it with a fully laden pack.  For someone still on antibiotics, it felt like quite an accomplishment.

At first, I thought I would cowboy camp away from the crowds at the campground.  (Cowboy Camp:  When there is little threat of rain, sleeping under the stars without a tent.)  Then I  found a sloped tent site, but the angle of slope was too much for restful sleep.  Finally, I came down to where there were many other campers and where there was a bear box.  With all my food, that box was a big  draw for me.

I set up opposite two very nice women who were bantering back-and-forth.  Eventually I went over to introduce myself to Serena and Evelyn.  I told them I was blogging, and they said I could take their picture and post it in my blog.  So, Serena and Evelyn, if you ever read this, you’re going to see yourselves in the blog!

You can tell just by looking them what a great attitude they had. Happy trails Serena and Evelyn!

Looking at tomorrow, I saw another long day.  Like Glen Pass today, I had a big climb to Pinchot Pass at the very end of the day, but at least it’s only one pass.  I hoped to have enough energy to make it, because I really didn’t want to start falling further behind.  I already lost two days in Independence because of my health, after all.  I decided an early start would be advisable, and I looked forward to escaping the Rae Lake crowds.

As the sun set and my cold dinner soaked, I reflected on the day.  It was a bear, no doubt about it (but maybe a small pun about it…).  But I had come through it and was back on the John Muir Trail.   We will see what happens next, but I was far more optimistic than I had been.  Amazing what 14 miles and a few antibiotics can do for a person’s attitude, right?

#8381. How to Field Dress a Deer Like a Pro: The Ultimate Step-By-Step Guide

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:10 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Learning (or remembering) how to field dress a deer can feel overwhelming, but if you have a sharp knife and a reasonably strong stomach, you’ll be able to figure it out. If you manage to do so without nicking the guts or yourself, that’s ideal.

Removing the guts is the bare minimum required for dropping a deer at a processor, and an essential skill every deer hunter should learn. A field-dressed deer is also a lighter deer, which makes dragging and loading it less cumbersome. And the sooner you gut a deer after shooting it, the better the venison will be. So, here’s a guide on how to field dress a deer in a few easy steps.

All you really need to gut a deer is a sharp knife and, if it’s getting dark, a good headlamp. Other deer hunters carry the kitchen sink with them and won’t field dress a deer without some or all of the following items:

Many experienced deer hunters can field dress a deer in minutes, while it can take new or casual deer hunters a half hour or more. The best way to gut a deer is to work slowly, use a sharp knife, and have adequate lighting.

Keep these gutting rules in mind before you get started:

Start by rolling the deer onto its back. It should be belly-up and evenly balanced on both shoulder blades. Adjust the rump and hips to ensure they’re as even as possible. If you’re working on a slope, rotate the deer so its rump points downhill and its head is uphill.

Ask a buddy to hold a leg. If you’re solo and the deer keeps slipping sideways or downhill, try wedging a log or stick under its rump or using paracord to tie a hind leg to a branch. Personally, I find paracord to be overkill, but will sometimes use my knee, shoulder, or armpit to anchor a hind leg or keep it out of the way as I work.

This step and the next can be done now or after opening the abdominal cavity. Grab a handful of the mammary gland, or testicles with your non-dominant hand and lift away from the deer’s body. Keeping your blade mostly parallel to the deer’s body, slice away at the base of the stretched hide until you’ve freed the reproductive organs, and toss aside. The goal is to avoid cutting into the organs and instead cutting under them.

This step can be done later or not at all, but I prefer to do this now (particularly when working alone) since it relaxes the tension between the hind legs and prevents your deer from rolling on you. It also creates more space to work while removing internal organs. I butcher my own deer and this does not sacrifice any of the meat on the hindquarters when done correctly.

Cut the muscle between the two back legs to expose the center of the pelvic bone. Find what looks like dead center on the meat between the two back legs and cut down (usually a few inches) from the top of the pelvis to the anus. Stay as close to the center as possible to avoid gouging the roasts on either leg. Don’t saw the muscle. Slice it instead, letting the downward pressure of your blade do the cutting.

Insert your knife tip into the side (not the center) of the anus. Keeping your blade pressed against the bone that encircles the rectum, cut around the rectum rather than through it. The goal is to cut the connective tissue so you can pull the tube of intestines out rather than dice it up.

This abdominal cut is often the most difficult for hunters, and the key here is not to puncture the deer’s stomach or bladder because you don’t want to get any bile or urine on the meat.

Prevent stabbing the guts by turning your knife blade up (toward the sky) and tilting it so the blade is more parallel to the deer’s belly rather than perpendicular. Working close to the base of the belly, grab a handful of hide and pull it up to create some space between the layer of hide and the organs beneath. Insert the tip of your knife and make an incision until you see (or more likely, feel with the knife tip) empty space below it. Keep the incision shallow and make the slit long enough to work a finger or two of your off-hand in the space. Take care to not insert the blade too far into the abdominal cavity.

Now that you’ve made an opening incision, apply even upward pressure with your knife blade to “unzip” the abdomen, or make a lengthwise cut along the deer from pelvis to breastbone. This is similar to using a pair of scissors to slice a piece of wrapping paper in a single, fluid motion. Don’t saw with your knife.

The organs you’re ultimately trying to remove lie in two groups: the guts (liver, stomach, intestines, bladder, kidneys, fat if present, etc.) and the vitals (heart and lungs). These two groups are separated by the diaphragm: a thin wall of purple muscle between the abdominal cavity and the rib cage.

Note: If you plan to shoulder mount your deer, do not split the ribs. You should only make your cut to the base of the lower ribcage (above) and stop there, since your taxidermist will need all that hide from the ribs to the tip of the nose (this is called the cape).

If you are planning on a skull mount or you aren’t mounting your deer at all, you can split the ribs if you want. Your blade will encounter some resistance once you hit the rib cage. If you center your knife, you can slice through cartilage in the breastplate before hitting bone. Some hunters use a hatchet or saw to split the rib cage open, but a stout fixed-blade knife will also work. Splitting the rib cage makes it easier to see (and therefore remove) the heart and lungs, but isn’t necessary if you are having trouble cutting through it. This step is especially useful if you suspect a broadhead is lodged in the rib cage.

Personally, I just carry a slim field-dressing knife when I hunt and skip this step altogether during rifle season. I don’t mind reaching into the rib cage to remove the lungs, heart, and windpipe by feel.

To access the heart and lungs in the rib cage (and ultimately free everything) you need to cut the diaphragm. Use the tip of your knife to puncture this thin layer of muscle, then circle the entire rib cage, keeping your knife close to the ribs. Once the diaphragm has been cut away, blood and jellied bits of lung usually slosh into the abdominal cavity. This is perfectly normal (and a sign of a good shot).

Work from the top of deer down toward the pelvis. If you split open the rib cage this part will be easier; if not, you’ll have to do it more by feel.

At the top of the chest cavity, you’ll see or feel a large ribbed tube. That’s the windpipe. Cut it crossways (perpendicular to the spine), then use a finger or two to grab ahold of it from the inside and begin pulling it up and away. This will begin to loosen the heart and lungs.

Grab hold of the heart and/or lungs with your off-hand and pull while continuing to cut connective tissue along the spine. Keep going all the way down to the pelvis and keep working until the stomach and guts come loose, too. Because all the organs are attached to the deer along the spine, it can be helpful to tilt the deer on its side for this part so the organs roll out of your way and reveal their connection point.

As everything loosens, just roll the guts and intestines out of the deer and onto the ground. Note: If you haven’t yet separated the rectum from the anus, the guts will still connect to the carcass by a single tube — that’s the lower large intestines, or colon. To free the guts and toss aside, slice the colon crossways just above the pelvis and tie it off (if it’s full) so pellets don’t spill inside your deer.

Read Next: How to Skin a Deer, Step by Step

To field dress big game with a hatchet, use it as you would a big belt knife, opening the paunch with a small incision at the base of the sternum. Then, tip the blade at right angles to the animal, with the handle up and your fingers spreading the skin close to the blade as you run it to the rectum. Do not try to cut the skin down into the animal; hair will collect on and dull the blade. Dump the entrails.

To quarter the carcass, hang it or set it belly-up on the ground. Loosen hams with careful strokes tight against the pelvis and through the ball joints. Don’t chop; use the blade like a knife, your fist around the hatchet head (inset). Remove the shoulders the same way, leaving the skin on unless you must remove it to let a big animal, like an elk or moose, cool in warm weather. The hatchet (or, better yet, a slim double-bit ax) excels at splitting the backbone. Hang the animal head down, rear legs spread, to facilitate this task. —Wayne Van Zwoll

It’s always best to gut your deer as soon as possible, but the window you have depends on the weather and the shot you made. If the weather is hot or even mild, the sooner you field dress your deer, the better. Within an hour of the shot is ideal in these conditions. If it’s cold, a deer can last longer before it needs to be gutted — hours or even overnight if you have to back out while blood trailing. It’s always easier to dress a deer when it’s warm and pliable.

The best knives for field dressing are usually a fixed-blade knife with a sharp blade. A smaller, handier blade makes certain tasks easier, like removing the colon and avoiding puncturing the guts. A larger, stouter blade is easier for heavy-duty tasks like splitting the ribs.

Field-dressing a deer isn’t difficult once you get the hang of it, and it’s usually easier with a buddy to help hold a leg or a light. Use a sharp knife, make slow, deliberate cuts at connective tissue. Do your best to avoid puncturing the stomach or bladder, but don’t panic if you do. More important is to avoid cutting yourself. The process may be messy or unpleasant, but ultimately you’ll end up with a cooling carcass ready for the skinning shed or processor.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8378. Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

“This is absolute madness,” said a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England. In a scene that couldn’t be more different from the past 28 years that he has spent walking around the world, Bushby stood underneath a giant Welcome Home Karl sign, made an appreciative speech, then begged off to continue walking the final few steps to his mother’s house, which he left back in 1998.

The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.

When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different. Bushby was 29 years old. He is now 57. When he began, he had around $500 in his pocket, a two-wheeled cart loaded with supplies, and an idea that most people would have dismissed as a fantasy. He was going to walk home to Hull, England, without using any transport. He would not return to the UK until he could do so on foot. He expected the expedition to take about 12 years. Instead, it has taken 28.

Bushby has spent more than 10,000 days and 50,000km pursuing that single objective. The Goliath Expedition has become one of the longest and most unusual human-powered adventures in modern exploration, and he is nervous about it ending. Speaking to The Washington Post as he approached home, he said: “My purpose and reason for living is about to end. It’s going to be difficult…trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”

Through Chile’s Atacama Desert. Photo: Karl Bushby

While serving with the Parachute Regiment, Bushby received a birthday card from his father, Keith, who had served in the British Army. In it was a story about special forces soldiers debating whether it was possible to walk from London to New York via the Bering Strait. Looking at a world map, Bushby began tracing the route himself.

But rather than stopping at New York, he extended the line south through the Americas, all the way to the tip of Chile. The result was an expedition that would take him from the southernmost reaches of South America back to his home in England.

“That was the moment the hairs on the back of your neck stand up,” he told GQ Magazine. “You think, well, that’s it.” He did some calculations, created a timeline on the “back of a beer mat,” and estimated the journey would take him 12 years. From that point, Bushby showed nothing but determination. At the start, most people doubted it was even possible. That only made him more certain that he wanted to try.

He gave himself two rules. The first was that he could not use any transportation, even self-propelled vehicles like bicycles or kayaks, to advance the expedition. The second was that he could not return to the UK until he had completed the walk. Those rules sound simple. In practice, they created multiple logistical nightmares and affected almost every aspect of his life.

Bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, with his equipment loaded onto a cart he calls The Beast. He was not an elite endurance athlete embarking on a carefully funded and organized expedition. He was a young former paratrooper with a few hundred dollars, a rough line on a map, and limited resources. He had no supporters or funding, and relied on gas station food or what locals gave him.

“The first years, you’re living the boys’ adventure dream, and it’s great,” he told The New York Times, “and then it really becomes a grind.”

The first few years took him north through the Americas, including multiple conflict zones. In Peru, he was attacked by a mob; in Colombia, he floated down the crocodile-laden Atrato River to avoid being spotted by armed men. Then he faced the Darien Gap, that infamously dangerous stretch between Colombia and Panama, ruled by drug and human smugglers, that almost all adventurers skirt around.

Eventually, he reached Panama. But emerging from the jungle did not mean he was free to continue. After crossing a restricted border zone without the necessary visa, he was detained for 18 days.

After making his way through the Americas, Bushby eventually finished crossing the U.S., where he had picked up a few sponsorships, and reached Alaska. The next major obstacle, and the one that catapulted his journey into world news, was the Bering Strait, the stretch of water separating North America from Russia.

The Arctic had already given Bushby a taste of its dangers. During the Alaskan stage of the expedition, he was rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on an ice floe that broke away from the coast and drifted out to sea, and had a standoff with a polar bear. He knew how risky the Bering Strait crossing would be.

In March 2006, Bushby and French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer spent 14 days crossing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia on foot. With 90kg sleds, they traveled across the shifting ice in temperatures that fell to around -30˚C, against the prevailing winds as the ice moved beneath them.

Wearing dry suits, they had to swim at points through the icy, slushy water. “All night long, you’re just listening to the grinding, and the ice is just like screaming,” he told The New York Times. “We actually had to evacuate the tent during the night because the thing started to break apart beneath us.”

They made it across, achieving a rare crossing of one of the world’s most formidable natural barriers. But reaching Russia did not mean the difficulties were over. Russian authorities detained the pair for entering the country without the required permission. They faced the possibility of deportation.

Crossing the Bering Strait. Photo: Karl Bushby

Russia would consume years of Bushby’s life. He had to leave the country every 90 days because his tourist visa allowed him to stay in Russia for only 90 of every 180 days. Then in 2008, his journey came to a standstill. He lost sponsorship and could not travel to Russia for a few years. In 2011, he resumed his trek, again in 90-day stints. Then in 2012, he was denied a further visa, and in 2013, he received a five-year entry ban from Russia.

Here, Bushby responded with an extraordinary protest. He walked approximately 5,000km from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., hoping to draw attention to his predicament and secure the paperwork he needed to continue.

The years of delay exposed another unusual aspect of the expedition. Bushby’s rules did not mean he had to remain indefinitely in the country where he was stuck. Nor did they prevent him from using transport for journeys unrelated to advancing his route home. However, he couldn’t fly back to the UK during these hiatuses.

When visas, funding, or political restrictions prevented him from continuing, he could fly elsewhere, take a break, and wait until circumstances allowed him to resume. But he could not use that flight to skip a section of the route. Whenever he returned, he had to pick up from the exact point where he had stopped. Most of the time, he decamped to Mexico. Its lower cost of living made it a practical place to wait. He also spent time in the United States.

Bushby and Dimitri Kieffer, 2006. Photo: Karl Bushby

The distinction mattered enormously to the expedition. Bushby could board a plane to escape a logistical dead end, but when he returned to the route, he had to pick up where he had stopped. He could not simply fly over the awkward section and resume walking on the other side.

The arrangement might seem to stretch the definition of walking around the world. But for Bushby, it was the only way to maintain his two original rules without spending years of his life waiting at a closed border. Some visa delays took years to resolve. And the longer the journey continued, the harder it became to predict when, or even whether, it would end. Getting across Russia alone took almost 10 years.

He lived cheaply but still needed money to survive on this near-endless journey. Some of it came from the sponsorships he eventually acquired. During what sounded like a particularly low point 15 years ago, on one of his hiatuses in Mexico while trying to overcome another logistical hurdle on his journey, he told Backpacker magazine:

I’m 42 years old and I’m broke and I’m homeless. I’m a professional parasite. I’m a professional hobo. I’m sleeping on other people’s couches. I’m 42 years old, and I have to walk other people’s dogs, just so they’ll feed me. My job is picking up dog shit!

The passage of time is one of the most striking aspects of Bushby’s story. His expedition began in an era before smartphones, Instagram, and the expectation of sharing every stage of an adventure online. The young man who left Chile in 1998 could never have imagined that nearly three decades later, people around the world would be following his progress toward his childhood home. The fact that so many people are following it still baffles Bushby.

While Bushby was away, life continued for the people he had left behind. His son, Adam, grew up, and his family had to get on with their lives without him. Adam was eight when he set off. He is now 36, with a family of his own, including a 12-year-old daughter whom Bushby has never met.

When his dad started the walk, Adam didn’t fully understand what was going on, or know how to explain it to people who asked. Over the years, they have tried to stay in touch and maintain some kind of relationship. At 14, Adam flew to Alaska to see his dad. It was six years after the expedition began and a turning point for him in accepting what Bushby was doing. “I did feel a bit awkward because at that point I didn’t really know my dad,” he told GQ Magazine.

They later spent 10 days walking together as part of a National Geographic documentary project. Adam described the experience as surreal, suddenly stepping into his father’s world. They have spoken regularly since, but as Adam put it: “[His] life went this way, and I went that way, two separate routes.”

In various interviews, Adam has explained that he had nothing against his father’s ambition, that he respects what he has done and is very proud of him. But also that growing up without him had been difficult.

Karl Bushby has not seen other members of his family for years. He met Adam when he stepped out of the water after crossing the English Channel back to England, but he has not seen his mother in over a decade, even though he will be living with her once he arrives back at his childhood home. He recognizes how difficult the situation will be and that it is due to his choices over the last 30 years.

“The relationship between me and my son is good, but there’s a lot to resolve there,” he told GQ Magazine. “I’ve got a granddaughter I’ve never seen, and then dear old mother, Lord. I have to live with my mother now. I’m going from a global adventure to living with my mother in a basement at 57. This is going to be a challenge.”

Life on the road has often been lonely, but Bushby has seen kindness and hospitality in every corner of the globe. “I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he told The Washington Post. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country, has been the same response.”

He has also had two significant romantic relationships during the expedition. He spent around seven years with a Colombian woman. Later, he had a three-year relationship with a woman from Japan. He met both while on the expedition, and it was also the reason both broke down.

After finally getting across Russia, Bushby continued through Mongolia, where he joined with other adventurers, including Angela Maxwell, to trek across the Gobi Desert with camels. After 1,130km and several disagreements, the group went their separate ways, and Busby continued into China by himself. In 2018, he crossed Kazakhstan and then made his way through Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Once again, visa issues ground the journey to a standstill. He could not get into Iran.

At the same time, the world was struck down by the pandemic. More years of waiting in Mexico began, even though Bushby still had a substantial distance to cover. Eventually, in 2022, he was on the move again. Once again joined by Angela Maxwell, he did something he had never intended doing during the expedition — swimming across the Caspian Sea.

Visa issues and geopolitics meant he was unable to cross into Iran. So he came up with a new plan. He and Maxwell went back to Uzbekistan and took a different route. They walked across the Kyzylkum Desert until they reached the Caspian Sea. A self-proclaimed terrible swimmer, he was completely outside of his comfort zone. Wearing a wetsuit and flotation equipment, he described his floating-and-swimming hybrid as floatimming. It might not have been the most elegant crossing, but after 32 days at sea, 27 of which he was swimming with Maxwell and two Azerbaijani swimmers in very choppy waters, he completed the 288km swim.

Back on solid ground, his next job was to get across Azerbaijan and into Turkey. Here, he hit a huge milestone. He crossed the Bosphorus Bridge on May 2, 2025. This meant he was back in Europe for the first time since he started walking.

The remaining distance to Britain was comparatively short, but the final stages were not straightforward. Once again, visa restrictions were the thorn in his side. Limited to traveling for 90 days at a time before having to leave Europe, he continued to use Mexico as a base as he waited for his 90 days to reset and tackled the remaining distance in short stretches.

He made it through Turkey, Bulgaria, and Romania before confronting the next issue. Bushby always knew one of the logistical challenges would be getting from France to England. He started trying to pull a plan together. Unsurprisingly, for someone who has walked across the world, his goal was to cross it via the Channel Tunnel. The issue was that this was forbidden. He had hoped to use their service tunnel, but his request was denied.

Karl Bushby speaks at a civic ceremony in Hull, England earlier today. Photo: YouTube

As he continued walking through Hungary and Austria, he attempted to appeal the decision, reaching out to anyone who might help, to no avail. “We have carefully considered his request and explored a range of possible options. In this instance, regretfully, we are unable to accommodate Mr Bushby’s wishes,” a spokesperson for the Eurotunnel told the BBC. This meant the only alternative was to get back into the water and swim the Channel.

Still walking, he had made it to Germany. Then he picked his way across Belgium and France, all the while decamping to Mexico, Canada, or the U.S. every 90 days, and trying to piece together a plan for swimming the Channel. This proved to be another headache regarding permissions.

French rules stop anyone swimming the Channel from France to Britain. He thought he had been granted an exemption, but in September, he learned that was not the case. After much negotiation, he finally got the go-ahead. On October 5, Bushby finally landed back on British soil at Shakespeare Beach near Dover after swimming the English Channel.

The crossing took three days. He spent around 20 hours in the water, spent the nights on a safety vessel, and dropped back into the water at his last-known position each morning.

After 28 years abroad, he was finally back in the country he had left in 1998. But rather than feeling joy, he told The New York Times he felt a real sense of loss. After three decades on the road, the prospect of just 400km to go was hugely daunting. “I’m about to lose my purpose for living,” he said. “It’s about to abruptly end.”

He is nervous about what comes next and reintegrating into a society he no longer knows. He is considering retraining as a teacher, as he loved giving talks in schools as he walked.

One big question is why Bushby has become so celebrated. He is not the first person to have attempted a long-distance walk around the world. Other adventurers have spent years traveling between countries, crossing continents on foot, or undertaking journeys without motorized transport, but Bushby has singularly captured the world’s attention.

Karl Bushby, back turned, leaves the civic ceremony to walk the last few steps to his mother’s house. Photo: YouTube

It might be the particular combination of his rules, or the fact that his objective is immediately understandable. He left home, and he is walking back. There is no complicated scientific mission to explain, no specialized equipment that the public needs to understand, and no obscure record category he is aiming for. The simplicity of it gives the story an almost fable-like quality, even though the journey was not simple at all.

With just two rules, the expedition is relatively easy to follow. Every delay matters because Bushby cannot simply skip ahead. He is forced to wait or find another solution when something blocks his route. The question becomes how he will get around it without abandoning his principles.

Then there is the sheer amount of time it has taken. People who first encountered Bushby’s expedition in their twenties are now well into middle age themselves. Initially, there were no updates on social media. Instead, there was the odd news article that cropped up every few years about the same man, still walking across the world. A story that seemed like an ambitious adventure morphed into an entire adult life on the road.

Bushby has not necessarily made the journey look enjoyable. His progress has depended as much, if not more, on navigating bureaucracy and finding support as on putting one foot in front of the other. Despite it all, he continued.

As the journey has hit an era where we can follow an adventurer’s progress in real time, every obstacle and milestone has renewed interest in the question that has followed Bushby for 28 years: Will he actually make it home?

Now that he has to confront a new question: How do you cope with coming home after three decades? “I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I’m suddenly going to find myself in?” he told the BBC in the days before the expected end of the expedition. “I think the old adage goes…the only thing worse than a man who can’t fulfill his dreams is a man who’s fulfilled his dreams…because then what?”

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8376. ‘Squirrels as Big as House Cats.’ We Competed in the Greatest Squirrel Dog Contest in the Country

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

“Neighbor down the road had a squirrel dog,” said Larry White as he led a cast of dogs and hunters to the woods. “Got its legs cut off by a mowing machine. Had to hunt that dog from a wheelbarrow.

“One day a friend asked to borrow the dog, so the owner explained that you had to push the wheelbarrow in whatever direction the dog pointed his nose. If he barked, the track was hot, so you pushed faster. When he looked up and barked, he had the squirrel treed and you got a shot. The friend came back late that night with no squirrels. His clothes were torn to shreds and his skin was scratched up and looked like a road map. ‘What in the world happened to you?’ the hound’s owner asked.

“‘What’s it look like?’ the friend snapped. ‘Your fool squirrel dog hit a deer and we ran that thing all day long!'”

Larry White was judging a cast in the 1981 World Champion Squirrel Hunt. His tale got a laugh, but it also emphasized the importance of handler/dog teamwork in any form of hunting.

A good squirrel dog works for the hunter by locating squirrels through scent on the ground and on trees as well as by seeing and following bushytails moving through the treetops. The dog’s manner of barking signals its degree of progress to the hunter. A good hunter works for the dog by staying keenly and constantly aware of what the barking means and by following almost within sight so he can get to the tree quickly and shoot the squirrel before it escapes.

Good competition squirrel dogs are more decisive, accurate and consistent than average squirrel dogs. They do the job with less wasted time and motion.

Squirrel-treeing talent always has been wherever you found it, but these days some unusual dogs are showing up in the woods. Chuck Trehern’s purebred Doberman pinscher learned to bark up a tree by watching the family coonhounds. Ronnie Liles’ 6-year-old Australian shepherd, Smokey, was never taught: he just started treeing squirrels. T.C. Jones won the 1980 Championship with a registered liver and white English pointer! Trophies similar to bowling trophies are awarded. The statuettes portray a dog barking treed.

Most squirrel dogs are not pedigreed, however. Two Illinois dogs were described as terrier and feist crosses. Randy Pannell, who trains 15 to 20 squirrel dogs every year, came over from Blue Springs, Mississippi, with a redtick coonhound/mountain cur cross. Fola Hart brought a Norwegian elkhound/feist cross from Virginia. And the 1981 winner was Orville Hart’s “Whiskey,” a 4-year-old Norwegian elkhound/feist from Leesburg, Ohio.

Feists, those wiry little mongrels that are intelligent enough to learn any job on the farm, are becoming rare because most people prefer to keep purebred dogs. As a result, many squirrel hunters are making their own mongrels by crossing two different purebreds. There’s a constant search for the best dog, and that’s one reason why Dick Sheets thought up the World Champion Squirrel Hunt.

Sheets reasoned that squirrel-dog competition would not only preserve and enlarge the sport, but that the dogs would improve through breeding. Perhaps breeds of purebred squirrel dogs of consistent ability would emerge from such an effort. The Yockanookany Coon Hunters Association of Ethel, Mississippi, agreed with Sheets and sponsored the first championship in 1980.

Yockanookany is Choctaw for “crawls on belly like snake” and also applies to the way hunters must cross a spongy swamp. The 100-mile-long Yockanookany Swamp is just two miles from the club grounds.

By 1981, competition had already influenced squirrel-dog breeding. L.E. Goutierez came over from Louisiana with two pups out of the 1980 second-place winner. The pups’ dam was Spot, his own small Chihuahua/feist cross.

Goutierez arrived a day early, pitched his tent and drove his dogs down the old Natchez Trace to the nearby woods where they could become accustomed to hunting new territory. The original Natchez Trace, which was once an extensive trading trail between the Indian tribes, runs right past the Yockanookany club grounds. The entire area is well forested with both hill-country and creek-bottom squirrel habitat.

Little Spot ran through the woods with her nose slightly down, searching for scent on the ground, on logs and on fallen limbs. Every tree got a sniff as she trotted past. But the squirrels weren’t moving. When Spot finally barked, L.E. didn’t become excited. “She scatter-barked,” he said. “It’s a cold track.”

Scatter barking is barking here and there instead of barking enthusiastically in one place such as on a hot trail or at a tree.

By the end of the championship hunt, Goutierez had learned one more thing about breeding squirrel dogs. “Have to get more size in my dogs,” he said. “My dogs can’t compete with the longer-legged, wider-running dogs.”

Four dogs were cast together in the first running of the championship in 1980 and many handlers thought that that was three too many. By nature, squirrel dogs do best alone. They’re highly intelligent, very independent and more than a little jealous of their relationships with their human partners. In 1981, a compromise was struck: only two dogs to a cast—male and female, if possible—and in weight categories of under and over 35 pounds.

The only reported fight occurred when the Doberman’s handler decided to be gentlemanly and let his competitor’s dog smell the dead squirrel, too. Getting to smell the squirrel is an encouraging reward of sorts and the Dobe was not ready to share that with another dog.

An impartial judge accompanies each cast, but it is up to the handler to “call” his own dog—that is, notify the judge when satisfied his dog has treed. As in coonhound competition, 100 points are earned by the first dog at the tree, 75 by the second. Unlike coonhound scoring, no points are awarded for striking (finding) a trail. This is because sometimes the trail is short, sometimes there is none and too many squirrel dogs are silent trailers. Also unlike coonhound scoring, tree points are not subtracted if no squirrel is found in the tree because squirrels all too readily travel from tree to tree.

If the squirrel is not found, the tree points are circled and do not count on the final score. Judges are allowed considerable latitude, however. If the squirrel is seen several trees away from the one the dog is treeing on and the judge is satisfied that the squirrel could have gotten there through the treetops, he can give the dog credit for that squirrel.

Six or eight squirrels an hour is not impossible in well-populated timber when the bushytails are really active. Ronnie Liles’ Australian shepherd treed 700 for him and his friends during the past two years. “The trick,” said Liles, “is to catch ’em stirrin’. You might not see a squirrel today. But you can come back through the same place tomorrow and see 10.”

Ronnie believes that the old hunters’ barometer, “If the cows are lying down, so are the deer,” also applies to squirrels. And as he says, the dogs are helpless if they can’t see, smell or possibly hear the bushytails. The squirrel that hasn’t been on the ground and is lounging on a limb or in a vine tangle probably won’t be discovered by a dog unless falling air currents allow the dog to “wind” it. This would happen mostly during the cool of late afternoon rather than during early morning when the warming sunlight causes air to rise.

Liles prefers hunting little cat squirrels (grays) in the big, swampy, bottom timbers. Shaking a vine spooks grays out of hiding faster and easier than it does fox squirrels. Other hunters choose the hills where more fox squirrels live because they don’t like the way grays often chase off through the treetops when a dog barks.

Randy Pannell minimizes that problem by staying fairly close to his dog and then getting to the tree fast. In competition, however, that’s not always possible. The second dog has five minutes in which to join the first dog at the tree. During that time, handlers and the judge stay clear.

Both Pannell and Fola Hart demonstrated the wisdom of walking apart from other hunters. At 79, Fola appeared to be walking far behind because of age. But he was the first to hear his dog bark treed while other members of the cast were busy talking.

The perceptive rapport between hunter and squirrel dog is nothing less than amazing. During a Friday afternoon cast, Orville Hart was reluctant to say that Whiskey had treed. “Them two dogs are looking at us,” he observed. “If they believed they had the squirrel, they’d be looking up the tree!”

When a squirrel was shot in Ronnie Liles’ cast, Smokey grabbed it and ran off with the second dog in hot pursuit. As Smokey raced past his master’s leg, Ronnie grinned. “That dog expects me to catch the other dog as it goes by. Then Smokey will bring me the squirrel. He won’t let the other dog have it. But if another dog gets to the squirrel first, Smokey won’t bother it.” Retrieving is an added nicety, but it isn’t rewarded with extra points during the Yockanookany competition.

Some dogs won’t bark if their masters happen to be present when the squirrel is treed, strongly suggesting that they have enough reasoning power to recognize that, in such a case, the boss doesn’t have to be called.

Read Next: The Ultimate Guide to Buying and Training a Squirrel Dog

One Mississippi hunter recalled a boyhood dog that would always dance around the opposite side of the tree, yanking and shaking every vine or sapling it could find. Invariably, this commotion chased the squirrel around to the gunner’s side. Since such a dog is quite rare, hunters often go in pairs, taking turns circling the tree and shaking the bushes after the dog has treed.

What’s it take to train a dog that shows interest in squirrels? Mostly, lots of time in the squirrel woods. But trainer Randy Pannell speeds things up with a slingshot and steel pellets. “Just hit the tree near the squirrel, and it will bail out or take off,” Pannell said. “The dog gets a sight chase through the treetops or maybe a short ground chase. This works best with gray squirrels, especially the young ones. And there’s no problem with game laws while training dogs because you’re not killing or hunting the squirrels.”

Never study treetops when the dog is in sight and isn’t treeing. A perceptive dog believes you see the squirrel and will start treeing. And never bring the dog running by shooting at something other than a squirrel. Fooling a squirrel dog ruins it fast.

The Yockanookany fox squirrels are flat out the most colorful in America. Some are rusty orange, as expected, but others are decorated with white noses, feet and tail tips and, occasionally, black scalps. Others are solid black. Two taken during the 1981 Championship were black with white tips. Southern grays are smaller than Northern grays, but the fox squirrels are bigger. Some, according to reliable reports, grow half again as big as their Northern counterparts and range—according to very unreliable exaggerations—up to the size of house cats, groundhogs and raccoons.

Yankee squirrel hunters are treated so many different ways during the Yockanookany event that they have to like some. They travel from as far away as Michigan to enter the event. “We welcome Yankees; it’s only the Damn Yanks we don’t like,” said one young Southern belle with a wink.

#8373. Everest and Ama Dablam Climbs Resume Despite Cyclone

The second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less. As the sun returned this afternoon, fresh snow hampered smaller teams on 6,000m and 7,000m peaks, but the highly supported expeditions on Ama Dablam are proceeding with barely a hitch.

No cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long. Leader Andrei Vasiliev told us yesterday from Kathmandu that he, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will return to the mountain in one or two days. The trio is well aware of the challenge they face on Everest’s West Ridge, completely alone and without oxygen.

The climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev mentioned he is under some pressure due to unidentified “unsolved matters” but still determined to tackle the climb. In his own words:

We know what needs to be done; the path is clear, and we must attempt to follow it. We’ve fallen ill. A massive amount of snow has fallen. You adapt quickly to new conditions. Once we’re back in the snow, the cold, and the cramped tent, it will feel as though things were never any other way.

The new snow dump has thwarted some teams attempting Baruntse (7,129m) in the Khumbu. Jan McManus of Ireland was among them, and he has called off his expedition after failing to reach Camp 1 due to deep snow:

It is unclear whether other climbers on the peak may still be trying. There were six large teams totaling 65 foreign climbers with permits for Baruntse.

On Himlung (7,126m), teams hurried to summit and get down and safely away before the cyclone hit. During the previous snowstorm at the end of September, a massive avalanche buried Base Camp, killing 16 staff members. Despite the tragedy, one of the deadliest in Nepal’s mountaineering history, the peak remained open, and guided teams came in large numbers to the mountain a couple of weeks after the accident. A total of 130 foreigners had permits. Teams summited on October 25 and 26, and then left the area.

Ama Dablam Base Camp is also covered in snow, but the commercial teams will nevertheless resume climbing soon. According to Jana Schneider of Germany, climbing with 14 Peaks Expeditions, a Sherpa team is on its way to reopen those sections where fresh snow has buried the ropes. “If all goes well, my summit push begins Nov 4 until Nov 6,” she wrote.

So far, 410 foreigners have applied for a permit to climb Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team first fixed the route on October 17, and dozens have summited since then. Despite the break forced by bad weather over the weekend, summits should continue throughout November.

One climber has perished on the mountain so far, and there have been some close calls. Paul Clarke of Australia and Xenia Santha of Hungary climbed Ama Dablam after attempting Dhaulagiri earlier this season. Their summit push was delayed as they found a 25-year-old climber in a serious situation at Camp 2. Santha and Clarke, who climbed without Sherpa support, gave the climber dexamethasone, spent the night with him, and helped organize an emergency airlift for the following morning. They continued to the summit one day later.

A high camp on Ama Dablam. Photo: Xenia Shanta

#8372. The Secret Shelter

After a grueling ascent, I reach the formidable summit of New Jersey, battling thin mountain air at a staggering 1,803 feet above sea level. I check out a location known as the Secret Shelter.

Don’t get too excited, I couldn’t get my lazy bones out of bed before sunrise, so there will be no pictures of a sunrise from Sunrise Mountain. There would also have been the small matter of the 5.3 miles I’d need to hike to capture such a photo. I’ll take my beauty rest, thank you very much.

The plan for the day is to hike north to Carnegie Road, turn around a find a place to camp. I say “find a place” intentionally because there is some question about the openness of the nearby “Secret Shelter” to hikers. More on that later. Also on tap is a short side quest to the New Jersey High Point, which you may recall has a large memorial tower marking the site.

Getting underway just before 8:00AM, the trail makes its way up Sunrise Mountain, a long, tree-lined ridge with occasional views West and East. Along the way the trail passes by the Culver Fire Tower, which is currently in use and not accessible for hikers. The best views of the morning were indeed right at the summit of Sunrise Mountain, which features an open pavilion positioned perfectly for watching sunrises. Oddly the nearby parking area doesn’t open until 8:00AM, more than half an hour after the latest sunrise of the year (tomorrow!).

Early morning view from Sunrise Mountain.

Early morning view from Sunrise Mountain.

Continuing north, the trail remained decidedly wonderful. After days of twisting my ankle on leafy rocks, the flat ride was just what I needed. I crossed the Deckertown Turnpike, captured a few more photos from the ridge, before reaching the High Point State Park HQ. The park office has a handy water bottle refilling station, restrooms, a gift shop, and rangers available for questions. I felt this was a good time to sit at the picnic table and scarf down my trail snack before the next stop, the New Jersey High Point. There was a high wind advisory for the area, and it was showing. I had to keep close tabs on my various bags to ensure they didn’t blow away which I chomped on my peanuts and sunflower seeds.

Preceding the observation tower is an observation deck provided a great view of the towering obelisk. I clambered down briefly before turning off the AT and up the steep trail to the tower. I was beat by the time I reached the monument, which had been built in 1930 as a war memorial/observation tower. It is possible to go inside the tower and up to the top. You simply need to open the front door and climb 291 stairs. After trekking up the steep trail to the tower I simply couldn’t wait to take on those steps. The information I had said the tower was open until 3:30PM, but when I reached the metal door it was latched and locked closed. I was positively dismayed, as you can see from the picture I took to capture my strong emotional reaction to such a brutal letdown.

The wind at the tower was incredible, I hadn’t felt this much wind since I was in the Whites. I tried to escape the wind by finding a safe side of the tower, but the wind was strong on all 4 sides, how does that work? I decided the best idea was get off the top of the mountain and continue my journey for the day.

View from the ridge near Sunrise Mountain.

View from the ridge near Sunrise Mountain.

The New Jersey High Point memorial tower.

View from the observation platform near the New Jersey High Point memorial tower.

View from the base of the New Jersey High Point memorial tower.

View from the base of the New Jersey High Point memorial tower.

View from the base of the New Jersey High Point memorial tower.

Awwwwww I don’t get to climb 291 stairs, shucks!

The New Jersey High Point memorial tower.

Once I was safely out of the wind I descended from the ridge that I’d spent all day on to hike in a valley for the rest of the day. The AT tracks northeast close to the Pennsylvania/New Jersey before turning to the southeast to follow, quite precisely, the New Jersey/New York border. The trail was mostly flat and passed through a few pastures. Just before the turn for the Secret Shelter, the trail passes over a ridge with a view of the high point tower. After a marshy area and several local roads stemming from the town of Unionville, New York, I reached Carnegie Road and turned south to retrace my steps.

This time around I would turn off the trail at a dirt driveway to scope out the Secret Shelter. The shelter was erected by James Macklin Murray, an avid hiker who completed the Appalachian Trail in 1989. After his hike, decided to give back to the trail community by building the shelter on his property. Rather than follow the model of traditional AT shelters, which are quite rustic, he hooked up electricity and running water. Sadly, Jim Murray, aka Backpack Jim, passed away on November 5th, 2025. The property is in jeopardy, but efforts are underway for the Trust for Public Land to acquire the property thereby allowing the shelter to continue operating. A commenter on FarOut, posting 2 days earlier, noted that there was currently a chain on a gate with a keep out sign at the entrance to the property. I was considering staying at the shelter, but obviously wanted to see for myself if it was still open first.

I turned down the driveway toward the shelter, keeping a sharp eye out for any deterring signage or chains, but saw none. The same path that hikers had taken for decades was still there leading to the grouping of buildings. I walked up to the building and found it unlocked with the trail logbook as well as several maps of the area still up on the walls. Even the hiker box had a few useful items. It certainly seemed to be operating as normal to me. I skimmed the log book and recognized plenty of trail names – Squirrel, Wit, Lancelot, 2Bears, and Quilt.

I knew it would be getting cold tonight and I was feeling increasingly swayed to stay at the shelter. I figured it would be warmer than my tent, and probably make it easier to get going in the morning. In the end I decided I’d rather be closer to my van and returned to the trail to hike south a little further.

View of the memorial tower from down in the Hudson Valley.

A view of the memorial tower from near the Secret Shelter.

On my way back to the trail another hiker was making his way toward the shelter. He goes by Rebar, and knew about my hike from fellow southbounder, Pebbles. I shared my findings on the shelter, including the fact that he would have it all to himself if he chose to stay there. We parted ways and I set a course for some streams I had passed on my initial trek northbound. I wanted to get as far south as I could manage in the fading light (and fading muscles). Conveniently, the furthest stream was reachable in that time and also had the most flat area for tenting. Despite some not so clean water flowing nearby, this stream was clear when I passed it earlier. Inconveniently, the water had completely changed. Something had dumped quite a lot of extra water in the time since I passed by. The water was a translucent gray, which sometimes results from farm runoff, or could be actual clay in the water. I decided not to risk and turned around to hike a few tenths of a mile north, I was pretty sure that water still looked good. It did, and I found a fine spot to pitch my tent for the night. By the time the day began getting dark I was climbing into my tent to rest up for the next day.

Would you drink water that looks like this? :p

#8370. 6.5 Creedmoor Vs. .300 Win Mag: Here’s the Truth About Cartridge Selection

Published Oct 30, 2026 1:09 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

One of the most common arguments we hear in favor of choosing larger cartridges for hunting big game is that a magnum cartridge will offer margin for error. When considering cartridges like 6.5 Creedmoor vs. .300 Win. Mag., the .300 has more energy, drives a bigger bullet faster, and, we assume, will do more damage than the 6.5. That means that if we don’t hit exactly where we are aiming, we are more likely to still kill the animal cleanly by choosing the magnum. At face value, the logic is sound. But how does it hold up when we start examining what the bullets actually do downrange? You might be surprised.

There are two schools of thought that commonly divide hunters when it comes to choosing cartridges. One opts for milder cartridges that have lower recoil and are generally easier and more pleasant to shoot well. The other wants the extra power to cover their bases. Everyone, of course, falls somewhere on a spectrum, and the categories aren’t mutually exclusive.

I’ve written a lot about why I think smaller cartridges are often the right choice for big game, and it generally boils down to two observations. First, with thoughtful bullet selection, I haven’t noticed a dramatic difference between the wound characteristics of smaller and larger cartridges — and the smaller rounds have produced consistently satisfactory results. Second, milder cartridges are more pleasant to shoot and, despite having no real limitations on the cartridges I have access to, that’s what I reach for consistently. I have the rifles and ammo to torch a hundred rounds of .300 PRC in a range session practicing positional shooting but, realistically, I’m going to pick a 6.5 Creedmoor, 6 Creed, or 22 ARC to do that. Practice with smaller cartridges can also benefit how you’ll shoot magnums, but there’s a lot of value in hunting with the cartridge that you train with.

You’ll commonly hear hunters argue that you should choose the largest cartridge that you can handle without flinching — especially for larger game. Lots of hunters consider this basic conventional wisdom, and it’s rooted in the belief that a larger cartridge, bullet, or more kinetic energy will result in a larger wound and will kill the animal more quickly. This makes up for some degree of shooting error, or will allow more forgiveness on less-than-ideal shot angles. Essentially, choosing a more powerful cartridge is viewed as cheap insurance.

There are many ways that bigger cartridges like the .300 Win. Mag. outperform smaller ones like the 6.5 Creedmoor. When choosing something for yourself, you need to know what the real benefits are, and decide whether they actually apply to you and your hunting. What does that look like in terms of margin for error? That’s exactly what we took a look at in the video above.

I took a 6.5 Creedmoor and .300 Win. Mag. to the range and fired the same line of factory ammo — Federal Fusion Tipped — from each into identical blocks of Clear Ballistics gel. This gel isn’t a one-to-one representation of flesh, but it is a homogeneous, consistent medium in which we can get a side-by-side comparison of two bullets. The blocks were placed at 200 yards with a Garmin chronograph positioned about 15 yards in front of the target to record impact velocity. The Fusion Tipped bullets were 140 grains and 180 grains for the 6.5 CM and .300 Win. Mag., respectively. The rifles were the same except for different barrel lengths — 18 inches for the 6.5 CM and 22 inches for the .300. Impact velocities were recorded as 2,233 fps and 2,526 fps, with the advantage going to the .300.

As expected, the .300 Win. Mag. load delivered higher velocity and more energy at the target than the 6.5 Creedmoor. The block was knocked off the table and was clearly hit harder with the 180-grain slug than the 140. However, the actual wound cavities were not much different. The expanded diameters of the recovered bullets were within .015 inch when measuring both the extreme diameter of the jacket (which would typically be smashed down flat in an animal) and the diameter of mushroomed bullet bodies. The .30-caliber bullet left a slightly wider overall wound cavity across its traverse, disrupting slightly more tissue, but the wound channels aren’t perfectly cylindrical either. The overall diameter of the wound channels and penetration were nearly identical.

To more closely estimate the difference in wound size, I measured the width and height of each wound channel every half inch from entry to the end of the expanded cavity — both were about 14 inches. Because I’m no longer spun up on my calculus, I plugged the data into Claude AI, and it calculated the estimated volume and generated simulated models. The wound channel cross sections are star shaped, not complete empty space, so this is only an estimate of the volume of gel affected by the permanent wound channel.

This demonstration shouldn’t be taken to mean that the 6.5 CM and .300 Win. Mag. are completely equal. They each have their advantages and disadvantages. The results, however, do track pretty well with other gel testing I’ve done, and what I’ve observed on animals. Those are that, with the same bullet construction, results don’t vary too much across most common hunting cartridges. In fact, things like penetration and wound cavity size can be more greatly influenced by bullet selection than simply picking a bigger or smaller cartridge.

Some hunters place a lot of weight in having a cartridge that “hits harder.” While we can see some of the effects in the movement of the gel blocks during this demonstration, and that delta in impact force could possibly offer increased effect to the central nervous system, it’s not a reliable predictor of how fast an animal will die, or how much room for error you have. What we can rely on is the damage the bullet does.

One of the real advantages of a magnum cartridge, with a thoughtfully chosen bullet, is that it can deliver effective velocities over longer distances. A disadvantage of a 6.5 Creedmoor, in common shorter barrel configurations, is that it will produce lower muzzle velocities and result in a shorter effective velocity window. Ensuring that your impact speeds are high enough to make the bullet work properly is critical.

Our field shooting exercise did demonstrate that you might be able to shoot a magnum just as well as the 6.5. If you can, then you are better poised to take advantage of a magnum’s real benefits. Over time, most people will find that they shoot milder cartridges more consistently. It is most important to choose a cartridge that you can shoot well and will practice with.

Read Next: I Shot the First Elk With the New 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak Ammo. It’s an Undeniable Elk Hunting Cartridge

Along with better equipment and more refined shooting technique, we are constantly learning more about terminal ballistics. Many of our long-held beliefs are simply a product of lore and oversimplified logic. If you’re a successful hunter and your favorite cartridge works well for you, we’re not asking you to change. But if you’re feeling the pressure to choose a cartridge that you don’t think you’ll shoot as well, because you feel that it’s powerful enough to make up the difference, you’re barking up the wrong tree. The smaller cartridges will work just as well on the good shots, and the big ones will do just as poorly on the bad shots.

An Indian passenger died and two more were injured when two helicopters crashed while landing near Everest Base Camp this morning.

The helicopters were operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two of Nepal’s largest companies. The crash occurred at the helipad on the outskirts of the village of Pheriche (4,371m). It’s a typical spot for helicopters to stop and refuel when on their way to and from Everest Base Camp.

As shown in the horrific video below, the two helicopters came from different directions, and both tried to land at the same time. Somehow their rotor blades collided. The inexplicable crash occurred in a wide, flat area with good visibility.

Vasanth Kumar, an Indian trekker, died on the spot, The Tourism Times reported. Shailesh Kishan from New Zealand and Rabindra Prajapati, a senior captain, were seriously injured. Both have been airlifted to hospitals in Kathmandu. They were all on board the Fishtail Air helicopter. The Air Dynasty chopper was carrying cargo.

#8366. Missouri Fourth Grader Has Already Taken Two Giant Whitetail Bucks This Season

Published Oct 30, 2026 4:01 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Noah Baker isn’t your typical young hunter. The Pike County, Missouri youngster is a hunting prodigy most sportsmen would be proud to call their son.

“He shot his first deer at age six,” his dad, Jared Baker, tells Outdoor Life. “He lives to hunt and fish. And we’d have to think about just how many deer he’s taken since that first one when he was still in first grade.”

October 25 was the last day of the Missouri early two-day youth gun deer season. Noah and Jared chose a hunting spot over a cut corn field late that afternoon near their home in Frankfort.

“The wind wasn’t great, and we just set up in a hillside haystack that overlooked a cut corn patch that was well below us,” says Jared, a 37-year-old heavy equipment operator. “We set a tripod rifle stand in the haystack, put Noah’s 7mm suppressed Remington rifle on it, and watched and waited.”

They got on the haystack about 4 p.m. on a hot afternoon. They hadn’t waited very long before a few small bucks and does started filtering into the corn to feed about 60 yards from where they were positioned.

“We were waiting for a big buck we knew was around that I named ‘Dwayne The Rock Johnson’, because he was so big and strong,” Noah says. “The deer’s head was huge, and I wanted him.”

The father-son team had two big target bucks they’d watched and planned to take this year. They’d also found shed antlers from the deer. Noah had shot the smaller of the two bucks — a 155-inch 10-pointer — with his crossbow on Oct. 2.

Now they were after the second buck – “Dwayne The Rock Johnson,” and it just so happened that the deer showed at 6:20 p.m.

“It happened fast,” Jared says. “We saw him at 80 yards, and he went into a grass patch to look at a doe.”

“I saw him first, dad was looking farther away when I spotted him,” says Noah. “Dwayne started to walk away, turning toward some smaller bucks. But dad used his grunt call, and the buck turned and looked at us.”

Noah had crosshairs settled on the deer’s chest and fired at the buck standing 80 yards away. The 140-grain Berger bullet put the buck down quickly.

“Noah and I just started fist pumping in the air,” said Jared.

Read Next: Here’s Why This Giant Missouri Buck Was Still in Velvet in Late September

They called some friends for help getting the giant 17-point buck out of the field. They didn’t weigh it, but a taxidermist who has the buck rough green-scored the antlers at 187 inches.

Noah’s other 155-inch 10-pointer also is with the same taxidermist for mounting.

“I’m going to hang both of them in my bedroom,” Noah says. “One on each side of my TV screen so I can watch them whenever I’m in there.”
