#8255. The Best Survival Food, Tested and Reviewed

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Regarding survival, a reliable food supply is high on the list of needs for disaster readiness. A well-rounded, easy-to-transport kit that keeps you nourished for days—without repeating the same bland meals—is crucial for morale and sustenance.

Many survival food companies are on the market, but not all have stood the test of time. Over the years, several have failed due to poor quality control and mismanagement. As a disaster readiness and survival training professional, I receive samples from many of these companies and, more importantly, have the unique opportunity to have hundreds of students test their products yearly. Additionally, I bring these samples to our courses to gather feedback from our instructors and participants. The insights shared in this article are based on decades of personal experience and the collective input of our students, providing you with a well-rounded perspective to help you make informed decisions about your food preparedness.

At the end of the day, no matter the crisis, we all need food to keep us going. While it’s true that humans can survive for weeks without eating, very few would willingly test that theory. The good news is that with the growing demand, more high-quality, nutrient-dense options are now available. After testing some of the best survival food on the market, these are our top picks for flavor, shelf life, and nutrition.

4Patriots has established itself as one of the leading survival food brands in the market. Proudly made and packaged in the United States, their products support local businesses while delivering high-quality meals. These meals are crafted for superior nutrition and taste, using fresh ingredients and whole grains, and are free from MSG. Preparation is simple—boil water, add the pouch, and within 15 minutes, you’ll have a hot meal ready to eat.

4Patriots packages their food in triple-layer Mylar to ensure long shelf life, which helps protect the contents from air and moisture. Customers can select from various kit sizes depending on their needs, from 72-hour emergency supplies to year-long provisions. Each kit is designed to provide one person with six servings a day, offering sufficient calories and nutrients to sustain energy. The meals come in various flavors, including macaroni and cheese, vegetable soup, and oatmeal. One of my favorite pieces of their kits is that many of the meals are named after people to add some morale build into it all.  No matter the kit size, 4Patriots offers a reliable solution for building a robust survival food supply.

A vital feature of an MRE is the built-in heater, which, once activated, heats your entrée, providing the convenience of a hot meal no matter where you are. However, there are some notable downsides. Many of our students, particularly those with military experience who have relied on MREs for extended periods, advise against using them for long-term situations. In addition to being heavy to transport, they can lead to digestive problems, ranging from constipation to more organ-related severe issues over time.

Providing a hot meal for your family during a disaster is more than just a practical necessity—it can help boost morale and alleviate anxiety, offering a sense of normalcy amidst the chaos. Mountain House meals taste delicious and require boiling water for preparation. Mountain House is a regular staple of meal choices in our classes. I see them often.

One of the great features is that the food rehydrates directly in the pouch, allowing you to eat from it, which means minimal cleanup afterward. With nearly 30 meal options, including breakfasts and desserts, variety won’t be an issue, and no one will find the meals repetitive.

Each serving offers about 250 calories, depending on the meal. With two servings per pouch, there’s plenty for even a hearty appetite or enough to share if needed. These meals are designed to stay fresh for up to 30 years and ensure you can access quality food for decades.

Crafted with Whey Protein Isolate as the primary protein source and fortified with high fiber while containing just 1 gram of sugar, these protein bars are perfect for daily enjoyment. Each Kirkland Signature bar offers 21 grams of high-quality protein and features real chocolate for a satisfying blend of taste and nutrition. Typically used for meal replacement and workout-focused diets, these bars conveniently meet your protein and fiber needs without compromising flavor.

In the context of disaster preparedness, these protein bars are an ideal addition to any emergency food supply. Their long shelf life, combined with their nutritional profile, makes them an excellent option for staying energized and nourished when fresh food may not be available. Lightweight and easy to store, they offer a reliable source of protein and fiber that can help maintain energy levels and support overall health during a crisis. Whether sheltering in place or on the move, these bars ensure access to essential nutrients in challenging circumstances.

Augason Farms is renowned for its extensive line of canned goods, which are perfect for long-term food storage and emergency preparedness. Their #10 cans are filled with freeze-dried or dehydrated foods, offering various essentials, such as fruits, vegetables, meats, grains, and dairy products. With a shelf life of up to 25 years, these canned goods are an excellent choice for those looking to build a reliable food supply for emergencies or everyday convenience. Each can is sealed for freshness and labeled with detailed preparation instructions, making incorporating these products into daily meals or survival situations easy.

Augason Farms’ canned goods are appealing because of their versatility and nutritional value. Whether you need individual ingredients like powdered eggs, instant potatoes, or freeze-dried strawberries, their products allow for flexibility in meal planning. You can use them in recipes or enjoy them independently, ensuring you have access to nutritious food options when fresh ingredients are unavailable. These canned goods are compact, easy to store, and offer large quantities, making them ideal for families, survivalists, or anyone seeking to stock up on essential food supplies that can withstand the test of time.

Peak Refuel is a top choice for disaster preparedness, offering high-protein, freeze-dried meals designed to keep you fueled during challenging situations. Maintaining strength and energy is essential in emergencies, and Peak Refuel meals deliver an impressive 40-50 grams of protein per serving. This high protein content ensures you get the nutrition needed to stay alert and physically capable when it matters most. Whether you’re sheltering in place or need to be on the move, these meals provide the sustenance required to get through physically demanding conditions.

Beyond their nutritional value, Peak Refuel meals are incredibly convenient for disaster preparedness. Made with high-quality, non-GMO ingredients, they rehydrate quickly with hot water and are ready to eat in minutes. The lightweight, resealable pouches are easy to store and transport, making them an ideal addition to any emergency food supply. Various meal options, including breakfast scrambles and hearty dinners like chicken alfredo or beef stroganoff, offer the nutrients you need and great taste to keep morale high during tough times. Peak Refuel’s focus on protein-rich, easy-to-prepare meals makes them an excellent choice for anyone serious about disaster readiness.

ReadyWise is a leading provider of long-term food storage solutions, offering various affordable, high-quality meals that are perfect for disaster preparedness. Whether you’re planning for a short-term emergency or looking to build a comprehensive survival food stockpile, ReadyWise provides convenient, easy-to-prepare options. Their freeze-dried meals only require water, making them ideal for emergencies or outdoor adventures where resources may be limited. With a focus on both taste and nutrition, ReadyWise ensures that their products not only sustain you during a crisis but also offer flavors you can enjoy.

One of the standout features of ReadyWise is its budget-friendly approach, making it a top choice for those who want to prepare without breaking the bank. Despite the lower price point, ReadyWise doesn’t compromise on quality or variety, offering satisfying and nutritionally balanced meals. This combination of affordability and convenience makes ReadyWise a smart investment for families and individuals looking to secure a reliable food supply for potential emergencies. With ReadyWise, you can build your preparedness plan without overspending, ensuring peace of mind for whatever the future holds.

To select the foods we tested, we received samples from a variety of reputable companies and also purchased additional products to ensure a wide range of options. With the help of our students, who have diverse tastes and preferences, we got a broad spectrum of feedback during the testing process. These foods were integrated directly into our survival and disaster readiness training courses, allowing us to evaluate their practicality, taste, and ease of preparation in real-world scenarios. This hands-on approach ensured that we tested the food’s quality and performance under survival conditions.

A structured approach to survival prioritization is best understood through the “Law of Threes” hierarchy. This principle outlines that our most immediate needs, in order of importance, are safety, thermoregulation, hydration, and finally, food. However, from a psychological and moral standpoint, food remains a constant desire, even though it ranks lower on essential needs.

We also took a multi-tiered approach to assessing these survival food options.  I am fond of saying that “hunger is the best seasoning in the world.”  That is true in the long term, but taste plays a role in the short term.  When assessing them, I emphasize both taste and cost-effectiveness. After all, it makes little sense to invest in provisions that are not enjoyable to eat. In addition to these factors, I consider the following critical criteria in my recommendations:

One of the most overlooked factors when choosing survival food is whether or not you enjoy eating it. Taste, texture, and how the food agrees with your digestive system are essential. While it’s easy to focus on stockpiling a large quantity of food, if you don’t like it, you’re essentially wasting money. Some may argue that you’ll eat anything in extreme hunger, but right now, you have the luxury of selecting food you’ll enjoy. Regularly incorporating these meals into your current diet helps rotate stock and prepares your taste buds for when disaster strikes. As the saying goes, “We do not rise to the occasion; we default to our level of training.” Why not start training your palate now?

Cost is another critical consideration when building a survival food supply. Most people must budget carefully, so simultaneously making large purchases may be impossible. A gradual approach works well for many, where small amounts are bought over time as the budget allows. This makes the process more manageable and helps you steadily grow your stockpile without straining your finances. If you face resistance from family members about spending on survival food, consider framing it as an insurance policy—something you invest in for peace of mind in case of a worst-case scenario.

Storage space can be a real challenge for those living in smaller spaces like apartments, condos, or tiny homes. It’s crucial to make the most of your space by considering the size of the packaging and the number of servings per product. This ensures you get the most food stored in the least space. Carefully evaluating your storage setup and choosing compact, efficient products can help maximize your shelf space and investment.

Storing survival food is best done in conditions that are dark, cool, and dry. These three factors will work together to slow down the degradation of the food. A closet in a spare bedroom, for example, might be a great location. A damp basement, perhaps not so much.

Most survival situations tend to last around 72 hours. However, in recent years, many emergencies have extended beyond that timeframe, and with global uncertainty, the possibility of more prolonged events is not just possible but increasingly likely. As a precaution, I recommend planning for at least one month’s worth of food for everyone in your household, ensuring you’re prepared for longer-term scenarios.

As previously mentioned, our primary needs follow a specific order: safety, thermoregulation, water, and food. For safety, ensure you have the tools necessary to protect yourself from both environmental threats and potential harm from others. This includes items to help you see in low-light situations and defend yourself if needed. Thermoregulation involves staying warm in cold weather and cool in hot conditions, so be sure to have adequate clothing and supplies to maintain comfort for at least one month without access to utilities.Water is an invaluable resource, and it’s crucial to have both filtration and purification methods to protect against bacterial and viral contaminants. In addition to these essentials, it’s wise to have signaling tools like bright-colored items, flashlights, and whistles to help attract attention if necessary.

Choosing survival food to keep on hand for emergencies requires a little homework and research. You shouldn’t buy several cases of something simply because the package looks enticing. Base your decision on facts, including budget and the quality of the food. Ease of preparation is also a factor, of course. In an emergency, you may not have ready access to things like stovetops or microwave ovens. Stick with things that require a minimal amount of preparation. Hopefully, you’ll never be in a situation where you must rely on survival food, but you’ll be glad you have it should the unthinkable occur.

For more than 125 years, Field & Stream has been providing readers with honest and authentic coverage of outdoor gear. Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. And when we write about a product—whether it’s a bass lure or a backpack—we cover the good and the bad, so you know exactly what to expect before you decide to make a purchase.

Highlights Education Caudill has a BBA from the University of Kentucky in Statistical Analysis. He is a Certified Master Naturalist from the University of Kentucky and a Level 2 Naturalist through the Kamana Naturalist Program. #8254. Go Further in Québec’s Winter Wilderness

Snowshoeing in Gaspésie. (Photo: Gaspésie © Gouv.Qc / I. Roberge)

Let this sink in: More than 92 percent of Québec is public land. Come winter, those millions of acres of woods, trails, and open glades get absolutely buried in snow, turning the province into a sprawling winter playground where opportunities for ski touring, Nordic skiing, and multiday snowshoeing abound.

All that wild landscape would be nothing without a trail system to match—which is why it’s a darn good thing that groomed trails and skintracks cover the province, courtesy of Québec’s adventure-minded culture and infrastructure. Cozy rustic huts dot the high country, Nordic centers pepper the lowlands, and there’s an extensive network of designated ski-touring areas across the region.

Behind Québec’s extensive network of winter trails and refuges lies a long tradition of winter travel and exploration.

Long before winter travel became a recreational pursuit, Indigenous peoples used snowshoes and knowledge passed down through generations to navigate the territory now known as Québec. Today, these snow-covered landscapes offer countless opportunities for exploration, from Nordic skiing and multi-day snowshoeing to backcountry adventures.

Today, Québec boasts 28 national parks and dozens of Nordic and cross-country centers. It also boasts plenty of grassroots backcountry ski areas, each complete with trail maps and designated runs. There’s no avalanche mitigation at these sites—they’re wild at heart—but the effortless parking, signage, and basic infrastructure make them a perfect stepping stone between sidecountry and true backcountry. Always remember to come equipped with the appropriate training, equipment, and avalanche awareness. And if you’d rather explore with a qualified guide, you can find businesses certified through Aventure Écotourisme Québec’s Quality-Safety certification program, which sets recognized standards for risk management, guide training and service quality.

Looking to do a little bit of everything? Try Vallée Bras-du-Nord. This all-season adventure center maintains both groomed cross-country ski trails and designated backcountry terrain. Its varied slopes and jaw-dropping views guarantee an unforgettable outing, while a collection of yurts and cabins make it a true ski-in, ski-out getaway. You won’t find a backcountry experience like it anywhere else in North America.

For a more homegrown vibe, head to Sommets du Fjord, a blues-and-blacks zone just beyond the charming village of Petite-Saguenay. The town sits right on the edge of the legendary Saguenay Fjord National Park—yet another ski touring and snowshoeing epicenter—which makes it an ideal multisport base camp.

Want to turn a great day into a great week? Treat yourself to a fully immersive multiday traverse through Québec’s snow-draped winter landscapes. Robust hut systems in national parks like Mont-Tremblant and Monts-Valins make it easy to plan linkups via Nordic ski or snowshoe, and village-to-village trips in the Laurentians like those along Les Routes Blanches offer chances to discover culture and cuisine alongside the stunning landscapes. Simply choose a trail to one or more of the parks’ remote refuges and use them as stopover points to cook, relax, and connect with your adventure buddies—and recharge by a blazing woodstove before hitting the trail again the next day.

The adventure doesn’t end when the skis or snowshoes come off. Beyond the trails, Québec’s welcoming villages, local flavors, and cozy inns offer the perfect setting to unwind and reconnect. Share a well-earned meal, raise a glass of a local wine or brew with your fellow adventurers, and relive the day’s discoveries. Because sometimes, going further isn’t just about the distance you travel, it’s about everything you experience along the way.

Your next winter adventure starts here. Whether you’re seeking powder-filled backcountry descents, multi-day Nordic ski routes or peaceful snowshoe expeditions through snow-covered forests, Québec invites you to explore further. Discover inspiring winter experiences and start planning your next expedition with Bonjour Québec.

#8253. This Is Why Your Trail Cameras Aren’t Working Properly

Published Nov 7, 2026 1:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

You’ve finally got your trail camera set up in the spot. Every day or two it sends you a photo of a giant old buck, and now all you’ve got to do is wait for the right wind to sneak in there and hunt him. And then, all of a sudden, the camera goes dead.

It’s a new camera, the battery life seemed fine, cell reception was decent … What the hell? Welcome to the often frustrating world of modern trail camera use.

I’ve been field testing and running trail cameras year-round for several years now and in my experience, there is no camera brand out there that’s immune to malfunctions and failures. But my experience pales in comparison to that of Rich Howell of Trail Cam Pro. Howell has been objectively testing and experimenting with trail cameras for more than 20 years.

I recently interviewed Howell on the Outdoor Life podcast and he shared several reasons why hunters see so many camera failures in the field. Some of it has to do with how we’re using the cameras, and some of it has to do with how the cams are made (which is usually pretty cheaply). Plus, Howell hints at where he thinks the future of trail cameras is headed, and it’s all about making a system that is more affordable and useful to hunters. It’s a conversation worth listening to ahead of the heart of hunting season.

In the meantime, here’s why our cameras often go down in the field, and what we can do to fix them.

Standard alkaline batteries often don’t have the required power to keep a trail camera running reliably, Howell says. If you’re getting fine daytime pictures, but blank, black images at night, it’s a good sign you have a battery issue as there’s not enough power for the camera to fire the flash. This can happen even when the camera is displaying decent battery life.

More expensive lithium batteries can work well, but they too can have issues. Howell noticed that about 1 in 20 lithium batteries would go bad very quickly, (like within days of use) and sometimes this was enough to prevent the camera from working.

Howell now suggests that hunters use rechargeable lithium batteries, which have proven to be more reliable. Having a pool of these batteries on rotation will help solve many trail camera power troubles.

When hunters first jump into the cellular trail camera game, they often like to get their photos sent immediately. In the beginning it’s fun to get a notification and then have that instant gratification of seeing a deer photo.

But it’s usually more effective to have a cell camera batch send images every 12 hours or 24 hours. This is a key way to preserve battery life, and it’s also a more useful way to analyze trail camera data.

Personally, I like to have cameras send every 24 hours and then I review all the cameras everyday in the morning. Looking at all the cameras on the property at once helps me put together activity trends.

Howell says that solar panels definitely can help keep your camera powered, but they often have issues in the field. First, you want to make sure that they are facing south to capture as most sun as possible. This can be a challenge if you want your camera facing north. And second, squirrels have a tendency to chew through solar panel wires. If you’re setting up your camera and panel in the hardwoods, there’s a good chance a squirrel is going to get to it. In other words, solar panels can be a useful tool, but they’re not a silver bullet.

If you’re using the stock camera strap, you’re just asking for trouble. The tag ends of these straps always seem to come loose (triggering the camera) and you’re never able to position the camera perfectly on the tree with them. Plus, other hunters can easily spot the strap, which is an important consideration if you’re hunting public land. Howell suggests using an adjustable tree mount to make sure you can position the camera exactly where it needs to go. You can find a wealth of  trail camera information on the Trail Cam Pro website and by subscribing to their newsletter.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8252. Hunting the ‘Old Ripper’ Was Almost More Adventure Than I Bargained For

Published Nov 7, 2026 4:00 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I had just come back from the service in 1954. My wife was expecting our first baby, and I was running a general store on Highway 97 just outside of Bainbridge, Georgia. Hardly a day went by that someone didn’t come in and tell tales of Old Ripper.

Old Ripper was a large black wild hog that lived in the nearby Fowltown Swamp. That hog tore up more fences, broke more gates, broke the backs of more female hogs and was chased by more hunters than any critter there has ever been in this country. Ripper had been shot by several people. My Daddy fired at him seven times with an M-1 carbine and believed he hit him, but the hog never fell. He had been hunted with dogs and he had killed plenty of dogs. There never was a hog hound that could hold him. The last time the boar was run with hounds, he killed two of the best hounds in the county with his slashing tusks, so no one else ever put their dogs on Old Ripper.

Old Ripper got his name because there seemed to be absolutely nothing he couldn’t rip up or utterly destroy. Farmers around Bainbridge went to the hardware stores and bought brand-new aluminum gates to put in the gaps he made in their fences. Within a week, the gates were often all bent and torn up where that crazy boar had stuck his nose under and bent them to get into a pasture or field. There was no hog wire or barbed wire fence that could keep Old Ripper out.

That boar was walking destruction. The farmers hated him not only for tearing up fences and gates, but even more because of what he did to their sows. Ripper would break into a pig parlor, tear up the pens and release all the sows. Then he would take them off for a stroll in the woods. Old Ripper weighed 438 pounds. So when he mounted some of the young sows, he broke their backs. Then the sows would have to be destroyed. The sows he did breed threw shoats that were as wild and crazy as he was. The piglets wouldn’t fatten and brought almost nothing at the market.

Everybody was out to get Old Ripper. My dad was accustomed to catching wild hogs. We used to catch them in the Fowltown Swamp, fatten them and sell them at the market. My daddy knew about trapping hogs. He built traps to catch Old Ripper. On two separate occasions Old Ripper did go into one of daddy’s traps, but he tore up the wooden stockades and broke out both times. My daddy wouldn’t stand for that, so daddy got a steel bear trap and set it for Ripper. When daddy went back the next day he found the giant tracks of Old Ripper and followed them to the trap. But instead of catching a renegade hog, he found the bear trap had been sprung by the big boar.

One reason Old Ripper became a legend was his ability to outthink the farmers and the hunters in our area. He had been around humans so much that in many cases he just outthought folks instead of using brute force. The people around our place began to think Old Ripper might be a supernatural creature. He was a boar, but he was a smart boar. No dogs could hold him, no stockades could enclose him, no fence could stop him and no man had been able to kill him for seven years.

Other episodes added to the legend of Old Ripper. One of the meanest things Old Ripper ever did involved Mrs. Ella T. Hand’s daughter-in-law, who was five months pregnant. She was in her kitchen and heard a disturbance out among her sows. She went out to the pig parlor and saw Old Ripper trying to tear the planks off the posts where she had her sows penned up. She picked up a rock and threw it at the old boar to try and run him off. When he saw her, he turned, looked straight at her and charged. Only a few steps away was a giant red oak stump that stood about three feet off the ground. The lady climbed up on the stump and began to scream for her husband. All the while, Old Ripper was going around the stump, snorting and blowing. He attempted to rear up on that stump and get to her but she stayed just out of reach of his razor-sharp tusks. For an hour the hog circled the stump as the lady screamed for help. Finally her husband came home. When he saw what was happening, he grabbed his shotgun from over the fireplace and ran toward the hog. At less than 10 yards, he shot Old Ripper in the side of the head with birdshot. The hog merely shook his head, looked at the man and trotted off.

To say Old Ripper was hated by everybody in the community would be a vast understatement. Every man and boy dreamed of killing that old boar, and plenty of work was forgotten by the men who hunted him. All it took to organize a community hog hunt was for someone to report that they’d seen Old Ripper. Every man and boy within earshot would grab a gun and head for the swamp.

I would have liked to have hunted Old Ripper, but I had mouths to feed. I didn’t have time to waste on that renegade boar. I had just bought a brand-new lever-action Marlin .30/30. I was proud of that gun and took it out behind the store to test it out. On that particular day, Mrs. Ella T. Hand happened to be sitting out in front of the store. Mrs. Hand was close to 80 years old. She always wore a sunbonnet, a long dress and about 90 percent of the time, she had a dip of snuff in her mouth. Mrs. Hand saw me kill a crow sitting in the field about 150 yards away with that rifle. I knew I’d made a lucky shot, but she didn’t. She told everyone for a month about how good I could shoot with that new .30/30.

“If that old wild hog comes back around my sows, I’m going to come and get you, Jack, and let you kill him with that new rifle,” she told me.

Well, about a month later, here comes Mrs. Ella T. in her 1949 pickup truck.

“Jack, that old boar is up in my field with some sows he run off,” she told me. “Now I don’t expect you’ll have any better luck than anybody else who has tried to kill him, but I sure wish you’d bring that new rifle up to the field and give it a try.”

I closed up my little country store and got into the front seat of that pickup truck with Mrs. Ella T. to try my hand at Old Ripper. I had five cartridges with copper-jacketed lead-headed bullets in my gun—the kind that open up but still go on through. There wasn’t any doubt in my mind that if I could hit that boar, the bullets would do the damage needed to put him down.

We drove to Mrs. Hand’s 40-acre peanut field, which backed up to the edge of Fowltown Swamp. I saw Old Ripper out in the middle of the field with four sows he had just broken out from their pen. The five pigs were all rooting in the peanuts. There was a hog wire fence around the field, with barbed wire on the top. The field, which was about 250 yards wide and about twice as long, was on a hillside. Old Ripper and the sows were up close to the top of the hill and I was down near the bottom. There was a dried-up creekbed that ran under the fence. From the tracks in the wash, I figured this was where Old Ripper and the sows had gotten into the field. The creekbed was only about two or three feet deep, but it was big enough for me to crawl under the fence and still stay out of sight. I could lay down in the bottom of the wash, crawl along on my stomach and Old Ripper wouldn’t be able to see me.

Until that day, I had never seen Old Ripper. I had looked at fences he had torn up and I had seen mud on the sides of the trees where he had rubbed. I knew he was a big boar, but I never realized just how big. When I saw Old Ripper standing there in the sun, his black bristles gathered in the rays of light and made him look a deep royal blue. He was a magnificent animal standing about four feet high, and he completely dwarfed the sows following him.

I said to myself, “Doggone your hide, Old Ripper! I’m going to try and get a little closer to you.”

The wash meandered from the bottom of the slope where I was uphill to where Old Ripper was rooting in the peanut patch. Lying flat on my belly, I would crawl for 10 yards and then peep over the edge to see where Old Ripper was. Each time I looked, the old boar was about 10 yards farther from the place than he had been before. It was just like he had a sixth sense that warned him of danger. He kept the same distance away, about 230 yards from me, from the time I first saw him until I decided to shoot. After I had crawled 30 yards, Old Ripper and his band of runaway sows were within 10 yards of a thick broom sedge field. I knew that if he got into that field, I wouldn’t be able to see to shoot him.

The wash was shallower and just barely kept me out of the boar’s view. The shot had to be over 200 yards. So I laid the rifle down on the lip of the wash, looked through the open sights and aimed at the top of Old Ripper’s shoulder. When I squeezed off the first shot, I saw the dust fly off the boar’s shoulder and heard the bullet make a dull thud when it hit him, but Old Ripper showed no sign of being wounded.

Then I stood up. Old Ripper reared up on his hind legs and bellowed like a wild bull. The hair on the back of my neck stood up. I had caught or killed more than 100 hogs out of that swamp, but I had never heard a hog make a sound like that.

When Old Ripper came down on his front feet, he was on a dead run, headed right down that hill. I knew that when he got to the bottom of the hill, he had business with me. I should have killed Old Ripper with that first shot, but he was far from dead. I didn’t panic. I knew that before the boar got to me, I would have time to fire four more of those .30/30 shells. I thought there was no way I wouldn’t kill him before he got to me. I had faced other wild hogs before.

With every shot, I believed I was pumping more lead into Old Ripper, but he never slowed. He still came on toward me. I took my time, aimed, squeezed, heard the report of the rifle, jacked another shell into the chamber and fired again. I knew I was hitting the boar, but he never missed a stride.

When Old Ripper was less than 50 yards away, I heard the hammer fall on an empty chamber. That was the loudest, most desperate sound I ever heard in my life.

I looked around and saw one lone cherry tree with no limbs on it about 30 yards to my right, but my feet wouldn’t work. I knew I couldn’t stay where I was, but I couldn’t go anywhere else. Old Ripper just kept on coming. I finally threw that gun down and began to run. Then I saw Old Ripper, now 20 yards away, running on two crippled front legs. I knew then that I had a chance to outrun him, but just as that idea went through my mind, the big boar fell and rolled to a stop about 10 yards away from me. He never moved, he never grunted and he never made another sound.

There was a slight breeze coming from that dead boar to me. Old Ripper’s odor was the strongest, rankest smell I ever have smelled. It was awful. I waited awhile to make sure Old Ripper was dead. Then I looked to see where my bullets had hit. The first had entered the shoulder. The second went through the hog’s loin and had gone into his stomach. Two other shots had hit his fore shoulders and entered the chest cavity. One bullet just flat-out missed.

Looking at Old Ripper, I was kind of sad that he was gone. Even if he was a renegade, he was a magnificent animal. There had never been a boar like him before that I ever heard tell of, and there never was another.

Mrs. Ella T.’s son James and her husband Ressie helped me load Old Ripper onto the pickup truck. We took the boar to Mr. Smoke Roger’s platform scales at Fayetteville, Georgia. The boar tipped the scales at 438 pounds. We struggled to reload the boar and then drove back to Bainbridge. Dr. Cooper, the veterinarian at that time, examined him. Below Ripper’s inch-thick hide was a sheath of gristle that extended from his huge shoulders to the middle of his back. This sheath had been Old Ripper’s armor and had turned the shotgun pellets and rifle bullets over the years. Dr. Cooper said the boar was between 8 and 10 years old and was probably a throwback to some of the European wild boars let loose in this country years before.

Read Next: I’ve Been Charged by Bears and Moose. Wild Hogs Are Much, Much Worse

When my daddy saw that the boar filled up the bed of that pickup truck, he could hardly believe his eyes. He had wanted to be the one who killed Old Ripper, but since he didn’t, he was glad it was me.

“That ol’ hog has cost farmers in this area thousands of dollars and many good sows, as well as being responsible for a lot of little pigs that weren’t fit to sell,” my daddy said. “I’m glad he’s gone.”

Since then the old Fowltown Swamp where Old Ripper used to roam and where wild pigs lived and bred for hundreds of years has vanished. Old Ripper’s haunts are covered by Lake Seminole today, but I remember it like it was when that boar was less than 30 yards away on a dead run bringing hurt to me, and I heard the sound of the hammer on my .30/30 falling on an empty chamber.

#8251. Scarpa Golden Gate LT Review: Moderate Stack Is So Back

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail shoes with a moderate stack are becoming harder to find. New trail models either have inches of soft, bouncy foam underfoot (sometimes with a carbon plate), or they are minimalist models that let your feet feel every pebble. Fortunately, a few that balance protection and ground feel still exist. I’ve just discovered one: the Scarpa Golden Gate LT.

Scarpa is an Italian mountain brand based in the Dolomites. Specializing in mountain climbing footwear, elite mountaineers historically wore the brand’s lightweight mountain shoes to cross rugged terrain. Scarpa’s trail running shoes reflect that heritage; they’re known for their rugged protection and firm, surefooted ride. But many trail runners who don’t live in places like the Alps or the White Mountains don’t need an indestructible mountain running boot. Enter Scarpa’s new trail shoe line-up.

The Golden Gate LT is Scarpa’s lightweight “door-to-trail” shoe meant for a broader trail running audience who want a single functional trainer on runs that bridge varied terrain, from asphalt to gravel to rocky singletrack. I put the shoe’s prowess to the test across Los Angeles’s urban streets, steep horse trails, and sandy beaches.

Weight: 10.5oz (men’s 9, women’s 10) Stack Height: 30 – 24 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm

+ Handles road-to-trail transitions smoothly + Stable base + Excellent traction – Fit too narrow for wide feet – Slightly sluggish on quick turnover

The Golden Gate LT may be a departure from Scarpa’s roots in many ways, but not in style: I received a hot orange-white colorway that immediately reminded me of the Orange Crush soda can and blends right in with Scarpa’s line up of mountain running shoes and ski boots. Though the flashy look isn’t entirely my style, I’m just glad it’s not a monster truck of a trail shoe.

Most of my test runs were on the hilly, paved roads of my neighborhood. Cruising through the familiar streets, I was happy to find that while cushioned, my landings weren’t squishy at all. Instead, I noticed a small bounciness in the midsole — like I was running on a shallow trampoline. That’s likely because Scarpa blended 20% PEBAX into the EVA compound midsole to provide extra responsiveness for what I call the “road” side of the hybrid shoe’s performance.

Taking the shoes uphill, the rebound was still there but didn’t do the heavy lifting for me. That changed, however, when I picked up the pace. With some downhill momentum, my stride lengthened, and any feeling of a firm trail shoe was completely gone. At quicker paces, the bounce takes over and helps maintain speed, feeling like an uptempo road shoe. Normally I don’t like shoes with much cushioning, but the upper’s gentle TPU-reinforced support wrapped my feet so nicely that I felt confident running faster and farther.

Later, I took them out for a long run mostly on trails, connected by some roads, to see how they held up on different surfaces. On the trails, the midsole bounce was less noticeable, which I appreciated, as bouncing over unstable surfaces doesn’t make sense to me.

Compared to other trail models I’ve worn, the lugs are far more flexible, providing amazing traction across sand, dirt, and rocks. The flexibility of the outsole kept my stride smooth and stable on uneven trails and helped the shoe maintain its beginning-of-the-run feeling late into a 14-mile long run. Overall, the outsole’s efficiency felt more alive on the trails than on paved surfaces.

If you’re crazy, like me, and sprint down steep trails, you’ll appreciate the moderate, 24 mm stack under the forefoot, making toe-offs effortless, helping short, quick strides remain stable, and ensuring that tight cornering is no problem. The 30 mm heel stack, however, which contributed to the smooth cushioning on the road, could sometimes feel a bit sluggish on steep trail descents. I prefer 4 mm-drop shoes to keep my steps quick and agile and maximize the thrill of heading downhill with my hair on fire. But if you’re more sensible and take it easy on descents, then the 6 mm drop shouldn’t be a problem at all.

Back on the roads toward the end of my long run, I felt the same road-shoe ride I get on my neighborhood runs. Though my legs were more tired after battling the dusty, hilly terrain, the flexibility of the upper and the outsole encouraged me to keep my pace until the end of the run.

Durability seems mixed so far: After testing the shoe for a month of road and trail runs, the outsole has progressively felt more flexible under my feet and can take on rocks and tough objects on the trails. The edges of the lugs have retained their sharp definition from when it was new, while the upper and overall cushioning still feel just as comfortable. The midsole bounce, however, is much gentler than when it was new (for better or worse), and the bright Orange Crush splash has since faded.

Quality moderate-stack trail shoes are becoming harder to find. If your favorite model lost its way in the “space-age arms race of trail super shoes,” as our editor Cade Michael aptly put it, and you don’t like feeling every rock beneath your feet through a thin minimalist sole, this one’s for you.

Runners with narrow or medium-narrow feet who prefer a tight fit should appreciate this shoe. The heel and midfoot’s gentle padding hug my narrow feet quite tightly, and the toe box has some room for toe splay, though it’s not wide — it’s right in the middle. This close-fitting shape is useful for tight cornering and platform stability, but if you have wide feet and need breathing space for your toes, the M2C H1, an Altra, or a Topo trail shoe might be a better fit.

So, is this the lower-stacked hybrid shoe that we’ve been waiting for? With its dual personality, the Golden Gate LT certainly handles roads and trails like it’s built for both. You can also totally wear this exclusively as a trail shoe for runs of any length. Though difficult trails with demanding terrain may not be its greatest strength, this shoe provides a comfortable, energetic ride on all other terrain, achieving exactly what it’s designed for.

#8248. Red Bull’s Newest Ski Film Is Made By Pros—But Is Surprisingly For Everyone

(Photo: Courtesy of Hai Yen / Legs of Steel / Red Bull Content Pool)

Unless all of your friends are die-hard skiers, you’ve probably endured the unfortunate experience of trying to explain ski films. For those used to tidy narratives and strong plots, it can be hard to see why a film that relies mostly on epic drone photography and loose plot development is worth several hours of someone’s time.

Thankfully, now you don’t have to. Filmmaker and pro skier Paddy Graham and his motley crew have done it for you. In his newest film, “We Can’t Not,” Graham writes a love letter to his favorite format, the ski movie. It’s also a message to his family, who appear in the film. The premise: This is Graham’s last hoorah, and before he steps away from the wild (and dangerous) world of steep skiing, he wants to help his family understand what exactly making a ski film entails.

“Paddy has been asked a lot about what he actually does, and why,” Red Bull Media House executive producer Sarah Stow told SKI. The film is essentially a response to the question Graham is trying to answer: Why keep making ski films? Why keep skiing such big lines? Why do you even do this? He can’t not.

The film opens up as many others do: a montage of big mountain skiing set to rock music, a few yew soundbites, and close-up shots of freeride jackets with sponsor logos. Then it takes a turn. We meet our protagonist and start to see the film’s thesis unfurl.

That’s the first moment that I realized this film was going to be different.

The idea of answering a legitimate question is what separates “We Can’t Not” from other films: the journey that the audience follows as Graham sits around a dinner table trying to explain to his children and parents what he does when he says he makes ski films is not unlike conversations we’ve had with our ski-film newbie friends.

The issue with many ski films is they’re created for an audience that already loves to ski; in “We Can’t Not,” the audience can be anyone. One way in which Graham does this is by introducing his cast to the audience like we’re meeting for the first time. Each castmate has an intro that explains his distinct “why”: why he loves to ski and why Graham chose to feature him in the film.

“We really wanted to introduce the athletes so audiences connect with them,” Stow explained, “which is such a smart move in a sport where we often only see goggles and helmets.”

The four other skiers: Kye Peterson, Markus Eder, Tom Ritsch, and Finn Bilous, all complement Graham’s conceit: They’re all a little maverick themselves.

But really, the story isn’t about the group of irreverent skiers—it’s about what compels a group of irreverent skiers to do something as outrageous as shooting another ski film. And, for that matter, why ski films ought to keep existing into the next generation. After all, Instagram and TikTok are full of more short-form ski clips than one could ever get through.

The response, at least according to these diehards? A passion for the sport that runs several standard deviations deeper than your average weekend warrior.

A point made clear by the team’s decision to rent out Hyperbowl, a VR film studio outside Munich that, according to Stow, is “more used to Hollywood productions than a bunch of pro skiers turning up.”

At Hyperbowl, a studio outside Munich that Stow says is “more used to Hollywood productions than a bunch of pro skiers turning up,” the cast found that sometimes the most radical lines exist many miles away from the mountain. The Alaska backdrops had to be scanned on location in advance, and Stow says it was the studio’s first indoor mountain ski shoot. Her verdict: the team was “pushing innovation in this film, not just taking the classic safe route.”

The film’s other big swing is its narrator. Sean Bean, a voice that Game of Thrones and Lord of the Rings fans may recognize, narrates the film. Stow says Bean, despite not being a skier, got so into the project that he became a method voice actor. For one of the final scenes, where he tells the audience the film isn’t over yet, she says he ran in from another room to get the tone right.

Ultimately, the meta-filmmaking in “We Can’t Not” helps to underscore the point of not only their ski film, but all ski films: If you love something deeply enough, no lark seems crazy.

While the film could have used a few female voices—there are no female skiers in the film, though many women lined the production teams for Red Bull — the bigger lesson of “We Can’t Not” resonates in its pure obsession with the art form.

For those who’ve struggled to wrangle their non-skier friends to the theaters, there is a story worth seeing here. For you and for them.

You can watch “We Can’t Not” for free on Red Bull TV, and in select theaters across the world.

It’s Halloween week and you still have no idea what you’re going to be. Everyone is “pretty tired” of you responding to what you are with an exhausted, “I just felt like running” in a goofy accent. It’s OK; we’ve all been there. And Trail Runner’s resident doodler and creative character costume expert, Bobby Peavey, has your back. He’s put together a curated list of archetypes from your local run club and Instagram feed that are sure to be a hit this spooky season.

This costume is perfect for your most bonk-vulnerable friends.  Dress them up as Bonkenstein and enjoy a night of constantly bringing them back from the dead with salty and sweet snacks.

Do you have the patience of a saint and the multitasking skills of Leslie Knope? Then the Race Director costume is the perfect choice for you. Your night is going to consist of making sure there are ample snacks for all, that trick or treating/holiday party schedules stay on track, that everybody stays safe and healthy, and about a dozen other things that everyone else surely overlooks.

When you select this costume for the spookiest night of the year, the assignment is clear: only speak in the past tense for the entire night. You’re full of nostalgia and cynical disdain for anything modern. You’re basically the Uncle Rico of the evening.

Time to update your watch to the current model, recharge your heart rate strap, and cover every inch of exposed skin with wearable storage.  Because the funnest part of your Halloween is going to be teaching all your friends about the newest and techiest gear on the market.

For this costume, it is crucial that you log more photos than miles.  You are in this costume purely for the likes and kudos. If you exit Zone 1 at any point, you’re doing it wrong.

No pacer or muling needed with this costume. Thanks to your vampire diet and a steady dose of nipple chafing, you’ve got all the nutrition you need to conquer any ultra distance!

#8246. How I Got Benighted (Twice) on Yosemite’s ‘Lost Arrow Chimney’

In the first installment in our Benighted series, Shino Jomoto shares with Climbing the weird and spooky tale from her night in the chimney on September 17, 2023—and what all climbers can learn from her epic.

With over two decades of climbing experience, Jomoto specializes in epics, which she defines as getting sandbagged on adventure multi-pitch climbs and big walls that take far longer than anticipated. But her biggest epic of all occurred in the storied chimney route (5.10a) up Lost Arrow Spire in Yosemite.

Earlier this week, a Yosemite Climbing Association (YCA) newsletter detailed the history of the Lost Arrow Spire, including the chimney route. First ascensionist John Salathé himself bailed near the top in 1946. The next year, he came back “for an all-out effort” that took over five days. “Pushing through the claustrophobic shadows of the Lost Arrow Chimney, Salathé and [Anton] Nelson endured searing heat, dehydration, and brutal physical exertion,” the YCA shared. “They spent four bivouacs dangling from crude hammocks tied to pitons driven into the wall.”

The Lost Arrow Chimney is also believed to contain a human skeleton. On March 19, 1961, 17-year-old Irving Smith died in a rappelling accident from the top. An American Alpine Club trip report shared that Smiths’ body remains in the chimney: “While a ranger and volunteer rescue party was preparing to attempt the difficult and dangerous removal, Smith’s parents and Park authorities determined that no further life should be risked, and that the body should remain at rest where it lay.”

A comment on the Mountain Project page of Yosemite’s Lost Arrow Chimney (5.10a) foreshadowed what was to come: “Don’t let the moderate grade fool you. After pitch 7, you are halfway done.” The Lost Arrow Chimney is 10 pitches.

Poor fitness, dehydration, and sleep deprivation conspired, and by pitch eight we needed headlamps. Too tired to continue, we did the only sensible thing: slept inside the chimney.

I started climbing in 2005, mostly out of a hatred for my corporate job. That led to years living out of a station wagon, trying to figure out how to rock climb. Fast forward decades later, I’m in the business of going on epics—a lot.

Jim Herson said you could write an entire print edition on just my epics alone. I’ve had near-death epics like lightning and hypothermia on a big wall. But I’ll put it this way: I can climb El Cap faster than I can climb the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The reason why I wanted to share this is that nine out of ten climbers will have an epic on the Lost Arrow. You might be able to climb 5.13, but try to climb 10 pitches of old-school chimney—see if you can still call yourself a 5.10 climber. I think everyone goes in with the confidence of the grade. Then they just get gut-punched by the old-schoolness of the climb.

On my Lost Arrow Chimney epic, we weren’t in danger. We never called YOSAR (Yosemite Search and Rescue). You’re just humbled in a silly way because it’s such a silly grade.

Aside from the likes of Chuck Pratt or old-school climbers, I don’t know anyone who’s ever redone this route. When you do a climb, you usually redo it. You want a redpoint or you go back again. Nobody is dumb enough to redo this climb. We’ve done it three times, so it really goes to show either how incredibly stupid we are, or how memorable of an epic it was that we just needed to clear the record.

The lore that Jim Herson shared with me was he knew a guy who climbed the Lost Arrow Chimney and then never rock climbed again. The reality is he went to med school and gave up climbing. But that was his last-ever climb. It just embodies the spirit of the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The first time John and I did Lost Arrow Chimney in 26 hours on October 5, 2019 as a party of three, and we were actually in decent shape.

The time we slept in the chimney a few years later, we were a party of two. We thought we were fit. But we did all the classic gumby moves. We got up too late and got lost on the approach. To get back on route, we had to rappel. It’s obvious on a topo where you should go, but at four o’clock in the morning, you get lost. And we didn’t bring enough water.

On the climb, we started losing daylight. My boyfriend started dry heaving from dehydration and lack of fitness. He stopped mid-pitch in a chimney—he couldn’t go on.

There’s nothing you can really say in the dark. We’re not Rocky Talkie people. We have too much pride for that. So we just had to communicate with a rope. Finally, I was on belay. I went up to him. We were mid-chimney—this wasn’t even a belay station.

John was like, “I can’t. I can’t do this anymore.” And he’s a 10-times better climber than I am. So I was like, “All right, I’ll go.” He was like, “Are you sure?” I was like, “We can’t sleep here. We can sleep in a lot of places. This is not a place to sleep.”

It’s always scary when a very experienced person says, “I’m scared.” John rarely says he’s scared. It takes courage to say that. When you’re in the dark, there’s nothing you do. You can’t start yelling and placating, you know? You just realize in that moment like, it’s a serious climb. And you’re still having to reconcile that with 10a.

So I went questing and found this chimney that was adjacent to the climb. It wasn’t a chimney you go through on route, but everyone goes by it.

We were two pitches from the notch. Should we suffer for six hours, then rappel and call it a day? Or suffer through the whole night? You make those calculations. We decided we might as well stay put, rather than burden resources to call for YOSAR or any sort of search and rescue. I think that’s the number one thing: Can you self-rescue?

We had brought a salad that we thought we were going to eat at the base. So we ended up at the bivy with a salad, but no water. It’s kind of hard to eat a salad without water. So all of my swear words were salad- or foliage-related. It doesn’t matter if you have a whole buffet, if you have no water, you don’t want to eat anything. So we were just staring at this salad in the chimney. It’s one of those things with the Maslow’s hierarchy—if you don’t have water, you can’t do anything.

We laid out both climbing ropes so that we were a little bit insulated from the ground. We did the bivy dance. It was flatter than most bivy spots I have slept on. We were really depressed, just waiting for daylight.

Back sleeping was impossible, so we were relegated to side sleeping for the next six hours. There was no way to sleep besides big spoon, little spoon. The walls were very cold. I put a giant sad face in chalk where I was. Another group went and did it later and said, “We knew where you bivvied ’cause there was a giant sad face.”

But we were so thirsty, the epic wasn’t over. We could hear Yosemite Falls. Our brains went: Maybe we can just hike over there. Another lesson is you’re not rational when you’re having an epic. So we lost another half day going to the falls. We were sitting in a pool of water that we couldn’t drink. And we realized we couldn’t cut over. So we had to go back. A day and a half later, we got back to the car.

Finally, on June 2, 2024, we got our redemption. We did it in a day and tagged the summit where people do the Tyrolean. It still took us all day—and we didn’t even free it. We had to pull on gear. It makes you respect the history of the first ascensionists—the lineage of people who have tried it and who have bailed. There’s an insane amount of really, really old bail slings.

You’re in there and it’s a vortex. It’s spooky. I’m not a mystical person, but there are hexes that have been kind of swallowed by the rock. It’s a freaking spooky museum of gear. When you’re in there, you have an appreciation for who climbed this before you and the style in which they climbed it, because it is terrifying.

I feel like I’ve gotten my chimney badge in Yosemite. There should be a club for it: the Lost Arrow Chimney Support Group. If you can summit the whole climb and rappel in a day, I would have mad respect. More people climb the Nose than the Lost Arrow Chimney. Anyone who’s dumb enough and adventurous enough to sign up for that level of masochism will resonate more with me than if you’re C1ing a 30-pitch climb.

If you survive nine or ten pitches of chimneys with your partner, you will be bonded forever, for better or worse. They’ve done all these studies about reality TV shows, like for love matchmaking. You put people in intense situations and they confuse their endorphins as romance, but it’s really just adrenaline. Part of it is trauma bonding. Some couples are more willing to climb the Lost Arrow Chimney than go to couples therapy.

The beauty of epics is there are way more fun memories than sending. Every sending story is so ephemeral. But when you’ve been sucker-punched so hard by something scary, or that requires lack of sleep, or incredible amounts of suffering, you remember those experiences for decades.

If you don’t have some delusional optimism, you will never get off the ground. That delusion will catch up to you at some point. But you have to have a little bit of fuel. As long as it’s not over your head or dangerous for you and others. Can you live well and safely enough to live another day? Go do it.

Delusion meets reality at some point, like when you’re having an epic. Benighted is a subcategory of epics—it’s in the taxonomy. There has to be some darkness involved, generally speaking, but you don’t need to have slept.

The easy way to know is when you end up at the parking lot, you see your best friends, and they’re like, “How was it?” The face doesn’t lie. You actually don’t need to say words. They see your face and they’re like, “That was an epic.”

John and I have an epic grading scale. It’s the reverse GPA.

Every time we finish, we rate them. The Lost Arrow Chimney was like a 5.0.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

Got your own tale of getting benighted? Submit it here.

#8245. Take a Break this Winter. Warren Miller’s ‘Days Off’ Is Coming to a City Near You.

After 77 years of iconic ski films, Warren Miller is asking a question never posed before: What do the world’s greatest skiers and snowboarders do on a day off?

Days Off celebrates skiing for skiing’s sake. This fall, Warren Miller’s new narrator and host, Katie Burrell, is taking audiences from backcountry laps to heli drops and the après in between with the world’s best to find out what they do when they slow down and rediscover the art of the day off.

Tickets are on sale now and run throughout North America until late December. Find a screening near you here.

Marty Shaffer, founder of backcountry ski company CaPow, knows how to take a day off. The film features his annual trip to Blanket Park Chalet in Revelstoke, British Columbia. Shaffer’s parents bought the helicopter-access-only A-frame cabin in 1986, a month before he was born.

“Back then, it was a bunch of granola munchers,” Shaffer told Outside. “For years growing up, it was hard to get people to ski with me.”

Now, he and his wife run guide-curated backcountry ski trips with their two young boys. Burrell was also Shaffer’s first employee, and bringing her back to the chalet held a special place in the film.

“The story and the segment are super meaningful for my family because we filmed, and then ten days later, we had our second kid,” Shaffer said. “It’s special to me because it’s a story that we were able to tell at a very specific time in our life, and the magic of our family.”

Shaffer invited Burrell on the friends-and-family trip, and when she accepted the Warren Miller hosting position, she asked if she could bring a film crew

“It’s a special time for us to be up there with family,” Shaffer said. “Working as a guide and having a small business, this is one of our only times to really enjoy Blanket with our family and away from all the chaos.”

Shaffer has been watching Warren Miller films for ages, and said this year’s film reflects on the importance of relationships, slowing down, taking time off, and getting outside.

The film includes seven other segments shot across three continents, taking audiences from the remote heli-skiing terrain of Alaska and high-alpine mountaineering of Chamonix, France, to legendary powder of Hokkaido, Japan, and the pristine slopes of Deer Valley, Utah. The journey continues through the heart of Canada’s best ski destinations—Whistler, Pemberton, and Banff—capturing the sport’s raw spirit through backcountry snowmobiling, skijoring, and endless alpine pursuit.

Burrell joins athletes and industry professionals on their days off—unscripted runs, backcountry lodges, and local traditions that live just beneath the ski industry’s surface.

Hundreds of showings are still on deck, spanning the U.S. and Canada. Some events will feature giveaways, others will have surprise guests, and all will build community and stoke excitement around our favorite season: winter

Other featured athletes include Sam Kuch, Craig Murray, Jess Kimura, Marie-France Roy, Christina Lustenberger, Guillaume “Gee” Pierrel, Craig McMorris, Sebastian Judge, Mark Sollors, Truth Smith, Court “Blackbird” Larabee, Mason Mashon, Kaylin Richardson, Ted Ligety, Chuck and Claudia Mumford, Pep Fujas, Sam Mitchell, Marty Schaffer, Kate VanHee, and Himari Takamori, Hinano Sakamoto, Shizuku Hanada, among others.

Warren Miller’s Days Off is presented with support from Mammut, Deer Valley, Brooks, REI Co-op, Swany, Silverton Mountain, DryBrew, and in production with Outside Studios.

#8244. At This Resort, the Owner is Driving a Snowcat, Turning Wrenches, and Fixing Broken Fences

I’d never ridden a ski lift with the person who owns the mountain below us before, so I’m not sure if this is common.

But as we chugged from the Ski Santa Fe’s base toward its 11,075-foot peak, Ben Abruzzo noted a chairlift returning to the base that sounded squeaky, a groomer that needed tending, and an orange safety fence that had fallen over. Abruzzo—whose day was charged with showing this writer around the mountain his family has owned since the mid-1980s—interrupted his responses to any of my questions on more than a few occasions, apologizing before speaking into a small walkie-talkie mounted on his chest. He instructed this person or that to address the various tiny issues that must pop up a million times a day on a mountain, acting more like a manager than the guy who owns the mountain.

Over the course of a single lift ride, it became clear how much Abruzzo not only cared about the experience of the roughly 250,000 visitors who enjoy his family’s mountain every year but also about the mountain itself. It makes sense once you realize that Ski Santa Fe is, in a way, woven into the very fabric of the person Abruzzo is.

“It’s all I’ve ever known,” said Abruzzo, as the lift neared Ski Santa Fe’s peak, the mountain he described as his “lifelong backyard.”

Owners and CEOs often love to say that their businesses are like a family. However, for the Abruzzos, Ski Santa Fe is not only their family business, but it’s their ancestral home.

Abruzzo is the third-generation owner of Ski Santa Fe, following in the footsteps of his grandfather, his father, and two of his uncles, who finalized the purchase of the mountain in 1985. It was hardly a lark, as the elder Abruzzo purchased the Sandia Peak Ski Area in nearby Albuquerque in the late 1950s.

Their familial sensibility permeates much of Abruzzo’s staff. His grooming manager has worked at the mountain for thirty years. His operations manager as well. The mountain’s ticketing manager bests them both, with 32 years of service.

“I think it’s because we treat our folks right,” Abruzzo said, pointing out that when he says ‘we,’ he doesn’t just mean his father, his late grandfather, his uncles, and any other Abruzzo who’s spent time working the mountain. “Our mountain manager, our operations manager, all of our full-time staff; they’re all invested because they’re all part of this community.”

Abruzzo started working on the mountain when he was 12, building mountain bike trails in the summer and working in the rental shop during the season. After commissioning as an infantry officer in 2001, Abruzzo deployed to Afghanistan with the Army’s 101st Airborne Division during the height of the Global War on Terror. Abruzzo returned home in 2005, working as an area manager at Sandia Peak. He relocated to Ski Santa Fe in 2010, eventually taking over the mountain shortly before the Covid-19 pandemic.

And even though he owns the ski area, Abruzzo still drives snowcats and still turns wrenches when chairlifts need tending. And he requires the same of all the mountain’s senior staff.

“We expect all of our managers to be well-versed in the blue-collar side of things,” he said. “And that includes me.”

Sitting high in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, Ski Santa Fe is about a 30-minute drive from the heart of the famously artsy city in northern New Mexico. Of course, snowy days and weekends might impact that commute time, Abruzzo admits, despite the fact that the mountain has its own dedicated road crew charged with plowing the two-lane road leading up to Ski Santa Fe. Still, as Ski Santa Fe is the only ski area in the vicinity, it’s a drive that never feels out of reach for locals and visitors alike.

In a more corporate environment, that dearth of options could provide owners an excuse to rest on their proverbial laurels. However, Abruzzo sees that scarcity as an honor to uphold. If people only have one option, it’d better be a good one.

With 88 total trails, almost evenly split across blacks, blues, and greens, a trio of terrain parks, and 1,800 feet of vertical drop, all serviced by a double lift, two triple lifts, two quad lifts, two surface lifts, and a high-speed detachable lift, the mountain is far bigger and more diverse than you might think when you hear “family-owned ski area.”

But beyond all that, Ski Santa Fe is known by locals and regulars for two main reasons: first, its off-piste skiing. And second, its snowmaking capabilities.

On the day we spent together, snow fell from the sky in big, thick flakes. It was one of the 20 or so powder days Ski Santa Fe gets each season. The tops of tall pine trees, buried in some 200 inches of snow, poked out of the thick layers of powder. It was a relatively unfamiliar sensation to this lifelong East Coaster who is far better versed in riding ice than powder.

Still, Abruzzo assured, even when it’s human-made, Ski Santa Fe’s snow is some of the best and most consistent there is.

“We make very dry snow,” he said before pointing out how the mountain’s 42 snow guns and five-million-gallon storage tank allow them to cover most of the mountain in snow throughout the season. “It’s dry to the point where we have had snow gun companies write us a custom setting. And what you get is a much nicer surface to ski on that stays nice longer.”

A little shy of halfway down one of our day’s runs, Abruzzo cut from one groomer to another and, suddenly, a rustic, two-story shack stood surrounded by a small sea of skiers and snowboarders, each of whom seemed to have a beer, a cocktail, or a hot chocolate in hand.

At 10,500 feet, on-mountain restaurant Totemoff’s sits higher than the peaks of many ski areas in North America.

And while there was no entertainment beyond some music playing over the speakers, Abruzzo assured me that Totemoff’s often plays host to live music. Above the bar, apartments for Abruzzo’s family and staff really hammer home the idea of how deeply entwined the Abruzzo family is 0n this mountain.

As we sat chatting over a pair of light beers, the talk eventually came back to the Abruzzo family, their lifelong marriage to this mountain. I ask him what it’s been like having three generations of Abruzzos run a mountain together. He quickly corrects me.

“Both of my kids work here,” he said with a laugh. “So, it’s actually four generations.”

#8243. After Testing 122 Pieces of Gear, We Found the Best Climbing Gear of Fall 2026

Gear testing above 12,000 feet on the golden granite of Chamonix's Aiguille du Midi. It's a hard job, but someone's got to do it. (Photo: Anthony Walsh)

Rock climbing season doesn’t end when snow hits the high country. Some of the best conditions of the year are right around the corner: cool temps, ample shade, and just the right amount of humidity in the air. Unless you’re sharpening your ice tools, don’t give up on the rock (or plastic) season just yet—with the right gear, you’re in for the best season of your life.

Climbing’s gear-testing team has spent all summer sweating it out with the latest and greatest so you don’t have to. We tested 28 harnesses, 27 pairs of climbing shoes, 30 pairs of approach shoes, 9 ropes, and 28 backpacks—a healthy mix of new items and longtime favorites. Some of the gear was good, some was great, and a lot of it missed the mark: bruised hips, sore feet, exploding packs—it’s all part of the gear-testing game.

2026 was the year of the hyper-specific shoe. Although notable all-arounders made it onto our list, the real highlights were the shoes who didn’t try to do too much. One shoe felt about as stiff as a crampon, with its new-age carbon insert, and powered us up numerous vert testpieces; another had about as much support as a woolen sock (but, like, in a good way!); and the best shoe I’ve ever used for offwidths is absolutely terrible for finger cracks. Perhaps 2026 is the year of the shoe quiver.

The harness is the one piece of gear that will make or break your day on the wall. In an effort to find the best climbing harness available, we put everything from fast-and-light alpine G-strings to beefy big-wallers to the test this year, taking them on trips from the cold Canadian alpine to the steep walls of Devil’s Tower to overhung sport routes at The Red.

Unlike this year’s crop of rock shoes, my favorite climbing packs worked hard to serve multiple niches. One versatile alpine-climbing pack carried anywhere from one to four days of mountain kit with ease. And a new haul bag might just be the last pack (and airplane carry on) a rock climber will ever need.

The best climbing ropes are a tough category of gear to review because, these days, almost all are well made and perform great right out of the package. It’s only after hard wear—climbing pitch after pitch in rain, snow, and ice, coiling and uncoiling on dirt and sand, and taking some big whippers—that a rope reveals its true colors.

Helmets are our best defense against rockfall and weird whippers while climbing outdoors. And after years of writing accident reports—often of climbers who took a seemingly benign fall, before something weird happened—I regularly note how fortunate the climber was to be wearing one. When shopping for a helmet, take the time to find one that’s comfortable, lightweight, breathable, and fits properly—because actually liking your helmet makes you far more likely to wear it.
