#8238. Backyard Ultras Are Booming. Here’s Why.

In quite the feat of boots-on-the-ground journalism, author Dan England raced Jess’ Backyard Ultra on August 9, 2024. (Don’t ask him about the race name grammar.) He also spoke with backyard ultra mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell, several other backyard ultra race directors, and key backyard ultra runners, including Harvey Lewis and Maggie Guterl. What he found is that the format of running a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until only one runner remains is about so much more than running in circles. Since this article was originally published on Outside Run in 2024, backyard ultras have further entered the mainstream with the rise of figures like Mark Dowdle, Belgium resetting the world record, and Team USA winning the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship.

It’s 8:55 P.M. on Friday, August 9, and I’m with a small group of runners huddled together in a tent on a farm near Greeley, Colorado, that momentarily shelters us from our bad life decisions.

Outside the tent awaits pouring rain and a mushy race course complete with the “Plank of Doom”—a pink makeshift “bridge” adorned in purple twinkle lights suspended four feet over a drainage ditch full of stormwater.

Before the starting gun of this backyard ultra goes off in five minutes, Jessy Nelson needs to make an announcement. I’m assuming it will be about safety. Instead, she tells us that she is not a narcissist.

Yes, Jess’ Backyard Ultra does carry her name. But she named the race for about a dozen friends, all named Jess. (Seriously!). She met them all in an online chat group during a 1,000-kilometer Great Virtual Race Across The States.

Nelson started the race on her farm for them in 2021 with the hope that one Jess could run far enough to qualify for Big’s Backyard Ultra—the original Bell Buckle, Tennessee, “backyard ultra” event that pioneered a quirky new kind of endurance racing format in which runners must complete a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until they can no longer accomplish the task.

For the record, this event is Jess’ Big Backyard Ultra, not Jessy’s. Understand?

We nod as the rain comes down harder. It would be a fun, goofy, quaint little race that seems to match the aesthetic of many backyard ultras across the world, except it’s been raining for three days, transforming the dirt roads on which we will run into what seems like gooey Jello pudding.

Nelson is worried. The Plank of Doom is seriously dangerous, she tells us. Sure, it’s pink and twinkly, but the four-foot fall that could result with any misstep could mean a broken ankle or, according to Nelson’s narrowed eyes, instant death. Nelson is so serious about the plank that she forces the four of us competing to vote to keep it on the course instead of bypassing it through a paved road 100 yards to the south. We vote to keep it, 3-1.

It’s hard to take anything Nelson says seriously, given that this is a race seemingly held on the set of Little House on the Prairie and that a stuffed toy squirrel named Skittles awaits us in a rocking chair at the turnaround to our 4-ish-mile loop. One of the Jesses befriended a squirrel in her backyard, you see, and that’s a tribute to her. Nelson once befriended an eagle, who would follow her during her daily 10-mile loops around her property. But now, she presumes, the eagle is taking cover. We are about to do the opposite.

Nelson’s odd race is now one of an estimated 500 backyard ultras held around the world that are certified by concept creator Gary Cantrell. You may know him as Lazarus Lake, or simply Laz. He is  probably the sport’s most famous race director and certainly  the quirkiest. Cantrell is known first and foremost for creating the Barkley Marathons, a grueling 100-plus-mile largely off-trail race in Tennessee that’s considered to be the world’s hardest running race to complete. While there’s only one Barkley Marathons, Cantrell’s backyard race format has boomed over the past five years or so.

There is no predefined end length or time in a backyard ultra, as long as multiple runners can complete each 4.167-mile loop within an hour. (Cantrell chose that peculiar distance because running 4.167 miles per hour is exactly what it takes to run 100 miles in 24 hours.) A race ends when only one runner remains to complete a lap and is declared the winner, while all other runners are relegated to did not finish (DNF) status with whatever total number of laps they are able to complete. The runner who completes the second-most laps in a race is often referred to as the “assist,” in the sense that their effort is ultimately what determines how long the race is allowed to continue.

Most backyard races are not like Cantrell’s Big’s Backyard Ultra, which, even though it maintains a grassroots feel, has gained worldwide fame and is filled with elite runners. Most backyard races are more like Nelson’s: small, fun and grueling little get-togethers that last a couple days and bring most runners to tears. Most backyard race directors are like Nelson, too; they have“real” jobs outside of race directing and simply love the format and camaraderie their events foster amid runners of all ability levels pushing  themselves beyond what they ever thought possible.

When Cantrell started his race and named it after his pit bull, Big, in 2012, he hoped to have enough interest for just one event. He was pleasantly surprised when people asked if there would be another race the following  year. Now tens of thousands will likely tune in to the livestream to watch this year’s race on October 19. Cantrell guesstimates more than 25,000 people have run in a backyard ultra event this year, and those are just in the races he’s certified: He knows there are probably dozens more who don’t bother with the paperwork.

“The continued growth really has been a surprise for me,” Cantrell said. Indeed, there are backyard races in 83 countries now.  Even the renowned Tarahumara tribe of Indigenous people from Chihuahua, Mexico, (aka the Raramuri people, who were profiled in the 2009 New York Times bestseller Born to Run,) have their own race, Cantrell noted.

Cantrell relishes putting on the world’s hardest events, almost to a sadistic degree. Only 20 individuals have finished the Barkley Marathons since he began it in 1986. It’s a race as ominous as its location, Frozen Head State Park in Tennessee. The race, over 100 miles with a staggering 65,000-feet-plus of elevation gain, is a miserable quest for survival through thorn-infested bramble, often terrible weather, and ridiculously steep hills on a “course” with no real route.

He started Big’s as another way to test people, and at times, it resembles Stephen King’s The Long Walk, a fictional horror story about 100 walkers who are forced to trudge hundreds of miles and are shot when they quit. Big’s format is also horrifyingly simple: Run 4.167 miles, a “yard,” in under an hour, and then line up and do it again, and again, and again, on the hour, until one person is left. No breaks from the on-the-hour start are allowed, not even to use the porta-potty, but if you finish the yard early, you can eat and drink to your heart’s content, sleep a few minutes, and yes, answer nature’s call. Last year’s winner, accomplished Cinncinnati ultrarunner Harvey Lewis, set a world record by running 450 miles over 108 hours—or four and a half days.

Cantrell now finds himself surprised not only by the race format’s popularity but also the allure many runners have found in the design. These backyard races are, like Nelson’s race, more about community and the comradery of people pushing each other to go farther than they ever have than about fighting your competitors to the near death. While the format becomes exponentially more grueling over time as variables like sleep deprivation escalate, for the first 24 hours or so, the backyard ultra format is an approachable way for many to cover a very long distance. And Cantrell admits that he likes what these mom and pop backyard races have become.

“There are a lot of aspects to it that I didn’t really consider,” he said. “I do know we get a lot of people who never thought they could ever run an ultra. It’s a race for everyone.”

Cantrell thought of the idea for a backyard race close to 50 years ago, when he was in high school struggling to keep up with the fast kids on his track team during interval workouts. He noticed by the end of an interval he was often a little closer to their heels.

“I’d get left in the dust early, but eventually, I’d wear them down,” he said. “So in a 4-mph race, I thought I could beat everybody.”

The idea stayed in the recesses of his mind until he could do something about it on his property in central Tennessee. He didn’t have the money to put on a big race, but with the format, all he needed was a stopwatch.

“This format doesn’t require very much,” Cantrell said. “I think that’s why it’s caught on.”

It’s also caught on because it’s spectator-friendly—both online and in person—perhaps more so than any other race not on a track. It not only made a household name out of Lewis but acted as a coming-out party for Courtney Dauwalter when the two went head-to-head for nearly 20 hours in 2020 and ran a total of 283 miles before Dauwalter outlasted him by a lap and won. Cantrell said this was another aspect of the race he didn’t consider, and it’s partly what makes it fun.

“Women are on an equal competitive footing with men,” he said, and indeed, Maggie Guterl also won Big’s Backyard Ultra, now considered the format’s national championship, in 2019.

The format, Cantrell said, is supposed to measure willpower, not VO2 max or speed or other aspects of physiological talent. There are enough races for that. Instead, Big’s measures grit—the one thing he had over those speedy, more talented guys on the track in high school.

“The most challenging part,” Cantrell said, “should be the distance between the chair and the starting corral.”

Tens of thousands were captivated last year by Lewis’s win, his second at Big’s Backyard, which Cantrell now livestreams and provides real-time written commentary. Lewis was already well known for winning the 135-mile Badwater Ultramarathon in 2014, but he wasn’t taken seriously as a trail runner when he first entered Big’s in 2017, he said.

“I like the trails though,” Lewis said. “I’m very strategic. They were doing it wrong. Everyone was running up the first hill, and I was in the back, just walking up. The next day, everyone walked up the hill.”

Lewis kept going even after making a lap by just a second. He eventually gave in after 200 miles, taking the assist, but it made him wonder just how far he could go. He decided to devote part of his life to it.

“Big’s is so great,” Lewis said. “You’re walking into an ultimate game board, with strategy, perseverance, and skill level. The course itself is nothing special, and it’s usually that way with a lot of them. The genius is behind the format.”

Lewis races at Big’s to win, no doubt, but as a teacher at the School for Creative and Performing Arts in Cincinnati his living does not depend on it. (Good thing, as there’s no prize money anyway.), Despite his competitive drive, he’s learned to relish in the non-competitive moments on the course and treasures his two assists as much as his wins.

Last year, he says his goal was as much to help get runners through the third night as it was to outlast them all. He remembers 2020 mostly for the way he and Dauwalter spent nearly a full day and night taking turns leading the race and pushing each other to approach 300 miles, a number that was, at the time, unheard of to run in this format. Lewis called it a “collaboration” instead of a race. It was a much-needed feel-good story during the pandemic delivered by two nice people.

“We were very encouraging of each other,” Lewis said.

This is one of the evolutions of the race that took Cantrell by surprise: Backyard races build community among runners with different ability levels because of the unique format. Many other ultras around the world are in intimidating places for beginners, but the accessible four-mile loop obliterates those fears.

Mandy Mullen, the owner of run.Windsor in Windsor, Colorado, changed the format from a 50K to a backyard race for her Weld Your Mettle ultramarathon because it helped foster that community aspect.

“There’s so much more to running than just running,” Mullen said. “In this the competition goes away, and it’s more teamwork. There’s zero of, ‘I want to beat this person.’”

Katie Stroud is the president of a running and walking club that’s existed since 1979 in Alice Springs, a small town in the desert of Australia. She hosted the second annual backyard ultra this year as a part of the races the club puts on.

“It’s such a terrific format for people to push their distance in such a wonderful and supportive way,” Stroud said. “It’s so much more than people running in circles.”

Indeed, Cantrell believes more people ran 100 miles in 24 hours, a benchmark so elite that races usually give out special belt buckles to those who do it, this year in backyard events than all the other ultramarathons around the world combined. The final two left standing this year in Alice Springs, Stroud said, were running buddies who just wanted to push each other to 100 miles.

“There are all these little moments like that in our event every year,” Stroud said. “It’s really cool to be there for that.”

Carl Worth was another one who caught the backyard bug. Even though he’d never run more than a half marathon, he ran the virtual backyard race during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020 and astonished himself by covering 54 miles. He liked the camaraderie and community of backyard running so much he began organizing the Banana Slug Backyard Ultra the following year in Oregon’s Champoeg State Park.

At this year’s event, the winner ran for 49 hours and 200 miles for a “Silver Ticket,” which qualifies him for Big’s Backyard, since the Slug was one of the six events where the winner qualified him for the World Team Championships.

But Worth prefers not to focus only on the winner. During the race, he puts up a spreadsheet on a TV—he’s a software engineer by trade—and posts everyone’s longest distance they’ve run. Whenever they break it, and many do, they can ring a bell, a tradition that Cantrell established at his own race. At this year’s Banana Slug event, 34 runners surpassed their personal bests.

“It’s a really satisfying thing to put on as a race director,” Worth said. “You get to see some amazing things.”

This is true for Jess’ Backyard Ultra as well. The sun rises, illuminating the gray sky and shining some welcome light on our muddy trails. Nelson decides to take a small nap at the house. Our fourth competitor rolled her ankle in the wee hours of the morning, making my friend, Bret Naber, the winner after 30 miles, but we decided to run through the night and see how far we could go. At 9 A.M., after 12 hours and 50 miles of running through the mud, we go home for a shower and some sleep.

This year’s Big’s Backyard Ultra on October 19 is the biannual international team competition, called the World Satellite Backyard Team Competition. Team USA will compete at Cantrell’s event in Tennessee, and the 15-member U.S. roster will have at least two women, Megan Eckert, who won the Saguaro Showdown Backyard Ultra in Mesa, Arizona, and Jennifer Russo, who won Ohio’s Backyard Ultra, as well as Lewis and Scott Martin, the three-time winner of the Banana Slug race put on by Worth.

Cantrell said there are 68 national teams, the members of which will compete simultaneously in backyard ultras in their home countries to earn points for their teams. It’s much like the Olympics—with each country enjoying a home field advantage—and it makes you wonder if this event will finally get ultrarunning there.

“I think you have to reasonably see how it goes,” Cantrell said. “A lot of things start up, and they are really popular, and then they fade out. Maybe somebody more politically skilled than me could get it there.”

But Cantrell’s favorite part about the race format isn’t the superstars, even if his own includes some of the most elite ultrarunners in the world. It’s that time isn’t a factor. It’s about the distance you run, and if you run a personal best, you get recognized for it, even if you finish 30 seconds before the bell.

“The age groups in other races are won by the same people over and over,” Cantrell said. “But in this one, everyone has their day.”

#8237. Space Mirrors Promise Daylight in the Dark, But Rescue Teams Aren’t Convinced

A floodlight operated by Reflect Orbital illuminates the night sky. (Photo: Kern County Sheriff’s Office)

In the middle of a dark night on the foothills of Mt. Whitney, onlookers were suddenly flooded by a cone of light 3 miles wide by 10 miles long.

The source was a high-powered floodlight, placed nearby as part of a test exercise by a startup called Reflect Orbital. The Los Angeles-based company’s mission is to “launch the future of sunlight” by placing a swarm of mirrored satellites in low Earth orbit built to redirect sunlight anywhere on Earth on demand. The ground-based floodlight was designed to mimic that effect.

Among a wide range of use cases including agriculture, entertainment, and defense, the company claims rescue as one potential use of its tech in the coming years.

On a country road outside Lone Pine, California, a handful of seasoned rescue volunteers and public safety officials would find out how much — if any — a light field roughly the size of Manhattan and twice as bright as a full moon would improve their chances.

Phillip Cash, operations leader for China Lake Mountain Rescue Group, said his team arrived at the site with optimism.

“My team is largely scientists, engineers, technicians,” he told DarkSky International. “We live for this sort of stuff.”

Group leaders reported to the San Francisco Chronicle and DarkSky International that they envisioned very limited uses for the technology in rescue. They struggled with glare, saw little promise of benefit for helicopter crews, and realized the light could also shut off unexpectedly.

In the test, China Lake MRG and Inyo County SAR rehearsed standard search-and-rescue tasks twice — once in the dark, once under the big light. Crews ran grid searches, stretcher carries, and rope rigging.

Cash first noticed the light made it easier to move around on the ground. His peripheral vision was improved, he told DarkSky, and he didn’t have to worry about stepping in a hole.

But from there, the efficacy mostly faded.

Glare was an issue. While that may or may not be the case with a satellite as the source, Cash noted most rescuers already wear hats at night for this very reason. Limiting any light from the sky or ambient sources preserves night vision.

Another limiting factor of the test was that the organizers placed white pylons in the field as rescue targets, instead of the usual manikins. This created artificial reflectivity that helped Cash’s team find their marks more easily. But, he told DarkSky, his team realized the light could have a problematic effect on actual human subjects — especially anyone lost.

“They’re more likely to go, ‘Oh, look at all this light. Maybe I can find my way back now,’” he said.

Cash was also doubtful it would help SAR helicopter crews locate or navigate at night, noting they already use night vision as standard practice.

His takeaway: For the most part, it’s better to leave the daylight in the daytime.

“It’s not going to make a huge difference to wilderness search and rescue except in a few cases,” Cash told the Chronicle. “We’re pretty good at working at night already.”

Officials’ minds remain open to the technology. A spokesperson for the Kern County Sheriff’s Office told Backpacker that they intend to let SAR groups lead the way on any future implementation. That’s particularly the case with a team like China Lake MRG, a nonprofit that supports its equipment bills mainly through fundraising.

“Given the circumstances, if we needed it, it would definitely be something we would utilize,” said Lori Meza, Kern County Public Information Officer. “But we have no idea what it would cost.”

That price tag could be a real issue. While Reflect Orbital has not officially published any pricing information for its prospective services, Sky & Telescope reported that the company plans to charge around $5,000 per hour for its services, with constellations of multiple satellites — necessary to recreate the kind of bright conditions the team experienced — costing far more. (By comparison, an Airbus H125 helicopter, like the Kern County Sheriff’s Office operates, costs about $2,500 an hour to run, according to charter operator Craft.)

“Most search and rescue teams, at least in California, will not be able to afford it,” Cash told DarkSky. “They won’t even think about affording it. We cannot pay for that sort of thing.”

Emphasizing that any cost was still unknown, Meza said Kern County officials only buy equipment for SAR teams in limited cases. She gave the example of a purchase of vehicles several years ago.

“We do provide certain resources, and there might be an isolated case here or there,” she said. “But a purchase like a contracted service would be a new thing.”

She added that the Sheriff’s Office isn’t taking a position on the technology itself, and that they were grateful to be part of the test.

Other observers are less neutral. DarkSky International has functioned as a sort of public watchdog on Reflect Orbital, lobbying for what it sees as responsible development. Its five principles of outdoor lighting have been widely adopted, and published by the U.S. Department of Energy.

DarkSky sees the same gap in the technology for rescue as China Lake MRG — usefulness, which is also principle one of five.

“The first question is ‘is it needed?’” said Drew Reagan, DarkSky senior marketing and communications manager. “And in this case, the rescue groups found the need was pretty minimal.”

Many of the potential impacts of Reflect’s plan are unknown, because the government has allowed it to move forward with no environmental review.

If its plans become reality, the change in the night environment could be massive. The Federal Communications Commission has given the green light for Reflect to launch its first functional satellite. Its launch plan would place 50,000 in orbit by 2035. Even if they weren’t de facto floodlights, Reagan pointed out, the reflectivity of that many satellites alone would noticeably brighten the night sky everywhere on Earth.

“This represents a fundamentally new technology that will have a direct impact. Not only for the dark sky community or astrotourists, but for migratory birds, for insects,” Reagan said. “It’s not DarkSky’s goal to plunge the world into medieval darkness. We want to be part of these conversations. We just want to make sure we look before we launch.”

#8236. My Ski Helmet Looks Perfectly Fine. Here’s Why I’m Replacing It Anyway.

Last February, on the final day of SKI’s annual ski test, I caught an edge in variable snow conditions while testing carving skis. I went, as we say, over the handlebars, landing directly on top of my head and compressing my neck.

I knew I’d hit my head, but at the time, I didn’t think much of it. It wasn’t until the following day that I began to understand how hard I’d actually hit the snow.

A few days later, I was sitting in my doctor’s office being diagnosed with a concussion and a neck injury. For months afterward, I dealt with headaches, neck pain, and sensitivity to light and sound. Some nights I’d wake up at 3 or 4 a.m. with pain radiating from the base of my skull, unable to get comfortable enough to fall back asleep. The hardest part was how unpredictable it all felt. I’d think I was getting better, only to have the symptoms flare up again.

The good news? I was wearing a helmet that may have spared me a much more serious head injury. The bad news? Now I have to throw that helmet away.

If I hadn’t developed concussion symptoms, I probably wouldn’t have thought twice about wearing it again. My helmet was brand new, and from the outside, there’s no obvious damage. But apparently, that says little about what’s going on underneath.

Needing a little extra convincing to toss out what looks like a perfectly good, well-fitting helmet, I turned to Madelen Fahlstedt, Ph.D., a biomechanical specialist at MIPS, a helmet-safety technology company. Fahlstedt holds a doctorate in medical engineering from Sweden’s KTH Royal Institute of Technology, where she researched head-injury biomechanics and accident reconstruction.

She explains that most ski helmets contain a layer of expanded polystyrene (EPS) foam designed to absorb impact energy by compressing or deforming. Once it takes a serious hit, that deformation is permanent, meaning the affected foam can’t absorb the same energy again.

“The outer shell can hide these deformations in the EPS. Even from the inside of the helmet, the deformations can be hard to detect,” Fahlstedt says. “To that sense, a helmet is essentially a one-hit-wonder.”

Traditional ski helmets are designed primarily to absorb the energy of an impact, particularly the forces associated with linear motion, when your head strikes something and comes to an abrupt stop. These forces can cause serious injuries, including skull fractures.

But real-world ski crashes aren’t always so straightforward.

When your head hits the snow at an angle, it can also rotate suddenly. That rotational motion can cause different parts of the brain to move relative to one another, stretching delicate tissues.

“The brain is typically more sensitive to rotational motion than linear motion because it has shear properties similar to water or gel,” Fahlstedt explains.

Both linear and rotational forces can contribute to brain injuries, which is why some helmet manufacturers have introduced technologies designed to address rotational motion.

MIPS, for example, doesn’t manufacture helmets. Rather, it develops safety technology that manufacturers can incorporate into their designs. So you might find a MIPS system inside a Smith helmet or a Giro helmet, even though the two models look, fit, and function differently.

Its best-known technology allows a layer inside the helmet to move about 10 to 15 millimeters during certain angled impacts. That small amount of movement is designed to reduce the rotational motion transferred to your head. Depending on the helmet, the layer might be visible or built into the padding.

MIPS is just one approach, however, and no technology can guarantee protection against concussion.

In fact, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is clear that no helmet is concussion-proof. Still, helmets provide meaningful protection. According to a 2022 review by the American Academy of Pediatrics, skiers and snowboarders who wear helmets have roughly 34 percent lower odds of suffering a head injury than those who don’t.

According to Fahlstedt, a helmet should be replaced after a significant impact, regardless of whether there’s visible damage.

The challenge, of course, is figuring out what counts as significant.

A helmet that rolls off a tailgate or gets knocked against the chairlift safety bar isn’t necessarily in the same category as one that absorbs the force of your head hitting hardpack. But a crash doesn’t have to look or feel dramatic to involve substantial forces.

Mine certainly didn’t. Without the concussion diagnosis, I’m not sure I would have considered it a significant impact at all. But as the CDC notes, concussion symptoms can take hours or even days to appear, so how you feel immediately after a crash isn’t necessarily a reliable indicator of injury. If you suspect a concussion, stop skiing and seek medical evaluation.

The same cautious approach applies to your helmet. When in doubt, err on the side of caution. Based on Fahlstedt’s advice and helmet manufacturer guidance, here’s when to replace your ski helmet and what to look for when buying a new one:

These standards establish minimum safety requirements, but they don’t tell you how one helmet compares with another. For that, Fahlstedt points to Virginia Tech’s Snow Sport Helmet Ratings, one of the most respected independent resources for comparing helmet safety.

Its ratings include 56 snowsports helmets and evaluate their performance in laboratory tests measuring both linear and rotational head motion. Rather than simply passing or failing a safety test, helmets receive a one- to five-star rating, giving skiers another way to compare their options. You can compare those ratings with SKI’s 2027 Winter Gear Guide, where we selected the eight best ski helmets for resort and backcountry skiing from 36 models we tested. Our hands-on testing evaluates factors like fit, comfort, ventilation, and usability on the mountain.

It’s tempting to look at nearly new gear, especially something that wasn’t cheap, and convince yourself it’s probably fine. But a helmet isn’t like a scratched pair of goggles or a jacket with a torn sleeve that can make it through another season with a little duct tape.

Mine has already done its job once. I’m not asking it to do it again.

#8235. The Dean Fidelman Interview: 6 Photos, 6 Decades

A portrait of Dean Fidelman in 1971, the year he arrived in Yosemite. (Photo: Warren Shelton)

Dean Fidelman arrived in the Yosemite Valley in 1971 as a teenager. Yosemite has been his home ever since—except for a blip in the ‘80s, when he set aside his passion for climbing to become a fashion photographer in New York City and Los Angeles. But a phone call saved him from what was, for him, soulless commercial work.

It was Lynn Hill who called, asking Fidelman to start making climbing photos again. She invited him to come shoot her on some climbs in Europe, where he also first met Chris Sharma. From there, he doubled down on his life’s mission to show “the art of rock climbing,” in his words.

Fidelman spent the first half of his career shooting in black and white on film cameras, including a Pentax 6×7. He processed his own film and developed his own photos—sometimes by night in the historic Yosemite darkroom of Ansel Adams. Eventually, he caught up with the times when filmmaker Renan Ozturk gave him a Sony a7R II mirrorless camera and he made the switch to digital—and full color. “In my viewfinder, I set the preview to black and white, but the capture contains full color,” Fidelman told Climbing.

Now, 55 years after arriving in Yosemite, Fidelman still calls the area home and continues to shoot climbers around Camp 4. Perhaps best known for his work capturing the Yosemite Stonemasters and Stone Monkeys, Fidelman has also sat down for interviews in a couple documentaries released this year, including The Dark Wizard about Dean Potter, and a film about the weed plane that crashed in Yosemite, enriching many of his friends.

Fidelman is also known for his Stone Nudes, nude portraits of climbers bouldering or free soloing. He started the series in 1999 and now estimates it runs 300 images deep. At least a few times a year, he still receives requests from climbers to shoot a Stone Nude—a phrase which he has tattooed on his hands.

We caught up with Fidelman to discover the changes and throughlines he’s observed across six decades of Yosemite photography, the challenges of revisiting his relationship with Dean Potter for The Dark Wizard, and the next iteration of the Stone Nudes project. For this retrospective interview, we also asked Fidelman to select one photo for each decade of his work, which you’ll find below.

This interview has been edited for clarity and concision.

Dean Fidelman: As the decades have progressed, the way that I think about making a photograph has changed. But the people haven’t changed as much. With the Stonemasters, I was just making photographs of my friends doing cool things in the desert. I wasn’t really thinking about anything besides trying to make the best photograph I could—and finding out what a good photograph was.

With the Stone Monkeys, from the late ’90s until 2010 or 2015, I was simply living in Yosemite in the meadow, sleeping down by the river. So I fit in financially with this group of people really well. When I asked someone to make a photograph with me, there was no hesitation.

Recently, I’ve done some photographs for Summit Journal of people on YOSAR [Yosemite Search and Rescue] and at Camp 4. The first thing someone would say when I asked if I could make their photograph was, “I’d be honored.”

That kind of put me on the back foot in a weird way. If I ask to make a photograph of you, it’s because I respect you, or there’s something about you that I really enjoy being around or seeing. So it’s more like you’re honoring me, because you’re going to be vulnerable in front of my camera for a moment. Once we get over that, it’s just like working with the people I’ve always worked with.

Fidelman: When Lynn reconnected with me, it was pretty much immediate—”there it is.” You think of your path in a linear way that leads to being the best at something, but that’s not how it works. I was doing my photography much more personally than commercially. When Lynn connected with that, I thought, “Oh yeah, the personal aspect of photography, I can do that.” She definitely sponsored me and opened that world back up.

Fidelman: Charles Cole at Five Ten and John Bachar at Boreal both used me for ads. But Charles especially would say, “Here’s $500, here’s $1,000. Here’s my camera. Just give me some photos, but make what you’ve always made—no pressure.”

When I got back into Yosemite, one of the first people I met was Dean Potter. He was super open to me. I met him through Bachar because they were giving him shoes at the time and wanted to make some photographs. We had an immediate kinship, and that brought me deeper in with the Stone Monkeys. Then you had Cedar Wright, who was just starting off at that moment in time, and everyone else just came out of that.

With the people who survived—and the people who didn’t—I realized I was making this visual record of friends, trying to express them in the moment. That’s what I’ve hopefully continued to do.

Fidelman: Honestly, my opinion hasn’t changed since the ’70s. It wasn’t like I just happened by when Bachar or Yabo [John Yablonski] or somebody was doing a solo. Sometimes Bachar would say, “Hey, I’ve got this thing figured out now and I’m going to do it. I want you to make the photographs.” Three or four of us would jump in his van, go down to wherever the solo was, and make these photographs.

Even back then, climbing magazines did not want to publish [free soloing photos]. I didn’t take it personally. The first publication that published my work was the National Enquirer. It was a picture of Bachar soloing with a headline like “Man Climbs Rock” or “Daredevil Climbs Rock.”

So I experienced both ends of the spectrum early on. I realized that what you’re making isn’t going to be universally accepted. But you’re doing it for the people who are doing these solos and the people who appreciate it. I wasn’t making all this stuff happen; it was happening in front of me and has continued across generations.

Fidelman: When film crews called 10 years after Dean Potter died to make a film, I was really kind of conflicted, but I approached it as professionally as I could. They showed me a rough cut of all four episodes. After I watched, I went into this horrible depression that I just got out of in the last couple months.

Fidelman: It made him very real again. Suddenly, I still think he’s alive. He’s existing. I can feel his presence, trying to come up really close to me and intimidate me—his voice and everything. Obviously, it’s storytelling, but it’s made me really question a lot of what happened and a lot of who I was. I think hopefully I’ve gotten that straightened out.

Fidelman: It means having a high respect for unspoken boundaries—how you carry yourself in that moment, what your objective is, and what you can ask of the person in front of you. With Stone Nudes especially, they are naked and vulnerable. There’s all kinds of trust going on there. You respect unspoken boundaries by observing someone to see how open they are to direction. But I’ve also found women have been mansplained with men trying to tell them how to climb.

And then with your friends, you’re on an intimate level because they know you, but suddenly there’s a camera up. They’ve seen your work and they’re honored. So you need to try to get rid of that awkwardness by bringing your energy back and refocusing.

Fidelman: I’m still working on the Valley Muse book. I made some new Stone Nudes this March that I really like, so I’m looking at calendars or possibly a book, gathering for another five or six years, traveling to favorite spots and places I’ve always wanted to go to.

Fidelman: There are a couple of photographs I want to make in Patagonia. It’s just a boulder in the middle of nowhere—and there was so much nowhere. There’s also a cool volcanic place in Venezuela. But next, I’m heading to Spain to work on deep-water soloing nudes in Mallorca.

Fidelman: Probably 2018, right when I stopped with the Stone Nudes calendar and Renan [Ozturk] gave me that camera. That’s probably the last time I went into a darkroom, unless the darkroom had a scanner in it and I was scanning my negatives. With a lot of my original black and white photography, I would process the film myself. I used to find these traditional photo labs up and down the coast.

After the last lab closed, I used Ansel Adams’s darkroom in Yosemite. They would let me use the darkroom from 10 at night until midnight. What was left of it was just a long sink and a heavy dark curtain. I’d be rattling cans at midnight and I look over and there’s a portrait of Ansel looking at me like, “What are you doing in my darkroom?”

Fidelman: Once I was shooting in the middle of the Merced River by the 120/140 junction. A friend was on top of the boulder posing while I was waist-deep in the river. Suddenly, a big tour bus pulled over and a bus-load of tourists piled out, pushing each other trying to take photos with their phones.

One time I was making photographs in Eldorado Canyon on that boulder right in the middle of the river with my friend Anora, a hippie. I went back to Yosemite and processed the film in Ansel Adams’s darkroom. I’m hanging out at the lodge and this person comes up to me—obviously a climber, but very clean-cut. He goes, “Excuse me, are you Dean Fidelman?” And I go, “Yeah.”

He sticks his hand out, with this big smile on his face and goes, “I want to shake your hand. You were in Eldorado Canyon about a month ago and you were making some photos. We were on the Bastille and oh my God, she is so beautiful. That was the most amazing day. My partner went home and bought a calendar even though he knew she wasn’t going to be in that one. But is she going to be in the next one?”

Then I made a Stone Nude of my friend Brian Ludovici, who’s a wonderful human and a super cool boulderer. He asked if I would make a photograph of him on Midnight Lightning (V8) with his clothes on. So I show up there and he’s just got this pair of short shorts on, right? This is his favorite boulder problem. He loves it. He worships it. And he goes up it and down it. I say, “Hey, man. You think you could do it nude?” Maybe four or five of his friends are there, all egging him on. He gets to where he’s pressing out the mantle, but he couldn’t do it. He put his shorts back on.

Then there’s this guy running full blast toward me from 100 yards away. He looks really closely at Brian. Then he stops and goes, “Dude, this was the most amazing day of my life. I looked from over there by the kiosk and there was a beautiful nude woman doing Midnight Lightning, so I started running to get a closer look. But it’s a dude.”

Fidelman: One fall. My friend Joey was like, “Let’s make a photograph.” I first met her when she was 16. She goes, “I want to make a photograph.” I go, “No, no.” Same with [Chris] Sharma. I go, “No, you have to wait until you’re 18.”

A couple years later, she’s in Joshua Tree and wants to climb the White Rastafarian (V2). First, I tell her she has to do it with her clothes and shoes on, so I can see that she can do it. She does it perfectly. But she can’t do it barefoot. So, she took her clothes off and we had a bunch of pads down, hidden by the bushes. Three of her friends were spotting.

She gets up to the crux and starts to bring her hand up and she blows. Her friends didn’t even touch her. She hit the pads, but sprained her ankle fairly badly. I felt really horrible, but I did put it in [a calendar]. I always make certain that [climbers] can do it at least with their clothes on first. Now I always tell the spotters, “If you’ve got to get in the photo, don’t even worry about it. Put your hands on them, even though they’re naked!” Unless somebody wants to solo something, but it’s not going to be outside the limits—ever.

Fidelman: I’m working on two books. One is a history of the Nose with John Long, Hans Florine, Ed Hartouni, and Sarah Conley. The other is a book on the Stone Monkeys with James Lucas. We’re getting the manuscripts and photo selections organized, with plans to publish over the next couple of years.

Fidelman: I’ve been working on archiving all the stuff from the ‘60s and Glen [Denny] was a huge influence on me, as well as Tom Frost and and a few others.

I understood two things very early on. One is if you’ve tied into a rope with people who have climbed with people like John Salathé and Royal Robbins, you’ve tied into a rope with all those other people, too. I tied into a rope with [Jim] Bridwell and lots of people that probably go back all the way to Salathé.

When John Long and I made the Stonemaster book, it was a fulfillment of my dream to make a book, but also of the understanding that if we allow those stories to die, we have no magic. All our beliefs are based on those stories and those legends.

I’m hoping maybe someone shows up, and I don’t care who they are. If I can see that passion and they’re really looking to provide that rope that we can all tie into, then my work would move forward.

#8234. The 7 Best Men’s Base Layers of 2027

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

What to know: Our team of expert testers wore 46 bottoms and tops made of natural and synthetic materials for skiing, running, and other winter activities. Their months of evaluation resulted in naming the Stellar Merino Base Top and Tights as the best overall base layer for men for its comfort and moisture management. Most versatile is the Flylow Hanmer Wool Baselayer Top for under $100.

The base layer (aka long underwear or thermals) is both the literal and metaphorical foundation of a proper layering system. A wrong choice makes the whole system fall apart. If you pick a layer that chafes or gets sweaty, you’re going to be miserable no matter how perfect your insulation or shell performs.

Even after testing them for over a decade, however, I’m still hesitant to crown a few as the best because base layers are highly personal. Someone skinning uphill in the damp Pacific Northwest needs something very different from a resort skier sitting on frozen chairlifts in Colorado. Your ideal fabric feel, insulating weight, shoulder fit, and myriad other variables may vary greatly from mine.

This year’s rough snow season in the western U.S. only reinforced how important versatility is in our gear. Due to inconsistent winter conditions, we found ourselves wearing these base layers not only while skiing and touring, but also during mountain bike rides, cold morning runs, gym workouts, and shoulder-season adventures where moisture management and mobility mattered just as much as warmth. After months of testing 46 bottoms and tops—because it is our job, after all—these are the best base layers that we believe will appeal to a variety of preferences.

Pros and Cons + Most comfortable wool layer in test + Best-in-class moisture management + Remarkable odor mitigation – No hood

Out of the 46 base layers we tested, the strongest pool we have ever drawn from, the Stellar Merino Base Top and Tights were the best base layering set in the widest variety of conditions. From 15-degree full-day ski tours in Colorado’s San Juan backcountry to 45-degree high-output mountain bike rides in Durango, the layers scored best in comfort, moisture management, fit, and odor mitigation. One tester put it simply: “Clear best in test.”

Sourced from Uruguay and produced in a family-owned factory in Portugal, the Stellar kit uses premium fine 19.5-micron merino wool fibers, which deliver both softness and stretch. The fit earned praise from our tester, who is 5’10” and 170 pounds, and extremely picky about how his base layers hug his body while he moves in the snow. “Both the top and bottoms were snug but never bunchy, with an ideal sleeve and leg length for unhindered movement,” he said.

Each layer features flatlock seams to reduce bulk, gusseted underarms for full range of motion, and an elongated back panel to block cold drafts. It moved moisture efficiently and transitioned from sweaty to completely dry in under 30 minutes. After a season’s worth of wear, odor buildup was minimal. “Still haven’t washed it!” said our tester, who cohabitates with his fiancée and hasn’t heard her complain. The only knock? No hood, which would’ve been nice to help the top transition to a standalone spring skiing piece.

Sizes: S-XXL Key Material: 100 percent recycled polyester

Pros and Cons + Silky smooth + Friction-free seams + Excellent mobility across multiple sports – Too lightweight for chronically cold skiers

Built with The North Face’s lightweight double-knit DOTKNIT polyester fabric, this shirt combines engineered holes in the face fabric and targeted yarn construction with a wider knit in high-heat areas like armpits. The marriage accelerates moisture transfer during movement, which testers appreciated during sweaty mountain bike rides, icy bump skiing in 45-degree weather, and early-morning runs in Ashland and Bend, Oregon. Despite weighing just 6.67 ounces, the double knit still delivered enough warmth for winter weather while drying quickly and remaining exceptionally breathable. No clamminess here.

Its standout feature was the construction. The low-profile merrow stitching (an overlock stitch that wraps the edges of fabric panels as it joins them) and slim athletic fit made the base layer almost completely disappear during repetitive movements like pedaling, skinning, and gym workouts. Thumb loops also prevented sleeves from bunching underneath outer layers during cold ski days and made transitions between activities seamless. While it kept us warm while we were moving, this is definitely not the thickest or toastiest layer in the test. Skiers who routinely run cold on frozen chairlifts will likely want a heavier option (read on for our recommendation).

Sizes: XS-3XL Key Material: 100 percent recycled polyester

Pros and Cons + Extremely breathable + Casual enough to wear anywhere – Minimal insulation in truly cold weather – Must be coupled with outer layer in wind

Patagonia has been making Capilene layers for over 40 years, and the new Capilene Lightweight Crew is proof that this signature fabric just keeps getting better. Made of 100 percent double-knit, recycled polyester, with HeiQ Mint odor control and a wicking finish, it weighs a scant 3.3 ounces. Those technical details translated directly into real-world performance during mountain bike rides, gym workouts, and early-morning runs where the layer consistently dumped heat and dried almost immediately. The odor mitigation worked so well that this top once went three full weeks of heavy use between trips to the washing machine.

Unlike heavier synthetic layers that can start to feel swampy once soaked, this one retained a dry, barely-there sensation even after sweaty intervals and long climbs. The fitted cut also helped the top transition comfortably between sports and life, and the stripes made it look more like a casual long-sleeve tee than a dedicated technical layer. We ended up wearing it so often that it became part mountain-bike layer, part workout shirt, and part accidental Zoom call uniform. Disclaimer: this is not a deep winter insulation monster. On truly cold days, it worked best underneath a shell and insulating layers, or alone only during high-output activities.

Sizes: S-XXL Key Material: 100 percent merino wool

Pros and Cons + Soft and comfortable + Fantastic warmth-to-breathability balance + Excellent mobility despite heavyweight feel – Too warm for spring touring

The Woolx Backcountry Leggings delivered some of the best next-to-skin comfort and thermoregulation this season. Built with heavyweight merino wool, they struck an impressive balance between warmth, stretch, and breathability that made them equally enjoyable during cold ski mornings, frigid dawn-patrol jogs, and recovery hangs at home.

Despite their thickness, the leggings moved exceptionally well during mountain bike rides and gym workouts. The fabric stretched naturally through deep squats, pedaling, and mobility work without ever feeling restrictive or bunchy under outer layers. While they didn’t dry as quickly as lightweight synthetics, they retained warmth even when damp. The fabric also resisted odor buildup during repeated workouts and back-to-back days of use—another advantage of merino wool in multisport layering systems. We’d recommend reserving these for the most frigid temps: during sunny spring ski days and warmer trail rides, testers overheated in them.

KUIU’s most advanced fleece to date, the Vital S3 Zip-T Hoodie is the base layer that can do it all. The soft-brushed fleece interior traps heat, wicks moisture, dries quickly, resists odors, and still gives you plenty of mobility on high-output cold weather hunts. Boosted by XLANCE®️ technology, the fleece is reinforced with an advanced polyolefin-based stretch yarn with built-in resistance to sweat, chemicals, heat, ozone, and UVA/UVB radiation. This means your hoodie retains elasticity and durability even across the most grueling treks—you’ll get the same fit and performance when you reach for it season after season.

Sizes: S-XXL Key Material: 100 percent merino wool

Pros and Cons + Remarkably breathable for its weight + Soft next-to-skin feel + Immediate warmth during cold starts and transitions – Too warm for sustained high-output efforts – Slightly bulkier under trim shells

The Ridge Merino Inversion Crew managed one of the hardest balancing acts: delivering substantial warmth without feeling stifling the second testers started moving. Made of 100 percent merino wool, it became a favorite during freezing dawn starts, snowy driveway shoveling, and post-ride recovery hangs. Superfine 18.5-micron fibers were impressively soft against the skin for such a warm piece—one tester wore it to sleep even after sweating in it during the day. Low-profile flatlock seams, raglan sleeves, thumb loops, and an extra-long cut minimized friction points underneath packs and outerwear, making it all the more cozy.

What surprised us most was how flexible and breathable the top remained despite its warmth. Heavyweight base layers often feel amazing when you’re standing still and miserable once your heart rate spikes, but the Inversion regulated temperature better than expected during moderate-output movement. This is still, however, fundamentally a cold-weather specialist. During hard uphill efforts and warmer spring conditions, it quickly became too much of a layer. It also felt a tad bulky when coupled with a very trim Rab shell—worth noting if you like tighter outer layers.

Sizes: S-XXL Key Material: Polyester/wool blend

Pros and Cons + Packs down to the size of a tangerine + Fast drying + Silky next to skin – Doesn’t work as a standalone layer in cold

Over ten days of skiing in the Japanese Alps, spinning lifts at Mount Ashland, and ski touring at Crater Lake, the Rab Syncrino Base LS Tee became one tester’s default when he knew he was going to get hot and sweat hard. Built with Rab’s lightweight Syncrino 125 fabric, it combines merino wool for insulation and moisture-wicking with polyester for strength, durability, and fast drying. We found this triad of attributes ideal for high-output touring, hut trips, and traveling in temps 40 degrees and below.

It packed down to the size of a tangerine, which one tester squeezed into his pack as a safety layer on hut trips and a two-week trip to Nozawa, Japan. He praised the next-to-skin comfort, saying it “felt like you didn’t even have it on,” and rated its mobility and sweat management highly. The single-jersey construction, low-bulk seams, drop tail, and set-in sleeves made it especially comfortable under other layers.

Even after sweaty skimo sessions and back-to-back cold days, it stayed fresh. “No matter how much I sweat, it [shone] in many environments,” our tester said. However, it was too lightweight to be a standalone layer during the winter months.

Sizes: S-XL Key Material: Merino wool/nylon blend

Pros and Cons + Wide temperature range + Highly breathable + Minimal friction during exercise – Fit is long for shorter users

The Flylow Hanmer Wool Baselayer Top was winter MVP for one tester after five big days of testing on his local ski hill, Mount Ashland. He not only appreciated the Hanmer’s incredible versatility in the mountains but also felt like he was wearing a normal, non-technical top around town thanks to its two-toned sleeves and casual style. “You could literally wear this every day in winter,” he said. Tested from zero to 40 degrees while skiing, running, and during three full-on nighttime skimo training sessions, the Hanmer consistently stood out for its ability to keep him warm and efficiently move his sweat at the same time—two attributes that often conflict with each other. “I would finish a skimo workout and rip off all of my other sweaty layers and keep the Hanmer top on and throw on my down jacket over it. It was amazing that it wasn’t soggy,” he said.

The Hanmer is woven from a blend of merino wool and nylon that Flylow claims is 50 percent stronger than comparable merino fabrics. While we weren’t able to confirm that number, we can confirm that it did not experience pilling after a full winter’s worth of testing. It proved warm, breathable, sweat-wicking, and also impressively odor-resistant even after days of heavy use. “It was noticeable how odorless it was; most of my other layers would carry a little stink after the same amount of use,” he said. Flatlock seams eliminate chafing, while a long cut makes layering easy. Thumb loops and a backpack-friendly raglan construction enhance usability during high-output movement. “The thumb holes are ingenious,” our tester said. With cozy skin feel and all-conditions reliability, the Hanmer is a layer that disappears in a good way.

Everybody is different, so dialing in the materials that feel the best against your skin is the most important part of the base-layer buying journey. In general, the best base layers are constructed of either polyester or merino wool, with spandex, elastane, or nylon spun into the fabric to increase stretch or durability. Polyester layers are usually cheaper and quicker to dry, while merino is more expensive, dries slower (but retains heat while wet), and is more odor-resistant.

Which is better comes down to personal preference: some love the soft hand of natural fibers, but even the most advanced, small-micron merino wool material can make someone with a wool intolerance miserable. If you can, try on any layer you want to buy. How it feels against your skin is paramount and differs per person. If something feels itchy in a dressing room, run from it, as it is only going to get more uncomfortable with prolonged use.

Once you land on a material that works for your skin, start looking into moisture management. If you sweat a ton, as many of the testers for this category do, look into lightweight synthetic base layers, as they have an excellent track record for moving moisture efficiently. If you don’t sweat much, then you can get away with thicker next-to-skin layers that will also be warmer when you’re not in motion.

In terms of design, base layers are pretty straightforward. To maximize comfort, look for upgrades like flatlock seams and raglan sleeves. These can prevent chafing, especially when wearing a pack.

When deciding what to avoid, we would suggest starting by looking at the label. Staying away from certain materials is a great way to minimize your chances of getting a bum base layer. Cotton is an obvious material to avoid for winter-specific base layers because it holds onto moisture and can become dangerously cold. Synthetics without some type of odor-mitigating technology might also not be your best bet for hut trips, winter backpacking, or high-output skinning because they can become unsavably stinky in one trip. If something is wool, check the micron number. A lower micron count (finer fibers) will be softer and more comfortable next to skin than a higher one.

We also suggest looking a little deeper at the wording of wool/synthetic blends. Purpose-built blends (which intentionally place wool and synthetics in different parts of the blend) can utilize the hydrophilic and hydrophobic natures of the fabrics to its advantage. An example of this is a material that has a hydrophilic synthetic next to your skin to grab moisture with a layer of a hydrophobic wool that will move that moisture away from you. If the blend is described as “intimate,” that means it weaves them together in a way that will deliver the worst of both worlds. An intimate blend creates a tug-of-war over that moisture that can leave you super clammy, so we recommend steering clear.

Due to the abysmal snowpack in the Pacific Northwest, category manager Joe Jackson had the most varied testing conditions for base layers he has experienced in more than a decade of testing the category. In addition to the ski days he eked out at Mount Bachelor and in the backcountry, he used these layers during more than 60 mountain bike rides, early-morning runs, and high-output workouts in his home gym. That broad mix of activities allowed him to evaluate not only warmth and next-to-skin comfort, but also mobility, moisture management, odor mitigation, and versatility transitioning between sports.

Skiing, however, remained a critical part of testing, as always. Testers used these layers during resort skiing, uphill touring, cold transitions in parking lots, and long days spent sweating under packs. We paid close attention to how quickly layers dried after high-output efforts, whether fabrics became clammy during sustained sweating, and how well the materials retained warmth after becoming damp. We also stress-tested mobility across all sports because the best modern base layers should disappear while you move instead of restricting you.

But this year’s low snow totals also created a more realistic picture for how today’s base layers are actually used by many outdoor athletes, as multisport layering pieces that need to perform just as well on trail runs and shoulder-season bike rides as they do under a ski shell.

Category manager Joe Jackson has been testing gear professionally as his main gig for over a decade. While he has tested everything from whitewater kayaks to sporks, base layers remain one of his all-time favorite categories. They can be absorbed into everyday life to get the type of testing reps needed to help tease out the nuance that makes a piece of gear truly special. They also don’t take up much space in his overburdened garage.

If you suffer from FOMO, do not follow Southern Oregon-based tester Yu Kuwabara on Strava—his output is absolutely bananas. He’s the kind of athlete who will climb and ski Mount Shasta (he has 37 summits) in the morning, then teaches a mountain biking clinic that afternoon on a casual day. The local race director and father of rippers logged hundreds upon hundreds of multisport miles and tens of thousands of vertical feet around Southern Oregon, as well as on a trip to Japan, to test the dickens out of these layers.

Durango, Colorado–based tester Ryan Pyles has enough energy to power a small city. He positively channeled said energy this winter with remote packrafting trips, dozens of days skiing in the backcountry around Durango and Red Mountain Pass, mountain biking, trail running, and skiing in his local resort of Purgatory. He worked as a science teacher while testing last winter and has also worked as an engineer. The two jobs arguably make him the perfect candidate to deliver solid feedback because of his ability to really get in the weeds with materials as well as distill that into understandable information.

#8233. The 7 Items That Got Me Through October (and the Rest of Fall)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Oh October, the month of mystery. Here in Boulder, Colorado, it’s when you wake up in the dark not knowing if it will be warm, cold, raining, or windy. The only thing you do know every morning is there will be even more much-larger-than-life-sized skeletons poking out of peoples’ lawns. (Why has this become a thing? As my friend Clare said on a run the other day, “people are desecrating their lawns with plastic trash!”)

Anyway, it’s a tricky time of year for running. Head out the door overdressed and you will end up a puddle of sweat that, depending on the weather, ultimately makes you cold. Leave underdressed, as I did for a tempo run two weeks ago, and your limbs will feel like they’ve been cursed by a witch who’s turned them to immovable ice.

But tricky conditions can be solved with treats. My trusty associate editor is, in his words, “going to the desert to do something stupid.” (Go Cade!) That leaves just me to round up our gear of the month. Here are the five items I kept packed in my Janji Ultrahauler (another piece of gear I can’t live without!) so I was ready for whatever I woke up to:

Kilian Jornet’s fledgling shoe and apparel company has stuck to relatively technical alpine equipment—until now with the Nnormal Cadi. This do-everything trail shoe is exceptionally comfortable thanks to a padded heel collar and tongue and a cushy midsole with 37 mm stack in the heel, 31 mm in the forefoot. It’s got a nice wide toe box (an obsession of mine as I work on my foot strength and toe splay). And with a Vibram Megagrip outsole it’s tacky on all terrain and in all conditions. I also appreciate the mesh upper, which is breathable on hot days and dries quickly on wet ones. It’s the only shoe I brought on a trip recently, which means I found myself wearing it for a 12-mile run around the Charles River in Boston—definitely not as energetic as your typical road trainer these days, but it got the job done just fine. It’s just a solid, dependable shoe.

It’s rained A LOT in Boulder this month. And by a lot, I mean more than zero times. I know I’ve lived here for too long because I’ve gotten soft and the only thing that got me through more than zero very dark, very wet mornings was this rain jacket from Arc’teryx. That’s because it’s actually waterproof. But it’s also super lightweight and breathable, meaning you don’t incinerate in your own body heat and end up wet anyway. Plus one for the cinch on the hood so you can actually keep it on your head while you’re running and another bonus for the vents under the armpits, which help moderate body heat. I know $450 is an obscene amount to spend on anything, but this is definitely a case of you get what you pay for.

When it comes to running pants and tights I am very, very picky. They can’t suffocate my waist, but they also need to stay put. They can’t bunch around the knees, but they also can’t be so baggy that the pant legs rub into each other. The Janji Altas Multi Pant is one of the few pieces that passes my stringent test. They are supremely comfortable thanks to a wide elastic waistband, and a drawstring lets you dial in the fit. They’re loose enough to allow for full range of motion, but they’re streamlined enough that I can wear them for harder efforts without getting annoyed. Why I really love them for this time of year is they are lightweight and breathable, providing just the right amount of insulation. And even better, they have nearly knee-length ankle zips so I often wear them for the warm up and zip them off for intervals—no shoe removal required.

There is something so comforting and luxurious about tucking into a comfy vest for a fall outing. Enter this fleece-lined vest from 7Mesh. It’s super breathable yet cozy thanks to a soft, woven outer layer paired with the light and ultrasoft fleece lining. I’ve been loving it for colder runs when a jacket feels like too much but a long sleeve isn’t quite enough. And I’ve also been loving it on the bike—especially because the vest folds into itself via a big back pocket, revealing little straps that let you fix it to your bike frame when you’re not wearing it.

Not too cold and not too warm, snug but not tight, these gloves are  a shoulder-season star. They’re so lightweight that I don’t think twice about wearing them for the start of a run before the sun rises and stashing them in a pocket as I warm up with the ground. I can use my phone with them on, carry my ballot (the midterms are on Tuesday!), as well as maneuver zippers and, if desperate, tie shoes. Plus the colors and patterns instantly boost my mood. (They came in so many fun options!)

One-star review for the name. Zero stars for the logo branded on the top of the collar. And yet, five stars for these socks. They are just that comfy and moisture-wicking. I am pretty skeptical of overengineered gear, but CEP has me thinking maybe there is something to developing stuff in a lab. These socks provide a gentle amount of compression and arch support while also being ventilated in all the places you want it. In other words: they stay put, and they keep my feet comfortable for a wide range of temperatures—perfect for fall running. Most importantly, my feet do not slip in my shoes. I repeat: no slippage here. My friend saw me running in them the other day and he said he also loves these socks so much that he ordered five pairs. Oh and they come in approximately one billion colorways.

I know, I know, it’s a crime to spend more than $50 on a hair product—much less two products. But hear me out: Colorado is savage on my wavy hair. When left unchecked, the dry air and harsh sun leech out every last drop of moisture, turning my hair into a wiry mess. Add in the rainy days of October (or my annual pilgrimage to Hawaii) and in years past I am ripping out chunks of matted hair every time I shower. Enter this fancy shampoo and conditioner. I am not exaggerating when I say this stuff has revolutionized my hair’s life. For the first time in 13 years since I moved here, my hair feels soft. And I can actually get a brush through it when I get out of the shower! You better believe I will be buying it again.

Many backpackers today will never pitch a flat tarp—they’ve lost ground as more secure and user-friendly ultralight tents have become ubiquitous. But if you’re willing to put in the effort to learn to rig one, you won’t find a lighter style of shelter—or a cheaper one. The Rab SilTarp Plus Solo is a perfect entry-level solo shelter for the tarp-curious. #8231. The Top 30 Ski Resorts in the West (2027)

Choosing a ski resort for your next trip is about more than snow totals and vertical drop. Sure, you want great snow, lifts that keep you moving, and terrain that makes you want to take one more lap. But last winter reminded us just how much conditions can shape a ski experience—and how difficult it can be to judge a resort when much of its terrain isn’t open or skiing the way it should. A lean snow year across much of the West made for a challenging season, and those conditions appear to have left their mark on this year’s rankings, even at some of North America’s most celebrated destinations.

Every spring, we ask readers to weigh in on the resorts they’ve visited, rating their experiences across 18 categories that span the full spectrum of a ski vacation. From snow, grooming, lifts, and terrain variety to dining, lodging, nightlife, and overall character, these rankings reflect the collective wisdom of skiers who’ve experienced these places firsthand. But this year’s results come with an added wrinkle: When terrain is limited and conditions are far from ideal, it’s not always easy to separate a resort’s inherent strengths from the circumstances of the season. The latest survey went out last April, and the results are in.

More Results: Looking For the East Rankings? Click Here.

The 2027 West rankings, below, reveal which resorts are getting the most right, where they truly shine, and where there’s room to improve. Some familiar names took significant tumbles. Others weathered the challenges and climbed higher. These shifts suggest that even resorts with exceptional terrain, amenities, and reputations aren’t immune to a difficult winter. At the same time, these are overall vacation-experience rankings, not a referendum on snow alone. Our reviews break down each resort’s biggest strengths and weaknesses—on and off the slopes—to help you figure out which destination best fits what you’re looking for in a ski trip.

Think of this as advice from your fellow skiers, informed by a winter that didn’t always make for easy comparisons. These rankings aren’t a one-size-fits-all verdict on where you should spend your winter vacation, nor do they tell the whole story of what a resort can deliver in a better snow year. Explore the rankings, see how your favorites stack up, and discover a few places that might deserve a spot on your list. And if you disagree with the results, even better. The Reader Resort Survey returns next spring, giving you another chance to weigh in and help shape next year’s Resort Guide.

New this season, SKI is partnering with Outside Travel to provide seamless hotel-booking options at many of the Top 50 resorts. Navigate to the resort’s personalized landing page next to the “Book Now” bullet to explore lodging by budget and/or location. More destinations are coming online soon, plus revisit for dining and après recommendations from the SKI editors. Join Outside+ for up to 10% off lodging rates.

Big-mountain skiing meets a bona fide ski town, with enough terrain, dining, nightlife, and family-friendly diversions to keep everyone happy—if you can navigate the crowds.

Don’t let Park City’s No. 30 ranking fool you: This resort has a lot going for it. Readers praise its sheer size, varied terrain, and off-mountain amenities, making it one of the West’s most well-rounded destinations for groups with different abilities and interests. With more than 7,300 acres of lift-served terrain, there’s room for just about everyone, from families cruising groomers and exploring beginner-friendly zones to experts hunting steep, gladed pitches like Condor Woods and the high-alpine bowls of McConkey’s.

Then there’s the town itself. Historic Main Street is the real deal, packed with restaurants, bars, shops, and places to stay, while the broader resort scene offers plenty to do long after the lifts close. Park City scores among the best in nightlife, après, dining, and lodging, and readers appreciate that non-skiers can have a vacation here, too. Families also give the destination high marks, thanks to its mix of terrain and off-slope activities. “I love how close the resort is to town and all the restaurants and other amenities,” commented one survey respondent.

Access is another major advantage. Salt Lake City International Airport is close enough that visitors can often land and be skiing within hours, making Park City an easy choice for a long weekend or a family trip. “It’s the easiest large resort to get to in the U.S. with an incredible amount of terrain,” said one SKI reader. But that convenience is a double-edged sword: Crowds can clog base areas and lift lines, while parking headaches and high prices leave readers wishing the overall experience were a better value. Lift bottlenecks remain a particular sore spot, but lift network upgrades coming for the 2027-’28 season hope to move the needle.

This season brings significant upgrades at Canyons Village, including a new enclosed gondola to replace the aging Cabriolet and a five-story parking garage. Those changes should improve the arrival experience, though new parking fees will add another cost for some visitors. Through it all, Park City’s appeal is undeniable: enormous terrain, a lively town, and easy access from a major airport. “It’s a big mountain with lots of options,” said one Park City skier. “Fun and varied terrain and (usually) great snow.”

“Good for both hard-chargers and solid intermediates.  Lots of varied terrain.  Easy to navigate without taking a lot of lifts.”

At Canyons Village, a new enclosed 10-passenger Skyway Gondola replaces the open-air Cabriolet, with a mid-station serving nearby developments and a five-story garage is expected to open in early December with $29 per day (free after noon and for carpools of four-plus).

On the events front, Shaun White’s The Snow League comes to the mountain Jan. 21–23, 2027, bringing elite halfpipe snowboarding and freeskiing competition, live music, and fan events. Park City has rebuilt its 22-foot Eagle Superpipe for the competition, and the pipe will open to the public after the event.

Jaw-dropping Lake Tahoe views, sprawling terrain, and a lively après scene make Heavenly as much about the good times off the slopes as the skiing itself.

At Heavenly, the scenery is almost as memorable as the skiing. Perched above Lake Tahoe, with terrain straddling the California-Nevada border, the resort delivers one spectacular lake view after another across 5,000 acres of skiable terrain. There’s plenty for a range of abilities, from mellow groomers for families and newer skiers to wide-open blues and approachable black diamonds. Even longtime locals can’t resist pausing to take in the view. “I’ve lived in the area for almost 20 years and those lake views still almost knock me off my skis,” confessed one Heavenly fan.

Heavenly earns high marks for nightlife, dining, and lodging, with stellar après spots, craft breweries, and live music around South Lake Tahoe, plus the casinos and entertainment of nearby Stateline, Nevada. Whether you’re looking to keep the party going or settle in for a long dinner after a day on the mountain, there’s plenty to do beyond skiing.

The biggest frustration? Getting around. Readers dinged Heavenly for crowded lifts, including the gondola, and guest service remains an area for improvement. Some base-area facilities could also use a refresh. Still, those complaints have a way of fading when you crest a ridge, turn a corner, and find Lake Tahoe stretched out below you in all its glory. “There’s no shortage of beautiful runs—especially when the sun is shining and the lake is visible from anywhere on top of the mountain.”

“Heavenly has great grooming systems, so no matter how bad the snow gets, the groomers are fun to ride.”

A family-friendly favorite with forgiving groomers, surprisingly adventurous corners, and one of the easiest getaways from Denver.

As the closest major Epic Pass resort to Denver, Keystone draws plenty of Front Range locals alongside visitors looking for a full mountain vacation. The good news is that both are on tap at this family favorite. The frontside can get busy, particularly on weekends, but there’s more to Keystone than its popular cruisers. Head farther out to explore The Outback or venture into Bergman Bowl, where high-alpine terrain offers adventurous intermediates and families a chance to explore beyond the usual groomer circuit. “Love Keystone and its low-key nature,” shared one fan. “Fun terrain, especially Bergman Bowl and the glades on The Outback.”

For families, Keystone has a lot to offer. Free parking, efficient lifts, a strong ski school, and a location just 90 minutes from Denver make the logistics easier, while base-area wagons help parents haul gear and tired kids. The village isn’t the most authentic, but it has what skiers need, plus fun-for-families extras such as character parades and seasonal events. Don’t miss the annual snow fort atop Dercum Mountain—it’s always a hit with younger skiers. “Keystone is the unquestionable gem of the I-70 corridor,” exclaimed one excited reader.

The resort also scores well for grooming, which is good news for skiers who like confidence-inspiring runs. But don’t assume the mountain is all mellow blues and beginner-friendly terrain. Stronger skiers can find challenging lines on North Peak plus glades in The Windows. Keystone may not rank among Colorado’s most demanding mountains, but those willing to venture beyond the frontside can find plenty to keep them interested. “There’s legit steep terrain here if you know where to look,” said a survey respondent.

Where Keystone falls short is local flavor. Its purpose-built village and convenient setup make for an easy vacation, but the atmosphere can feel more functional than distinctive compared with Colorado’s historic ski towns. Still, for families and Denver-area skiers who prize convenience, well-groomed runs, and straightforward logistics, Keystone remains a dependable choice.

“In a bad snow year (which this one was), Keystone’s snowmaking and grooming made it possible for them to outdistance everyone around them. This was the place to go all season. More than half of my total ski days were here this year.”

Keystone officially debuts Kindred Resort, its first premier luxury ski-in/ski-out hotel, at the base of the River Run Gondola. The new property brings upscale lodging and easy slope access to River Run Village.

Western spirit, family-friendly skiing, and a lively town make Steamboat a welcoming all-around getaway, even when the snow doesn’t cooperate.

Readers appreciate a resort that feels welcoming rather than intimidating, and Steamboat checks that box once again despite a small slip in the rankings. On the mountain, Steamboat offers a satisfying mix of groomers, tree skiing, and more adventurous terrain. Mahogany Ridge’s advanced and expert glades and bowls expand the options for stronger skiers, while the double-black glades Christmas Tree Bowl rewards those willing to venture beyond the cruisers. Still, challenge remains a weaker category in the survey, so experts seeking relentless steeps may want to temper their expectations.

For families and mixed-ability groups, though, the range of terrain—and the resort’s strong service culture—makes it easy to build a ski day that works for everyone. Steamboat scores high once again for its welcoming family vibe.
