#8230. Meet the French Soldiers Who Get Paid to Climb Hard Alpine Routes

Dream jobs come in all shapes and sizes. Some might consider my job at Climbing dreamy. Others might hope to hangboard their way into professional climbing one day. My former colleague Duane Raleigh once made a very serious list of climber “dream jobs” that included roofers, fast food cooks, and snow shovelers.

I am here to tell you that none of these jobs are the best climber jobs. The actual best job for a climber, without any shadow of a doubt, is to be a member of the French military’s 27th Mountain Infantry Brigade. Why?

Allow me to describe the group’s latest work trip.

Last Wednesday, October 14, Sergeant Konrad Piontek and Corporals Amaury Fouillade and Clovis Paulin stood on the 6,654-meter summit of Peak 41 in Nepal. On the 1,400-meter North Face, they had just opened a stunning new route linking long sections of vertical ice with burly rock roofs and pitches of deep snow. They called the line Bon Matin (ED+ WI5+ M6 A1 90° snow), which translates to “Good Morning.” (Not sure what “ED+” means? Check out this article about international alpine grades.)

The three first ascensionists were part of a team of six from the 27th Mountain Infantry Brigade, better known as the Groupe Militaire de Haute Montagne, or GMHM. They had arrived in Nepal in mid-September along with a military doctor. After a period of acclimatization, the group split into two rope teams according to their skill level and how well each had adjusted to the altitude.

The Piontek-Fouillade-Paulin team eyed an attractive, unclimbed smear running plumb down Peak 41’s north side, to the left of a Korean team’s route from 2016. They began climbing on October 11 and summited after “four days of particularly committed climbing,” according to a statement shared with Climbing.

Over the 1,400 meters of the face, the team had to deal with numerous steep and poorly protected pitches, including sections of vertical snow. “We weren’t expecting pitches as steep as that, especially in snow,” said Corporal Paulin in the statement. But they also climbed what can only be described as truly classic mixed terrain: solid rock and squeaky ice, hanging above tons of exposure.

After summiting, the team descended the peak’s southeastern aspect via 15 rappels and significant downclimbing, turning their outing into one massive loop back to basecamp. “Reaching the summit was a real physical relief,” said Corporal Fouillade. “The mental release came later.”

Officially, France’s 10-person GMHM is tasked with “mastering extreme terrestrial environments, particularly vertical terrain and high altitude,” said a spokesperson to Climbing. This fluency in alpine terrain aims to contribute to the development of the entire French army’s mountain capabilities.

“The whole point of the GMHM is to practice high level alpinism,” said the group’s spokesperson. “What is learned regarding mountaineering or cold weather environments is passed on to the French mountain units, but the GMHM has otherwise no militaristic purposes.”

Similar mountain-military units exist across the globe, but—tragically—nothing so geared toward climbing excellence exists in North America. (If you happen to have a French passport and the pre-requisites, I’d be refreshing this recruitment page regularly.)

As far as we know, there is no fixed contract length for GMHM members; some alpinists have been part of the dream team for years and years.

In addition to one high-altitude expedition each year, the group travels to Greenland to teach the Groupement de Commandos de Montagne (literally: “mountain commandos”) about how to thrive in cold weather. They also take minor trips to develop rock and ice climbing skills, whether that’s locally in the French Alps or abroad to Yosemite. In plain terms, that means that 10 climbers get to occasionally don camo and earn a decent government salary to climb full time, around the world.

Did I mention the GMHM is the ultimate dream job?

#8229. Avoid California’s Crowded Trails With These 5 Quiet Coastline Hikes

There’s no shortage of spectacular hiking in California. Big Sur, Yosemite, and Redwoods have achieved international renown––and for good reason. But if you want to escape the crowds, the less congested San Luis Obispo coast offers scores of trails, uncrowded wilderness, and stellar vistas along Highway 1.

These routes invite you to hike on hills turned gold by spring flowers, spot seals in coastal reserves, and explore both long and short routes near cozy coastal towns—all without fighting for a parking spot at the trailhead. Integrate these hikes into a road trip along the iconic Highway 1, or just visit for an active getaway. San Luis Obispo’s landscapes are beautiful, the food is delicious, and, for the nights you’re not camping, there’s great lodging.

Named for the abundant yellow wildflowers that paint the hills gold every spring—namely bright yellow poppies, Deerbrush, and wild mustard—this unique park along the Morro Bay estuary is home to riparian environments, coastal scrub, and pines.

Scores of trails weave across 8,000 acres of wilderness and offer views of Morro Bay. But for epic views of the coast and a solid taste of all the park has to offer, start at the Hazard Peak Trailhead on Pecho Valley Road and hike out on Hazard Trail to the peak. From there, you can retrace your steps back to the junction with Canyon View Trail. Take that and descend a series of short switchbacks to Islay Creek Road, which will spit you out just down the street from the Hazard Peak Trailhead. You can also extend the hike by doing the full Hazard Peak loop, which is about 11 miles.

Located in the Lopez Lake Recreation Area outside Arroyo Grande, this trail climbs up and along the western ridge of the county park. Wildlife sightings of deer, birds, even black bears, aren’t uncommon. The last section of trail involves a steep climb to the peak, but the 360-degree views of the Oceano Dunes and coast to the west and surrounding Santa Lucia, Caliente, and Sierra Madre Mountains are worth the effort.

Start on Wittenberg Trail at the end of Lopez Dr. and branch off onto Duna Vista Loop Trail. Duna Vista Spur Trail will lead you to the peak. Hike directly back on the southernmost part of the loop for a slightly shorter route (8 miles) or split off onto the northern section for the full 8.8-mile trek. A day-use fee of $12 per vehicle is required.

This beautiful coastal walk isn’t a challenging one, but give yourself plenty of time to complete it: You’ll want to stop and soak in the wide ocean views, sea stacks, and wetlands. Most of the hike is along bluffs, but opportunities to descend and explore intertidal areas at low tide abound. Expect to see plenty of sea lions and bring your binoculars to try to spot an endangered snowy plover.

Start at the North Ocean parking lot on the edge of Cayucos and take Estero Bluffs Trail along the coast to the end of the park and back.

There’s more to this hike than classic California coastal scrub. In fact, as you climb over rolling hills, you’ll score views of Morro Bay and jagged Morro Rock, a volcanic plug in the estuary, and even drop into shady live oak groves. Volcanic peaks pepper the periphery, and opportunities to spot wildlife abound, including any of hundreds of bird species that follow the Pacific Flyway.

The state park’s trail system is extensive, but this route is a nice loop that touches a lot of the trails on the east side. Start at the parking lot on S Bay Blvd. and take Quarry Trail to Canet Trail, followed by Chumash, Crespi, Park Ridge, and Live Oak Trails. That leads you right back to the parking lot you started in. You can customize the length by combining various side trails, including to the top of Portola Trail, a small summit, which adds about a mile. A state park pass or $8 day-use fee is required.

This rugged trail leads into the Santa Lucia Wilderness within Los Padres National Forest, finally reaching an 80-foot waterfall that streams into an azure pool. Much of the trail slowly climbs through the woods alongside a creek and lush riparian zone in Big Falls Canyon. However, if you continue onward past the trio of falls, your efforts will be rewarded with sunny views of the surrounding Coast Ranges.

Start at Big Falls Trailhead on Upper Lopez Canyon Road and hike to the junction with Hi Mountain Trail. Return the same way. The last section of Lopez Canyon Road to the trailhead can be rough, so 4WD is recommended.

Eat: Gardens of Avila, located within Sycamore Mineral Springs Resort and Spa in San Luis Obispo, offers elegant dining, homegrown ingredients, and garden paths for after-dinner strolls.

Sip: Wineries abound. Oenophiles who appreciate organic and regenerative farming should visit Chamisal Vineyards in Edna Valley.

Explore Town: Los Osos offers welcoming coffee shops, local art galleries, and fine boutiques. Avila Beach is worth exploring for sunny waterfront vibes. Cayucos is home to classic seaside tourist scenes complete with souvenir shops and antique stores.

Campgrounds are in no short supply along Highway 1, and the San Luis Obispo area is no exception. Most of the state parks, like Montaña de Oro, Morro Bay, and Estero Bluffs, have their own developed campgrounds. Morro Beach also has a campground along the coast. Those can be booked online or in person, but they fill up quickly, especially on weekends. During the winter, these campgrounds are closed, so you’ll need to seek out dispersed camping or other lodging options.

Dispersed camping is strictly prohibited along Highway 1. However, some nearby mountain areas allow it. Check out TV Tower Road, Carrizo Plain National Monument, or Williams Hill Recreation Area.

Want to break up your nights outside? You have options. San Luis Obispo and nearby towns have plenty of hotels, BnB’s, and more luxurious accommodations. For a splurge, check out La Lomita Ranch, a chic and colorful former stable with painted tiles, terracotta, and horses in San Luis Obispo.

#8228. Lindsey Vonn Is Headed for Her 9th Surgery. She’s Still Thinking About Skiing.

Lndsey Vonn inspects the slope before the second official training for the women's downhill event at the Tofane Alpine Skiing Centre during Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games (Photo: Stefano Rellandini/AFP via Getty Images)

Lindsey Vonn is just days away from her ninth surgery in as many months, and the three-time Olympic medalist is still thinking about skiing.

On November 9, Vonn, 42, is heading into what’s slated to be the final surgery on her left leg following her severe crash during the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics in February. In an exclusive interview with Forbes, the alpine skier detailed her upcoming surgery.

“The plan is to remove all of the hardware, finally fix the ACL, and hopefully that’s my last surgery,” she told Forbes.

In February 2026, Vonn started the Olympic downhill race despite rupturing the ACL in her left knee just days earlier. After taking an aggressive line through the first few turns, Vonn clipped a gate just 13.4 seconds into her run, pushing her off course at the Tofane Alpine Skiing area.

The impact sent her spinning through the air before she crashed onto the icy surface, ending her race. Vonn was eventually airlifted to a hospital and diagnosed with complex fractures of the two bones in her lower left leg. Doctors put three plates and up to 20 screws in her leg, but couldn’t fix her ACL until her bones healed properly, she told Parade.

In the weeks following her initial surgery, Vonn shared that her injuries were so severe that she had to undergo an emergency fasciotomy, a procedure used to treat acute compartment syndrome. This potentially life-threatening condition occurs when pressure builds up around muscle groups, restricting blood flow or damaging muscles, tendons, and fascia. Colorado-based surgeon Dr. Tomas Hackett performed the complicated operation that saved her left leg from being amputated.

In a video shared to Instagram, the ski champion is sailing on a hydrofoil, writing that the event “was a big step in my recovery that made me incredibly happy. It may not have been snow but … it was one step closer to skiing.”

“I know I won’t be doing this, or much else, for quite some time after this next surgery, but I know I’ll get back to it,” she continued. “Eventually, I will.”

She said she expects to be on crutches for about four weeks and still has at least six months of rehabilitation in the works.

In 2010, Vonn became the first American woman to win Olympic gold in downhill skiing. Wherever she winds up, whether it’s slopeside or downhill, Vonn will always be our favorite comeback story.

#8227. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”

#8226. The Best Ski Packs of 2027, Tested in the Backcountry

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Our 14 testers ran 18 packs through a season of fast transitions, steep bootpacks, and long days to find the best of 2027. (Photo: Rick Sorensen)

Overview: The best backcountry ski packs of 2027 include the Ortovox Venet 30 ($170) for most skiers, the Raide EX55 ($599) for expeditions, the Dynafit Radical 30 Snow Pack ($190), and the Rab Descendor 40 Ski Pack ($200) for ski mountaineering. Our 14 testers—men and women—evaluated 18 packs over a full season in Colorado, Utah, Alaska, the Alps, and more, judging fit, weight distribution, access, and durability.

When traveling in the backcountry, it’s not just what you bring but how you carry it. Intuitive access points make finding and stashing items easy, and externally fastened gear needs to stay secure without blocking pockets. But making the most of capacity is arguably the most critical feature. As our testers make tracks farther out in the mountains and become more self-reliant, they tend to reach for higher-volume packs that can fit everything they need without overloading them to the point of a skin track gear explosion. We factored comfort into all of it while testing 18 packs, narrowing the field to the best backcountry ski packs of 2027 for every type of ski adventure.

Pros and Cons + Triple-zipper access + Huge hipbelt pocket – A-frame carry blocks pack access and the diagonal carry strap was a little tricky to access

Ski packs work best when you can avoid taking them all the way off and rooting through the main compartment when you need to pull out gear. That means shorter stops in the skin track—if you stop at all—which helps you keep momentum and body temperature up on cold days. The Venet 30 features triple-zipper access to the main compartment, which let our tester quickly grab his water flask while skinning around Hemavan, Sweden, and Helgeland, Norway. The large hipbelt was also a tester favorite. “While I loved the elastic waist on the Ortovox Freerider, the normal hip strap with the pocket on the Venet was a huge plus for general touring,” said one. “On longer days I kept snacks in it and on more freeride days I kept a GoPro, for which easy access allowed me to actually remember to pull my cam out before descents.”

Testers called this the most ergonomic and versatile pack they’ve used from Ortovox, thanks to its simplicity, the comfortable adjustability of its straps, and its full-contact back panel. The mini top pocket was well sized—not too deep and easy to access—and the hidden mini pocket in the avalanche tool compartment was useful for carrying an emergency bivy and small med kit, keeping them “out of the way” of the rest of your gear.

This pack’s ideal use is general touring with the occasional bootpack, but it’s capable as a more technical bag when ropes may be required. It performs well as a freeride sidecountry bag or on longer tours—comfortable for mellow days and functional for technical ones.

Features that would make this pack even more user-friendly: a small zip on the right back side to mirror the bottom zipper for water access, the ability to carry two ice axes (the elastic cord holds only one), and easier access to the pack when using side ski-carry.

Pros and Cons + Modular volume + Rolltop closure – No external helmet carry

Schlepping all your gear on a big hut trip or expedition-style endeavor has long presented a dilemma: how to carry a pack big enough for everything at basecamp while also having a daypack small enough for lighter missions. Bringing two packs is inefficient, but skiing with a few items jiggling loose in a giant frame pack feels cumbersome. The Raide EX55 expands to 75L and carries enormous loads, then cinches down once you’ve emptied most items out, so it skis like a little daypack. “During our big four-day ski traverse out of Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, I’d get to the base of a couloir, fill a bivy sack with all our junk, cinch the pack down, and boot up like I had a regular ski pack on,” said our Mammoth-based tester. “It skis incredibly well given how much gear it can swallow.”

Raide accounts for the added weight with thicker shoulder and hip straps and better load lifters than its smaller counterparts, the LF30 and LF40. All of it is ideal for heavier hauls. The EX55 doesn’t just turn into a giant sack and skimp on key features. You can still deploy your probe without taking off your pack—ideal for glacier travel of any kind—and the same goes for the shovel with the pack on one shoulder. Testers called the ski carry systems excellent, and being able to grab an ice tool without removing the pack is invaluable in steep bootpacks. “This pack strips backcountry skiing down to its absolute essentials but lets you do it on a bigger scale,” said one.

The one complaint we heard was that the EX55 lacks the external drop sleeve found in the LF30 and LF40 for carrying helmets and skins, so when the pack is loaded for overnight carries, it’s tough to stuff skins in and out of the front zip pocket. It also makes the pack very tall when fully loaded with a helmet inside.

Weight: 2.31 lbs Size: Women’s, Universal

Pros and Cons + Thick back panel padding + Easy-access diagonal-carry bungee cord strap – Not ideal for those who pack extra gear

When you’re banging out hot laps, your pack should feel like part of your body. This one holds tight to smaller female torsos and disappeared on the back of another Sierra tester last spring as she skied 1,500- to 7,000-foot days on Mount Shasta, in the Eastern Sierra and at Lake Tahoe’s Rubicon Peak. “This pack skied really well, and gear that’s good enough to disappear is my favorite,” she said  after testing other packs with hipbelts that didn’t curve as ergonomically as this one.

Testers appreciated the top, rear-panel, and side zips, which made it easy to organize their stuff inside and keep things like crampons and water readily accessible. The avy gear gets its own pocket with a wide zipper, and an ice axe can be removed without taking the pack off, as can skis with a skimo-style diagonal carry bungee strap.

At 30 liters, it’s right on the edge of fitting everything you might want to carry on a day tour. “When I went out to the Norman Clyde Couloir, conditions were cold and windy, so I wanted to carry more than I usually do for a day tour,” said our tester. “The pack fit snacks, 1 liter of water, a hardshell, a puffy, ski and boot crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a slender rescue sled, avy gear, a small first aid kit, and two pairs of gloves. I was definitely worried about busting the zipper, but it held all day.” The load lifters worked well to support this weight, and the thick back panel kept hard items like water bottles from poking into her back. If you prefer to bring this much stuff or more on most outings, you may find this pack a little too small.

Pros and Cons + Spot-on fit + Long side zipper accesses items of any size – Wobbly elastic diagonal ski carry

Spring ski mountaineering missions can mean longer days, longer approaches, and extra gear—crampons, more water, sometimes ropes—so you need a pack that carries it all in an efficient, functional arrangement. Loading it up is one thing; accessing it is another. The Descendor 40 balances both with a few key features. Our Colorado-based tester was a big fan of the side-access zipper, which is functionally useless if it isn’t long enough. This one is plenty long, and it was the only access point he needed while touring. He could easily pull out anything inside, including a large DSLR camera, skins, and a food bag, and he opened the rolltop closure only during full transitions.

The pack also has the best integration of hydration features. “On the right strap, there is a perfect pocket to carry a soft flask, including a strap to secure the flask against jostling,” our tester said. “I have lost soft flasks while skiing in other packs and am not worried about that on this pack. On the left shoulder strap, there is a small zippered pocket that is an appropriate size to carry items like gels, sunscreen, lip balm, etc. Overall, these features made it easy to stay hydrated and sunscreened on a fast and light ski tour.”

Testers lauded the comfortable back panel, wide hip straps, padded shoulder straps, and load lifters when needed. The pack carries weight well and fits true to size.

This pack is designed for long, efficient ski tours and glaciated summit pushes where ropes and technical gear are needed. It has features for ski mountaineering and carries additional gear like ice tools, with a gear loop for carabiners and a system for quickly strapping skis to the pack. The rolltop is an attempt to make the pack more versatile—a 40L pack that can act as a 25L—but it needs some refinement to better accommodate smaller volumes. Our tester also found the elastic strap for diagonal ski carry too long, and his skis bounced around while bootpacking couloirs.

Built for fast pow laps and and slackcountry days, the Dakine Heli 2.0 is everything you need to stay well equipped on your next mountain adventure. From diagonal ski and splitboard carry to vertical or horizontal snowboard carry, it doesn’t matter your style—it can get your gear wherever you need to go. The pack’s fleece-lined pockets keep your goggles smudge-free, and the snow tool sleeves keep your smaller items organized and accessible. And maybe most importantly, RECCO Technology helps keep you searchable in case of an avalanche or rescue.

Weight: 2.1 lbs (35L, S/M) Sizes: S/M, M/L

Pros and Cons + Easy access to inside storage + Removable snowboard carry straps – Avalanche tool pocket is too large

It’s a bold move to update a classic product, but Black Diamond took a leap on the tried-and-true Cirque by making several big changes. The brand added a side zipper to access the main compartment and more durable materials, including a PFC-free 210D nylon fabric and Dynex grid that’s stronger than the older version and more water repellent. Testers loved these new features and didn’t encounter any durability issues during the whole season of slamming the pack on and off in quick transitions with sharp ski edges and tools rubbing on the outside.

The new Cirque 35 excels on spring missions in the alpine, where quick access to crampons, an ice axe, and other gear is key. “I love a roll-top pack, and this is one feature that I really appreciate,” says one tester who toured it during winter and spring days around Aspen, Colorado. “I was able to throw in an extra layer for tours without hesitation because of the space it offered and how easy it was to get in and out, especially with the large side zipper.” The diagonal ski carry system with a bottom loop and top webbing strap with a hook was quick and easy to deploy in transition, and the ice-axe bungees were a breeze to unfasten on unexpected sections of steep terrain.

Our 6’1″ tester thought the pack was a bit short, and some disliked the hassle of opening both the webbing hook and roll-top buckle to get inside. Snowboard straps are sturdy but removable when you don’t need to carry a board on your pack.

Pros and Cons + Excellent freedom of movement + Compact fit – Limited carrying capacity

Skiing or snowboarding with too much extra space in a backpack allows the contents to rattle around inside, which can be an annoying distraction. Our Montana tester didn’t have that problem when hiking the ridge at Bridger Bowl, their local ski resort, with this compact, 15-liter pack with clever pocket placement and internal organization. Thanks to the low profile, it was comfortable enough to wear on the chairlift, and the fit felt snug while riding, too, with padding in all the right spots on the upper back, hips, and shoulder straps.

“It didn’t flop around at all like bigger packs do when empty, nor did it limit my movement in bumps or when really laying down carves,” another Montana tester said after securing the pack’s wide, sturdy hipbelt. They rode with this pack at Bridger Bowl in sub-freezing temperatures, requiring extra fuel and layers, and didn’t feel that it was too bulky. He also appreciated the glove-friendly A-frame and vertical ski carry options on short sidecountry hikes and bootpacks, along with snowboard straps and an internal avalanche tool compartment for sidecountry missions.

Overall, this is a small, space-efficient pack with smart pockets (fleece-lined goggle and external side zip) for short missions just beyond the gates or for fully-supplied resort laps.

Packs come in various sizes to fit different torso lengths, so measure your spine from the base of your neck to the top of your hips and choose your size accordingly. Torso lengths generally range from 15 inches, or size XS, to 20-plus inches, or size L. Because fit is the single most significant factor in pack comfort and carry, we recommend going to your local gear shop wearing the layers you plan to tour in and trying packs on. The hipbelt should securely wrap your iliac crest, and the back panel shouldn’t hit the back of your head when you’re wearing a helmet.

If half-day backcountry tours are your norm, choose a lower-volume pack, 20 to 30 liters, that fits just the essentials—shovel, probe, water, extra layers, snacks. If you typically spend full days in the backcountry, you’ll want a higher-volume pack, 30 to 40 liters, with room for the extra supplies you’ll need out in the elements. For overnight trips and expeditions, look for a 50-plus-liter pack.

Also make sure your avalanche shovel and probe slip easily in and out of the dedicated avy pouch in an emergency, and that the pack is big enough and organized enough for how you tour. Don’t be afraid to size up if you’re unsure how much space you’ll need—a few extra liters of empty space won’t weigh you down much. If you want to secure your skis to your pack, look for an A-frame or diagonal ski-carry strap system and back-panel suspension that can support the extra weight. The same goes for your helmet: most packs have integrated helmet carry, but not all do, so double-check if it’s essential to you.

Always carry avalanche safety equipment when traveling in the backcountry. That means wearing a beacon and carrying a shovel and probe in your pack. You’ll also need extra layers, a helmet, sufficient hydration—including something hot in an insulated bottle on longer backcountry days—snacks, a first-aid kit, and a basic repair kit.

To nail down the best ski packs of 2027, we seeded 18 products with 14 different testers. Each tester was matched to packs according to their planned objectives, body type, ability level, and testing environments. Then we set testers loose in the mountains, mainly in Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, Washington, California, and Alaska, with a few trips to Scandinavia and the Alps. Testers jammed gear into packs, stuffed them shut, and pushed them to their limits on both rugged and mellow ski ascents and descents.

We focused on newly designed packs with practical, ski-specific features that make traveling on snow easier, safer, and more enjoyable. We also brought tried-and-true, unchanged models into the mix so you’re seeing the best of what’s available. Comfort is a must, even for packs meant to carry smaller, lighter loads, as is durability, so we asked testers to evaluate straps, back panels, and hipbelt carry alongside the quality of materials.

Every time a pack went out, testers filled out feedback forms assessing fit, weight distribution, ease of access, and even pocket size and placement. Testers noted how easy it was to find what they needed, transition in the skin track, and carry their skis and boards on their backs while climbing steep couloirs. After a full season of rigorous testing, we selected the cream of the crop and reviewed those packs here.

Scott Yorko is a former gear editor for Backpacker, SKI, TransWorld SNOWboarding, and Outside. He lives in Colorado, where he splits his ski time between the world-class resorts around Aspen and the backcountry terrain of the West Elk Mountains. He loves to chase storms and visit pow-shredding friends, many of whom tested this year’s crop of ski packs in places like Alaska, Jackson Hole, the Sierra, Utah, and the Colorado Rockies.

#8225. This Climber Just Broke Dean Potter’s Half Dome Speed Record By Free Soloing ‘Snake Dike’

Michael Reese on the summit of Half Dome after breaking the trailhead-to-summit speed record (Photo: Courtesy of Michael Reese)

On October 28, 32-year-old American climber Michael Reese set a new fastest known time on Yosemite’s Half Dome, breaking an 11-year record set by the late Dean Potter. Reese climbed the 2,000-foot batholith from the Mist Trailhead to its summit in 1 hour 12 minutes 58 seconds, following Potter’s original line up Grizzly Gully and free soloing Snake Dike (5.7 R; 800ft). He broke Potter’s previous record from May 3, 2015, by about six minutes.

Potter, who famously competed with Hans Florine to set the speed record on the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft), saw the Grizzly Gully to Snake Dike line as a step toward blending trail running and climbing; he was aiming for a sub-two-hour time from trailhead to trailhead. He died 13 days after setting the record in a wingsuit accident at Taft Point.

Reese grew up in Boulder and came to climbing from running and triathlon. In September, he set a new speed record on the First Flatiron, at 7 minutes 51 seconds. After interviewing him last week in Boulder for a deep dive on the culture of free solo speed climbing, Reese told me he was headed for Yosemite the following day. I wished him luck. Having climbed both the First Flatiron and Snake Dike, I knew the latter would be a different game. The grippy, coarse sandstone of the Flatirons is a far cry from the slick, polished granite of Yosemite.

A few days after his Half Dome lap, I caught up with Reese to talk about his extensive training, the day itself, his safety margins on route, why he’s hoarded the same shoes as Potter since 2021, and why he thinks Potter’s record has stood for over a decade.

The following has been lightly edited for concision and clarity.

Michael Reese: Since I got into climbing in 2014, Dean Potter has been one of my idols, probably the one who I looked up to the most. The reason for that is he’s a hybrid athlete, you know? I come from a background in triathlon. I really like to mix cardio and strength. So Dean Potter was such an amazing individual because he had a professional-level aerobic and running fitness in addition to being one of the best free soloists, one of the best speed climbers, and one of the best BASE jumpers and highliners in the world. So I said, “Wow, how amazing is this individual to mix disciplines into territory no one’s ever seen?”

In 2021, one of Dean Potter’s good friends told me about this as a potential record to try. He became one of my main climbing partners. Of course, you know, this is 2021. Dean Potter had passed away years before. I went in 2021. I got totally destroyed because the approach was way too technical. I got lost, turned around in Grizzly Gully. It’s just such technical terrain. I went back on occasion, and started to learn the very complex approach of Grizzly Gully of alternating slabs, mazes, trees.

Bit by bit, I learned every year. I first went for a speed attempt in 2023. I went again in 2024, but I was really far off. I did 1 hour 37 [minutes] both times because it was really hard to figure out where to go. I wasn’t in as good of shape as I am in now, so I needed more fitness; I needed more practice.

Finally I came back this year, being in a lot better shape, spent two weeks practicing the route, then gave it a go.

Reese: Sixteen times before going for the record. Eight times free solo. Eight times with ropes and practicing the moves.  I practiced the crux 10 times in a row each lap, going back and forth across memorizing holds.  I didn’t really tick anything.  I jumped up and down until I purposefully would slip [while being clipped in]. I’d purposefully slip and find, “Okay, it took this amount of mistakes to actually cause a fall.”

Reese: Yes. The [complexity] of the Grizzly Gully approach, which is probably a low fifth-class approach with a lot of slabs. It has everything. It has running, it has steep, fourth-class dirt. That’s why I consider it the premier of technical mountain running, mixed running, and climbing, because you’re constantly switching gears.

Reese: We always did it a combination of simul-climbing and pitching it out. We would basically simul-climb to the crux section or sections. And then on those crux sections, I would be leading, and I would stop and [built a] traditional anchor and belay them up. That way they could give me a good belay for practicing the crux section.

Reese:  There was a lot of things that almost made it where I wouldn’t have been able to get the record. For example, I had gotten very sick just from being out in the cold. I had a cough. I had rolled my ankle two days before. So I was trying to nurse all these things, and I was just right on the fence of being like, “Am I healthy enough to go through this?”

Reese:  I’d scouted it out two days previously. Then I had a nice rest day where I just went for a picnic. I tried to ice my feet and I taped up my ankle.

My girlfriend started hiking a few hours before me to get in position because I wanted her to get some footage at the base. I hung out in Curry Village and rested. I did my typical routine where I drink a tablespoon of matcha powder to wake myself up and get amped up. I drank a ton of electrolytes because I knew that dehydration could be an issue. It was a very sunny day.

I went to the parking lot, I got on my shoes, and I put on gaiters to try to prevent a rock from going in[to my shoes in] the very dirty terrain. I had on just my watch, shoes, and shorts. No shirt because it was getting warmer. So then I did my typical warm up. I jogged for 15 minutes. I went up Grizzly Gully for a little bit to warm up my steep hiking muscles. I did some 30-second strides to get my heart rate elevated.

I  sipped some water, but tried not to overdo it, did some more strides, and then I meditated for a few minutes just to get in a good head space and say, “This is what I’ve been training for. This is my opportunity and it’s time to live in the moment.”

Reese: Not particularly. People looked at me like I was kind of crazy. Why am I sprinting back and forth at the trailhead? Why do I have no shirt when it’s 40 degrees out?

Reese:  Yeah. I connected my watch to GPS and began the effort from the Mist Trailhead on the pavement there. I had to swerve around some tourists for a minute and then I turned into Grizzly Gully. I didn’t see anyone [else] until I got to the base.

Reese:  Around noon. It was a pretty chill there, about 40 degrees. I wouldn’t mind it to warm up a little. And also because I needed to be very careful about other parties on route. Most places I could pass a party, but in a few places, like those first few pitches in the crux section, it could have been devastating to have a party on the way there.

Reese: I figured starting later would improve my chances of other parties at least being out of the crux section and a little bit further up, and, and that did luckily work out like that.

Reese:  Yeah, that’s a good question. A little bit of both. There’s a lot of places where the beta would vary so much I can’t rehearse everything. On the other hand, as you know, there’s a couple sections that the dike splits into two sections, and I do have each section rehearsed. So for the most part, I have options, and it would be okay besides that crux section. That would be pretty catastrophic.

Reese:  That’s a really good question. I do always prioritize safety. So if I came across a party and they were both in the anchor, or for example, if there was maybe just a just a follower that was securely on a tight top rope and it wouldn’t add any risk to them … and I was on record pace, I would be pretty keen to find a way to make it work, and maybe ask them just not to move, and I could tiptoe around. If there was a case where there was like a leader on the crux who was not looking solid, and I thought that going through would add risk to them or me … I would maybe bail on the attempt. Safety does come first. So yes, I would bail.

Reese:   I was going really hard, but I was saving just enough gas that I knew I wouldn’t, like, completely buckle on the crux. Then I hit the climb and felt really well. I instantly knew it was gonna be a good day on the rock. I was just kind of detecting every minuscule dish, kind of nailing the beta. And there were the people filming me at the crux section, cheering. I’d rehearsed it so much, it felt like a treat just to get across the crux and nail everything and feel really solid there. I still didn’t know if I would get it because I was gonna have to climb it faster than I ever had for the record still.

But it just flowed so well. So I did Snake Dike in 10 [minutes] 55 [seconds]. There was a special moment where I knew I would get the record because I knew I needed to finish them in, you know, 16 minutes or something. I knew I had done them in about 12 or 13 before. [That day] I did them in about 11 minutes. That Death March—that was the crux. As you know, that steep stuff after the Snake Dike, I was starting to kind of buckle, and I had a headache from dehydration. My knees and arms were starting to kind of buckle from lactic acid. But I knew I’d get the record, but I also just wanted to do the best I could and make a time that would last. So I pushed to the summit, sprinted across to the true summit, past the cables to the highest end on the north end. There was a party hanging out there.

I ran and tagged the summit, breathing hard. They were like, “Geez, dude,” like, “What did, what did you do?” I couldn’t even… My response was just dry heaving ’cause I’d gone so hard.

Reese:   The Five Ten Tennies. I bought a big stockpile of them before they went out in 2021 because I knew they were some of the best shoes and may not be made again. It’s the same ones that Dean Potter used on his attempt.

Reese:    I think the length of time honestly was kind of borderline. I think anything longer, it would be important to have something. Anything shorter, you don’t really need it. You do have a good point there. This actually was kind of a borderline scenario . Everyone’s different. For me, this one was right on the fence of bringing anything or not. And it depends on the day. If it’s a hot summer day, maybe I would change and bring something. Under the same conditions, I’m happy with not having anything.

Reese:    I think it’s because of how unique and special the line is. The magic is that most peaks, the fastest way is gonna be running around to the summit. On El Cap, the impressive nose record, you know, an hour 50… you can run around El Cap faster than that. You could run around the side and get up there in under two hours.

On Half Dome, it’s interesting, because from the Mist Trailhead to the summit, you summit up the cable. Most people go up the cables in the Subdome. So that requires running around everything, whereas Snake Dike allows a very direct line to the top.

One reason I think it’s lasted so long is Dean Potter was such an amazing athlete with his combined running and climbing. He had this high level of running combined with being able to solo Snake Dike, obviously a very easy free solo for him. So there are people that may be able to run a little bit faster, but they can’t solo Snake Dike. There are people that can solo Snake Dike, but they have nowhere near the fitness.

There have been some amazing athletes like Nick Elson from Canada.  He was able to tie Dean’s time by taking the shortcut through the forest and running around, splitting Liberty Cap and Broad Nick, shortcut through the forest to cut the switchbacks, and then up the cables.  Now everyone, including myself, starts at the Mist Trailhead. Which is an extra 60 seconds. [Editor’s note: Elson’s trailhead-to-summit time was 1 hour 20 minutes 57 seconds. He currently holds the round-trip speed record on Half Dome, with 2 hours 3 minutes 52 seconds].

When people said, “Oh, is Dean Potter’s vision really the best to go up Grizzly Gully and Snake Dike?” I think what I did proves that Dean Potter had the vision because Nick Elson, being one of the best trail runners… He’s extremely fit, one of the best athletes. I wouldn’t be able to beat his time by eight minutes to the summit off of pure fitness. So the eight-minute difference shows that Dean Potter’s line, the Grizzly Gully-Snake Dike, is just faster than the shortcut through the forest and going up cables.

Reese:    The honest answer is I don’t know. Maybe someone will get really motivated and beat it sooner rather than later. Maybe it’ll be another really long stretch. I tried to put enough of a difference where it’s gonna be a little bit hard.

Records are made to be broken. I’m not gonna be surprised if it’s broken one day. I don’t know when that’ll be. The thing is, it’ll probably have to be beaten by Grizzly Gully-Snake Dike, because it’s already been shown that some of the best trail runners can’t go under 1 hour 20 minutes by any other means running around. I think and hope it’ll have to be done by someone comfortable soloing snakes, like a runner-climber hybrid. Which makes Half Dome so special. The fastest way to the top is by climbing. It’s gotta be done by a climber.

#8224. Two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia, Leaving Officials to Look for Answers

A young grizzly in British Columbia (Photo: Colleen Gara / Getty Images)

Two hikers are dead after a suspected bear attack on Indigenous lands in British Columbia, provincial wildlife officials say. The incident comes just a year after a bear encounter in the same area left four people seriously injured.

Rescuers discovered one body on the afternoon of Nov. 2 near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, leading to a search for a second, missing victim.

That search concluded late Tuesday night when searchers found the second hiker dead. Officials with the B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) believe both were attacked by a grizzly bear, and efforts are ongoing to locate and trap any bears in the area for assessment.

Authorities and family members have since identified the pair as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her daughter, 20-year-old Selah Reed.

“It is not yet clear whether more than one bear was involved,” BCCOS Investigator Jeff Tyre told Backpacker. “Any captured bear will be assessed. If it is determined to have been involved in the attack, it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety.”

Family members first reported Balcarras and Reed overdue on Sunday, Nov. 1. Police and SAR operators found the first human remains on Monday afternoon, and called BCCOS due to evidence that suggested an animal was involved.

The victims’ remains have since been returned to their families, and the Snooka West Trail remains closed.

In the wake of the deaths, tribal authorities of the Nuxalk Nation, the First Nations people who live in the Bella Coola valley, expressed their support. Samuel Schooner, elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said in a statement that the tribe understands firsthand the trauma this incident will inflict on the victims’ family members and on the survivors of last year’s attack.

That incident occurred near Highway 20 on Nov. 20, 2025, when a grizzly attacked a local school group taking a lunch break. Adults were able to repel the animal with bear spray and a bear banger, but not before it severely injured four people, including three children. The four individuals were rushed to the hospital in varying conditions, and seven others required care at the scene.

No one died, and investigators continued to search for grizzlies in the area, eventually determining three bears could have been involved. Over the following two weeks, officers captured eight adult and juvenile grizzlies for forensic testing. All eight animals were eventually collared and relocated after they could not be forensically connected with the attack.

A total of 24 officers were involved in the response to that attack. Some reportedly drove 14 hours overnight to hand-deliver samples to the Alberta Wildlife Forensic Laboratory. BCCOS described both the response and the incident as extraordinary.

“In my 34 years of experience, I have not seen an attack like this with a large group of people,” Kevin Van Damme, with BCCOS, told Global News at the time. “So this is extremely rare and I think the public needs to understand that part.”

As 2025 field operations concluded, the Conservation Office reported decreasing bear sightings and pointed out that grizzlies in the area typically transition from hyperphagia to denning in or around December.

It’s unclear how long the current search will continue. A spokesperson for BCCOS said investigators were unavailable for comment due to heightened field activity.

“Our thoughts are with the family of the victims during this tragic time,” the agency said. “We are in contact with the family to offer any support we can as we continue to investigate this incident.”

#8223. Vail Has Free On-Mountain Grills— Here’s Where to Find Them

Skiing isn’t exactly a budget-friendly sport. Between lift tickets, equipment rentals, and overpriced on-mountain meals, the costs can add up quickly. But tucked away at one of Colorado’s most famous ski resorts is an unexpected way to save money on lunch. Instead of spending a small fortune at an on-mountain restaurant, skiers can bring their own meats and grill them slopeside.

My husband and I have done exactly that; we packed our own meat for a midday cookout between runs at Vail Ski Resort. It’s one of those experiences that feels almost too good to be true, especially at a resort where even a casual lunch comes with a price.

And while saving money is certainly part of the appeal, there’s something special about taking a break from skiing to grill your own lunch surrounded by the Rocky Mountains.

Located in Blue Sky Basin, Belle’s Camp offers a different kind of dining experience. Rather than ordering from a menu, guests can bring their own food and use the public grills to prepare lunch.

“Belle’s Camp is meant to be a different kind of on-mountain dining experience,” says Kevin Delonay, Vail Mountain’s senior director of food and beverage. “Guests bring their own food, gather with friends and family, and make lunch part of their day in Blue Sky Basin.”

It’s a surprisingly simple concept. Pack whatever you’d like to eat, carry it with you while skiing, and head to Belle’s Camp when you’re ready for lunch. Burgers, hot dogs, and steaks are all possibilities, although you’ll want to consider how easily your food can be transported in a backpack.

Visitors should also pack whatever they need to enjoy their meal, including any necessary utensils, condiments, and other supplies. Since you’re carrying everything onto the mountain, keeping things simple can make the experience much easier.

The grills are available during Belle’s Camp operating hours when Blue Sky Basin is open, although availability is subject to mountain operations and weather conditions.

“There are plenty of places at Vail where we cook the meal for you,” Delonay says. “Belle’s is special because we provide the setting and guests create the experience themselves.”

One of the biggest advantages of grilling your own lunch is the potential savings, especially for families or groups skiing together.

At Vail, a typical on-mountain cafeteria lunch can cost around $20 per person, while a more upscale dining experience can cost considerably more. At The 10th, Vail’s full-service restaurant at the top of Gondola One, a Wagyu cheeseburger is listed at $45. For a family of four, a lunch on the mountain could add up to $80 to $180 before drinks or other extras.

Keep reading: Everything You Need To Know About The Hottest New Ski Lunch Trend

Instead, visitors can stop at a grocery store before their ski day and stock up on ingredients for a fraction of the cost. For example, a pack of hot dogs, buns, and a few toppings could feed several people for around $15 to $20. Burgers are another relatively inexpensive option, while those looking to make lunch more of an occasion can bring steaks.

Of course, the exact savings depend on what you purchase and how many people are in your group. But for families or friends already spending hundreds of dollars on lift tickets, rentals, and other ski expenses, packing lunch is one of the easiest ways to cut costs.

And unlike eating a cold sandwich on a chairlift, grilling your own meal gives you a chance to sit down, relax, and enjoy a warm meal on the mountain with a new sense of appreciation.

Despite being one of the resort’s more unusual experiences, Belle’s Camp isn’t necessarily something every first-time visitor knows about.

According to Delonay, much of its popularity has developed organically, with skiers introducing their friends and family to the experience.

“Belle’s Camp has really grown through word of mouth, and I think that’s part of its charm,” he says. “People discover it, bring their friends back and start their own traditions.”

That’s part of what makes the experience so memorable. Some visitors might stop for a quick burger between runs, while others turn lunch into a full-blown gathering with friends.

“We see everything from a simple lunch with friends to groups that really turn it into an occasion,” Delonay says. “That creativity is part of what makes Belle’s so much fun.”

For my husband and me, grilling lunch at Belle’s Camp was a fun change from the typical ski resort dining experience. It’s not every day you get to cook your own meal in the middle of one of the country’s most famous ski resorts.

If you love grilling your own lunch on the mountain, Vail isn’t your only option in Colorado.

Loveland Ski Area, near the Continental Divide, also lets skiers bring their own food and cook lunch without visiting a traditional restaurant.

The resort has four on-mountain cabins that the public can use for free, each equipped with propane grills. Visitors are welcome and encouraged to pack their own food and prepare a meal during their ski day.

It’s a particularly appealing option for families and groups who want a warm lunch without paying on-mountain restaurant prices. But beyond the savings, it’s also a fun way to slow down and enjoy a different side of skiing.

After all, some of the most memorable moments on the mountain don’t happen on the slopes. Sometimes, they’re as simple as grilling lunch with friends and family between runs.

#8222. 7 Exercises to Help You Survive a Multi-Day Ski Trip, According to a Physical Therapist

Autumn belongs to apple orchards and slow cookers, unless you’re a skier. Then it belongs to gear hunts, fresh wax, and lift ticket research. The excitement lasts from the first turning leaf to about 10 P.M. on opening day. Then day two arrives. Your quads burn, your calves feel tight, and you wonder why you skipped those hip and groin stretches.

To understand why day two hits so hard, I spoke to Milica McDowell, DPT, owner of Clearwater Physical Therapy in Bozeman, Montana. She has 20-plus years of clinical experience, grew up skiing at Alyeska Resort in Alaska, and is married to Paul Herberger, a retired Freeride World Tour skier turned coach. So she knows a thing or two about the day-two body aches.

On day one, McDowell says, most skiers feel “absolutely nothing…except for adrenaline.” On day two, the tables turn and “most of us feel like we’ve been hit by a snowcat overnight.” She links the inevitable discomfort to three causes.

The first is eccentric loading, which happens when a muscle works while it lengthens, like the lowering half of a squat. In one study, 24 fit skiers spent four hours on the slopes. A day later, they still had reduced eccentric strength in their hamstrings and quads. McDowell calls the result “itty-bitty microtraumas in our muscle.” A 2019 research review puts soreness from unfamiliar eccentric work at its worst 24 to 72 hours after.

The second is a gap between gym fitness and ski fitness. Strength training and cardio help, McDowell says, but they’re “not specific to the demands of carving turns for hours on end.” A study of elite racers shows skiing leans on slow lowering and long, steady holds. While physical therapist Matt Hastings points to slow-tempo lifts and wall sits, McDowell notes that it’s “really really hard to prepare for hours in that flexed ankle and flexed knee position.”

The third is altitude. Thin air makes it harder to deliver oxygen to your muscles, so fatigue sets in sooner, and Cleveland Clinic says headache and fatigue can show up within a day or so of arriving.

As McDowell puts it, “it’s harder work to do the work.” Some soreness is normal, but it rarely lasts more than five days. If you wake up feeling hungover “without knocking back too many après PBRs,” McDowell says, thin air might be why.

None of that is a reason to skip day two. The best time to fix it is before you go. McDowell’s plan starts four to six weeks out, with three strength moves and one cardio drill. Start light, because new eccentric work causes its own soreness.

The last three moves on the list can be used as a five-minute warm-up.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Drop as deep as feels comfortable, then rise without locking out your hips and knees. Pulse for 20 to 30 seconds, building to 60 to 75 seconds, for four to six sets. It can “mimic the demands of repeated turns,” McDowell says.

Pop one heel up and hold the kettlebell on that side. Hinge down with a flat back, then stand tall with glutes fired. Most fit people can use 25 pounds, McDowell says. Do 12 to 20 reps for two to four sets.

It’s “just a fancy lunge,” McDowell says, with your back foot on a bench or step and a weight in one hand. Herberger suggested this one. Do eight to 12 reps for two to five sets.

McDowell likes short bursts of hard effort, 30 to 60 seconds long, followed by three to four minutes of rest. Aim for your heart rate to climb toward about 75 percent of your max, which the American Heart Association estimates at about 220 minus your age. If you have heart, kidney, or metabolic disease, talk to your doctor first. If you’re new to exercise, start lower and build.

McDowell’s warm-up starts with stairs, squats, or burpees until your heart rate climbs 20 to 30 beats per minute above resting. Then run through three moves for your calves, quads, and hips.

It copies your ski boot position and gives you “a nice stretch into your Achilles area.”

If you’re sore on day two, three, or four, lie on your side. Pull your heel to your seat and take slow breaths. A review of 99 studies found stretching didn’t reduce soreness, so think comfort, not cure. The same review found light movement and massage eased soreness, so take a walk between ski days.

A lunge with a twist toward the ceiling. It’s “a fantastic way to warm up your spine, rotators, core, and lower body all in one.” Herberger suggested this one too.

Day two sends the bill whether you plan for it or not. Joe Puchek, 73, has skied for 71 years, and he told SKI to “make the decisions today to allow you to ski tomorrow.” The wax can wait. The squats can’t.

#8221. The World’s Most Cinematic Trail Running Is Hidden Above the Arctic Circle

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

Hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

On my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

The Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!)

Combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

Although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

The vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

While there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

Lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

It’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

Weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

Getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

Traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s important to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

Designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.
