#8220. In His Own Words, a Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain

Honza Špička on Huascarán (Photo: Courtesy of Matěj Žák)

My name is Jan “Honza” Špička. My climbing partner, Matěj Žák, and I are two alpinists, climbers, mountaineers, skiers, and endurance athletes from Nove Straseci, a small town in the Czech Republic. Although we have known each other since childhood through our families (and the local ice hockey team), our climbing paths only crossed a few years ago. Since then, we have spent three seasons together in Peru’s Cordillera Blanca and two seasons in Argentine Patagonia. We have roped up together a few times on Czech sandstone as well. We are no professionals, though; rather than extreme lines, what we have behind us are moderately difficult routes climbed in our own style: clean and fast.

Our speciality? Long days in the mountains and a fast, lightweight approach. We take nothing on an expedition that we cannot carry on our own backs.

Huascarán is the highest mountain in Peru and the highest point in the entire tropics. Its south summit reaches 6,768m and the north summit 6,655m; the two are separated by a broad col called La Garganta (“the Throat” in Spanish) at roughly 6,000m. Huascarán lies at the heart of the Cordillera Blanca, the most heavily glaciated tropical mountain range in the world, and it gave its name to the surrounding national park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985. Because the Earth bulges slightly at the equator, the gravitational acceleration on the summit of Huascarán is among the lowest anywhere on the planet’s surface; a person there measurably weighs a little less than at sea level, by a matter of grams. The summit of Huascarán is also the second most distant point on Earth from the planet’s center, right after Chimborazo.

The mountain is named after Huáscar, the Inca ruler who fought his half-brother Atahualpa for several years over control of the Inca Empire. Atahualpa eventually defeated his brother and had him executed. The American mountaineer Annie Smith Peck, then over fifty years old, climbed the north summit in 1908. The higher south summit held out until 1932, when a German–Austrian expedition made the first ascent.

Huascarán, however, also has a darker side to its history. In 1962, a huge mass of ice broke away from the mountain, and the resulting debris avalanche swept down onto the towns of Ranrahirca. Then, on May 31, 1970, an earthquake off the coast triggered a far larger and more extensive avalanche from the north summit, which within minutes buried, among other places, the entire town of Yungay. The earthquake and avalanche combined took the lives of approximately 67,000 people. It was the deadliest single avalanche disaster by death toll in recorded history.

This tragic event unfortunately also carries a strong Czechoslovak mark. It was right here, in the valley between Huascarán’s north summit and Huandoy Sur, that a Czechoslovak expedition was camped—and the whole expedition became a victim of this mountain.

If we take into account the victims of 1970 and all the climbers who have died on its slopes, it is probably the mountain responsible for more human lives than any other in modern history.

The ascent itself, via the Normal Route, is not particularly difficult, but Huascarán’s glaciers are retreating fast, and so today some routes that were relatively straightforward climbs just a generation ago involve significant objective hazards. In the six years that I have lived in Peru, I cannot remember a year when Huascarán did not claim another victim. There have even been years when it allowed no one at all to reach its summit.

The start of our trip began on Friday, July 11, in the evening in our favourite “pollo a la brasa” restaurant. Our whole group, which we called the “Cayesh crew,” met for a shared dinner to load up on a solid dose of protein before what was to be the main climbing objective of the season for all of us: Huascarán Sur. It has to be said, though, that for none of us was Huascarán the center of the universe. We all had it in “one day, maybe, I’d like to, if it comes to it…” mode, but there was certainly no obsession with this “fat one.” I already had three unsuccessful attempts behind me, but even so I wasn’t insisting on “bagging it.” Yet somehow the appetite, the motivation, the hunger for it arrived. And essentially by coincidence it arrived not only for Matěj and me but also for our friends from Peru. In the end we formed three teams of two.

I have known Saul—formally, Freddy Saul Mendoza Lizana—since 2021; he was essentially my first climbing partner here in Peru. Since then we have been through a lot together—in the mountains, on the crags, at home, and in the pub. He was like my Peruvian brother. We were so close that my wife Alča and I were already counting on a little room for Saul for when we one day return to the Czech Republic and settle down somewhere.

Agnieszka is a Polish “machine” with several 8a/5.13b sport routes to her name. She had seen plenty in the mountains, too. Definitely no lightweight.

Alejandro “Chicho” Ugarte Jordan was a professional photographer from Lima. His main interest was unique mountain images captured with his DSLR or his drone. We had known each other since 2022 through the Skiing Peru project, which we were both part of. We often spent time together with our girlfriends in Lima outside the season, too.

Artidoro “Arti” Salas Gaitan was a pure Huaracino—someone who comes from Huaraz. He was born in the town at the foot of the Cordillera Blanca and lived there his whole life. He ran the Big Mountain hostel, well known among climbers. I personally have known him since 2021, when I spent my first season in Huaraz at his hostel.

Our expedition began on the morning of Saturday, July 11, when we loaded the van with heavy packs. Under the watchful eye of—as Matěj called him—our adoptive father Paul, our friend and the owner of the cozy Cayesh Guest House bed and breakfast, we set off for our starting point, the village of Armapampa in the Yungay area. From Huaraz, it was about a two-hour drive. Besides the six of us, Alenka came along, too, having arrived from Lima that same morning, as did Míša, a Czech woman living in Nepal who had just popped over to Peru to see friends. The girls, however, were only going on a day trip to the hut and back down the next day.

On the edge of the beautiful village of Armapampa, we unloaded our gear from the van, ate the last gluten-free cinnamon rolls that Alenka baked for the trip, and shouldered our heavy packs. Matěj took a group photo and we set off towards Refugio Huascarán, our base camp. We reached the refugio at 4,650m spread out over quite a wide time range (Matěj first, at 2 hours 45 minutes, and Saul and Aga last at a little over 6 hours). Who knows where and why they lingered; apparently they were finishing off their avocados. Either way, the trail was easy and there was no rush, so everyone went at their own pace.

There was no one at the hut apart from us, so we enjoyed it immensely. The evening was a very friendly affair: dinner, beer, guitar, and singing in four languages mixed together. And, of course, planning the climb.

This is where the first, relatively pivotal moment came. Aga wasn’t feeling well—to be precise, she felt pretty crap—so she decided to walk down with the girls. That left the five of us Mohicans. Saul immediately arranged with the lads to form a three-person team. At the time, it seemed to me a good idea. Saul is the most experienced of the three, and the team would only be stronger for it. In hindsight, I blame myself that we didn’t tell him to stay with Agnieszka; Aga was his big “project.”

After breakfast at the hut, we packed our rucksacks, took a group photo, and set off. The girls headed down; the lads headed up. None of us had any idea that this would be our last photo together, and that the girls would never see Saul, Chicho, and Arti again. Just writing this sentence brings tears to my eyes.

The second day of the climb up Huascarán was easy going. A few hundred vertical meters led up to the glacier, then a few hundred more traversed over a gently angled and relatively safe glacier to the spot where Camp 1 is set, at about 5,300m. Matěj and I arrived first, and shortly after us Arti and Chicho, with Saul behind them. We pitched the tents, melted water, cooked food, took photos, rested, and fine-tuned the details for tomorrow’s summit push.

Huascarán is normally climbed via the Garganta col, where Camp 2 is placed at 5,950m, and from there climbers make for the summit. All of us, however, were heading for the El Escudo (“The Shield”) route, which is technically harder but objectively safer,and of course more fun. It is a roughly 600-meter long ice face at 60 to 70 degrees. Thanks to its shape, there are no seracs hanging above you, no cornices, and far fewer things that can come down on your head. Unfortunately, there is little room for a Camp 2 there, so the Escudo is usually climbed from Camp 1 straight to the top, with the descent via the Normal Route.

We set our departure time for 10 pm. While the sun was still up, we crawled into our sleeping bags to get at least a little sleep and recharge the batteries a bit. We all knew that brutally hard work lay ahead.

This was it: summit day. Matěj and I got up at 9:30 p.m. so that we could leave at 10. We could hear the lads sometime before 9. In the end, we left more or less together: the lads at about 10:15 pm, we a few minutes after them.

Given the profile of the route over the Escudo, the plan from the start was to climb in pairs. Later, we became a pair and a three. You cannot climb this with five people on one rope, and none of us ever suggested it. The same applies to the descent.

The first part of the route was probably the most dangerous section of the whole ascent. It was a zone of crevasses and seracs of a size you will not encounter in Europe. There were a few sections of steep ice, but it wasn’t outright hard; it was just that something could come down at any moment. This section was shared with the Normal Route, which then branched off to the left towards Camp 2, while we headed right towards El Escudo.

We reach the bergschrund in less than two hours, with the lads following an hour or so behind us. Here we re-tied onto the full length of the 60m rope and racked up all our gear. In the process, I dropped my radio somewhere into the bowels of the glacier, and Matěj set off upward. The terrain wasn’t hard, so we simul-climbed on a single rope. Matěj climbed three to four pitches this way until he ran out of ice screws. On his last two snow pickets, he built a belay and let me through. My section was more hard snow than ice:easier climbing, less fun, but with correspondingly worse protection. I had three snow pickets on my pack, but I wanted to save those for later, for the belay anchors. After climbing some six pitches on just a handful of screws, I topped out over the lip of the Escudo, where I brought up Matýsek. (Editor’s note: “Matýsek” is a Czech nickname for “Matěj.”) By then, we were at 6,300m. It was cold as hell, with the sun still nowhere in sight. I dropped a glove and started feeling properly ill from the altitude. From this moment on, I suffered like an animal. The section from the top of the Escudo to the summit was endless; it wasn’t as steep any more, but it was long, and the soft snow did nothing to help our progress.

Sometime before 9 a.m. on Monday, July 13, though, we stood on the summit of Huascarán Sur. We didn’t really feel much joy, because we knew the worst was still ahead of us: the way down. On top of that, the summit was a completely flat plateau. You could play soccer on it, only you’d have a long way to go for a stray ball. Even so, weakness came over me and I cried. It was my fourth attempt, with my partner and childhood friend, and exactly a month to the day since our dog, Pisco, was poisoned. I cried again just remembering him. But the joy was there, too, although the main part of it was supposed to come down below. And it did come. But only for a moment.

We didn’t linger on the summit. There really was nothing there. After a snack, a little tea, and the summit photo, we headed down. No one had been on the summit for about two to three weeks, so there were no tracks and no trail. Our only guide was the offline mapy.cz app, which traced the Normal Route. But it was the route that was walked an unknown number of years ago, so we treated it as a rough indication only. We re-tied into classic glacier-travel mode, roughly 15–20 meters apart, with the rest of the rope coiled around each of our bodies.

A few minutes from the summit, on the empty, white, flat plateau, I saw something that looked like the windblown hint of a trail. Before I even got there, something happened and I was falling through the air into an icy hell.

A crevasse. With no sign whatsoever of its existence, it had been waiting there silently for its victim. I remember precisely the feeling of flying into the void. It was as if I were falling for an eternity. Suddenly, I felt the rope come tight, and I knew that was Matýsek. But I keep falling. In that instant, I was certain that in a moment, Matýsek would come flying in after me and we’d both be dead.

But a miracle happened—a miracle called Matěj. The rope bit again and I stopped. He bloody well caught me. I was hanging about 12–15 meters down in a crevasse that runs 100m in each direction and could easily be 50m, 100m, or 300m deep. Who knows? Below me, I saw nothing but icy hell. The crevasse was completely covered with a cap of fine snow. Zero chance of seeing it.

To my own surprise, I didn’t panic; I knew exactly what to do. My only connection to our world was the rope I was hanging on and whatever Matěj had rigged up there to keep me in this world. I clipped a Micro Traxion onto my harness as a self-belay and climbed up the vertical ice wall towards the surface as far as I could. I felt so OK that I even took three photos inside the crevasse. When the line of the rope stopped me from climbing any farther, I swung out into space. I ascended the rest on prusiks.

In a little under half an hour, I was out, back on the surface, back in the world. Only now did I breathe out.

Matěj and I fell into each other’s arms and began to grasp what we just survived. It would have taken very little for him to come in after me, and no one would ever have found us. In hindsight, I see it as an enormous miracle and a measure of enormous skill on Matěj’s part. He saved our lives. And maybe it was at this very moment that we realized this really was no joke and that things were getting serious. We continued the descent very cautiously, and we were genuinely scared.

We reached the edge of an ice wall where the Normal Route was supposed to be, but there was nothing there—nothing at all. There was no question of searching for a way through this labyrinth. The wall looked to be about 20m high, with a ramp below it along which we hoped to traverse off left toward the Normal Route.

We rappelled off two snow pickets into a relatively safe spot surrounded by seracs. I remember looking at the leaning towers next to us and thinking that one deep breath would be enough to bring the whole lot down. Still, we felt a certain safety in our little hollow. Finally, we had a bit of time to catch our breath, eat and drink a little, and get in touch with the lads.

Before I could do that, they called me. They said they were about 200 vertical meters below the summit. But it was already late, around 12 to 1 p.m., so their plan was to traverse off towards the Normal Route and descend by it.

I told them to try to find our tracks and our rappel, and to really watch out for crevasses, because I had just fallen into one. We confirmed that everything was OK and that we would meet in the evening at Camp 1, or if need be, at base camp, depending on the time and our energy. If I had known that this was the last time I would speak to them, I would have told them so much more.

A little later, while searching for the route on the map, my phone slipped out of my hand and vanished somewhere below. But I didn’t dwell on it. I knew we had other worries. It was just a shame to lose the photos from inside the crevasse.

Another unpleasant rappel off a 25-meter serac, and we were on the slope leading towards the Garganta. By now the weather had turned and visibility had dropped to a few tens of meters. But we were already in the Garganta, at 6,000m. All we needed now was to find Camp 2, which was just a flat patch where tents stood two days ago. From there, there should be some tracks and a route down.

We wandered about a bit, but eventually we found Camp 2 and there really was a hint of tracks. Shortly before that, the summit shook off its cloud, and we saw the lads above us at about 6,300 or 6,400 m. It even looked to us as though they were closer to the Normal Route than we were. We were really relieved.

The route from Camp 2 to Camp 1 is the most dangerous crux of the climb. It is a zone of avalanches, collapsing seracs, and crevasses. Later, Matěj and I agreed that we both felt as if we were living in some kind of virtual reality, outside our bodies, just waiting for the video game to end. Maybe that was why I didn’t really register the risk.

We arrived back at Camp 1 at sunset. With our last reserves of strength, we packed up and continued down to the refugio. A hot dinner and a bed was, after all, a big draw. And it was only a little under two hours more.

We reached the hut sometime before nine in the evening, after 23 hours on our feet. We asked for something to eat and a beer, then went to sleep. We thought about the lads and somehow had no doubt that they were fine and that they were at Camp 1. After all, we saw them a short way above Camp 2.

In the morning, we woke up at the hut completely wrecked, but suddenly also happy with what we’d achieved. We expected the lads to turn up any moment, and then we’d race down into the valley. The news from the lads, however, was different.

Saul wrote that they couldn’t find the way down and had to bivouac somewhere above Camp 2. But they were OK, he said; they survived the night up there without any camping gear. They were tired, Chicho was apparently feeling ill, but all were OK. They would try to find the descent route. From then on, we were to communicate with Chicho, as Saul’s battery was dead.

We still had no idea that things were bad. But neither did the lads. Because things weren’t bad yet. We managed to download our GPS track onto a phone and send it to the lads as a mapy.cz link. Up above Camp 2, there was occasionally a signal, so we communicated with the lads via WhatsApp.

At 9:10 a.m., Chicho wrote asking us to send our route. At 9:15 a.m., we sent the mapy.cz link and it was delivered.

At 10:16 am, Chicho sent a photo and a video from where they were. They sounded fine; Camp 2 was visible below them. At 10:18 a.m., we sent them a crib sheet of roughly which way to go down, including a sketch drawn onto their photo. This was delivered. At 10:21 a.m., we asked Chicho whether he had our route on mapy.cz. This was the last message delivered to Chicho. After 10:21 am, no further messages were delivered. From then on, there was no communication from them.

Since the weather was beautiful, the lads were fine, and there was no signal lower down towards Camp 2, it never occurred to us that the lads might be in trouble. We were certain they had descended lower, lost signal, had flat phones, and so on—but were descending. There was essentially no reason to think anything else. They werebujacos”—tough guys. They had survived a night without sleeping bags at 6,400m, and now they would just run down to us, to the girls, to lunch, to a beer.

Given these assumptions, we knew we had several hours of waiting before they would appear above Camp 1, which could be seen from the hut. Meanwhile, we tried to contact them by radio and by phone, in case they happened to come into signal. But still, we were completely calm.

When about 3 p.m. came and there was no sign of them, though, it seemed odd to us. It had gone on too long. We decided we would go up and look for them. They were probably tired and frozen, and another night up there would be truly critical.

We ate, brewed tea, and took all the clothing we had. In the meantime, I called a friend, a guide, down in town so that he knew something was going on and could start rounding up help if needed. But there was still a chance alive in us that they were at Camp 1, asleep in the tent, and simply had no way of letting us know. Down in town, a group of volunteers was already getting ready to set out to help. There is no organized professional mountain rescue in Peru.

But there was no one at Camp 1. By then we sensed that things were bad; we just didn’t know how bad. On top of that, a snowstorm was moving in.

The message we sent down was clear: It was official, we needed help. The lads were somewhere up there. We were going up for them. We knew that down in the valley things were already under way and would keep going without us. But we had a different task: to find them and bring them down.

We pack all their sleeping bags as well and set off up into the gale. Matěj created a Garmin messaging group and made our position trackable online. He realized more than I did that we were heading into real trouble.

I have friends up there – my “churaks,” my “hermanos.” I registered nothing.

For the first time in my life, I was faster than Matěj. In my head, I knew they were up there, frozen and exhausted but alive, and that we were their only chance.

In these conditions I would turn around on any climb of my own; I would never go on. But now it wasn’t about me. It was about the lads. The moment we gave up, they would have no chance.

We got as far as above Camp 2, to 6,000m, but there was nothing anywhere. That was shortly before midnight. Just gale, snowfall, a temperature I’d estimate at around minus 30 degrees, and not a trace of the lads.

By this point I knew things were very bad. In this weather, no one survives up here for even an hour. Matýsek was very afraid of going down because of the avalanche danger and pushed for us to stay at Camp 2 and somehow sit it out with all those sleeping bags. I knew that if we stayed, we would be dead within the hour. In the end, I convinced him that we had to go down. That was about 50/50. But staying up there felt to me like 90/10.

The descent was horrific. Avalanche terrain was everywhere we looked, with giant seracs over our heads almost the entire way. Visibility was near zero, and our tracks drifted over with snow. Nevertheless, our guardian angel was on duty again and guided us down. We get back to Camp 1 sometime around 3 a.m. on Wednesday, July 15. There I well and truly collapsed, mentally and physically. We crawled into the tent for a while and waited for the first group of volunteer rescuers, who, as we already knew, were on their way from the refugio.

Even in the tent and in a sleeping bag, 700 vertical meters lower, the weather was terrible, and it was here that Matýsek told me we were one–all. He had saved us above that crevasse, and I had by insisting that we go down.

The first rescue team reached Camp 1 just after first light, sometime after 6 a.m. It was five people in all, three guides and two aspirant guides, and among them my good friend Szymon, who was the only one closer to me than Saul. That was all. We handed over all the information we had and let them go up. We would head for the refugio, where further teams were supposedly bound: one to set up a support base at Camp 2, another at Camp 1. Supposedly lots of people were coming.

Unfortunately, we were in Peru, where everything does not quite work. We met the Camp 1 team below the glacier—five lads, all friends, climbers, and volunteers from Peru, Colombia, Spain, and the Czech Republic. No Camp 2 team ever came, and in fact, there never was one. The five lads up above had packed late in the evening and set out from Huaraz to help friends in need. In a single push they climbed to over 6,000m. But because of the lack of support and the conditions up there, they had to turn back in the afternoon and descend to Camp 1. That essentially ended any realistic chance of finding the lads alive. I personally had known already at Camp 2, which we had climbed to in our attempt to find them, that there was almost no chance left.

From then on, great chaos set in across the whole organization of the rescue and search. As I already mentioned, Peru has no mountain rescue service; there are no rescue helicopters, no rescuers, no system, no protocol, no designated person to take charge of any coordination. Everything happened through the WhatsApp group that Matěj created when we set out for the lads. Everything was done on the basis of volunteers, friends, guides and family members.

Eventually, the police, the high-mountain police (Policía de Alta Montaña), and apparently even the army joined in to help. But their help consisted solely of transporting volunteers by helicopter from the town of Caraz to the refugio at 4,650m, and the first helicopter took off 24 hours after the official call for help. What’s more, it flew up empty, to assess the situation, only to find that another police helicopter had been sitting on the “helipad” by the refugio for several days, badly parked, and that its pilots were afraid to take off in it.

In the end, some transport up did take place, but effectively only on the following days. If someone down below had been able to coordinate it, they could have sent the line of volunteers towards base camp on foot, with a herd of donkeys, on the very first day of the search (July 15), and they would have been there far sooner than waiting until the next day to see whether anyone would get a place on the helicopter.

The entire rescue, and subsequently the search, was run by volunteers and the families. It was they who hired private companies with advanced drones, they who coordinated everything, mainly with the police, they who did everything they could. I myself went back with two volunteers a few days later to a point just above Camp 1 to attempt a further search with drones—without success. The zone where all the clues ended—GPS signals, the location of the last photos, the hint of the last tracks, and so on—is at around 6,500m. Camp 1 is at 5,300m, and most drones simply cannot fly that high and that far. Only the advanced police drones can, and they in turn lacked experienced pilots willing to risk it. Going higher wasn’t possible because of the conditions on the mountain. So, a stalemate. In the end footage from the suspect zone was obtained, but there was not a trace of the lads.

After almost detective-like work by many friends—using the GPS signal from their watch as requested from Garmin headquarters, footage from private and police drones, plus footage from the guides who went all the way up during the search, information from us, and the lads’ last photos—it appears that the lads missed our belay station by literally a few meters, and that while crossing a snow bridge over gigantic crevasse systems it collapsed beneath them.

When I first wrote this report, it had already been more than three weeks since I last saw the lads, since I last spoke to them. Still nothing has been found today, and in my view it will be hard for anything to be found. The scale of everything on Huascarán is utterly absurd: crevasses several hundred meters wide and deep, seracs the size of apartment blocks… Sure, this isn’t the Himalaya, and it doesn’t look like it, either. Huascarán looks like two lazy fat blokes lying side by side. But beware of it. That mountain is mean and hostile, and although on paper it isn’t hard—the Normal Route was reportedly graded only AD/AD+, the Escudo D—it is no game. You are playing for your life at every single step.

I don’t think that either we or the lads made any fundamental mistake; it was simply that Matýsek and I had a large dose of luck, while the lads had a little less of it.

I am not writing this story for sensation. It is just one real story with a tragic ending. If at least a few of you take something from it—ideally some kind of lesson—it will have served its purpose. As we all know, the mountains give, but sometimes they also take away. We unfortunately now know that this is no empty phrase but the hard truth.

Editor’s note: This trip report has been translated from the original Czech into English with permission of the author. Place names and local terms (La Garganta, El Escudo, refugio, Huaracino, pollo a la brasa) have not been translated from the original Spanish.

#8219. What’s Your Hiking EDC? Backpacker’s Editors Share Their ‘Every Day Carry’ Gear

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Associate Editor Will Brendza's EDC requires three to four pockets, but prepares him with tools, fire-starter, light, and his favorite pair of sunglasses. (Photo: Will Brendza)

It seems like everywhere online people are sharing photos of their “Every Day Carry” (EDC) kits. Watches, pocket knives, key fobs, and other day-to-day, on-your-person gear are photographed in a spread and posted to socials with a quippy caption. Often, it’s tactical bros who just want to show off their knives and handguns. For others, it’s an opportunity to flash a Rolex or humble brag about their expensive whip. It’s an internet trend that’s exploded among gear nerds, collectors, survivalists, and preppers.

But what about hikers? We’ve all got a dedicated list of gear we wouldn’t hit the trail without. How would the EDC trend look if you shook people down on the trail to find out what was in their pockets?

We wanted to know. So we’re starting with Backpacker’s editors—to see what our trail EDC looks like and how it’s different from person to person. We’re curious what others’ might look like, too. Tag @backpackermag in a photo of your hiker EDC on Instagram, and we’ll check it out.

Here’s what our team is never leaving the house without. #hikerEDC

The most important piece of gear I keep on me is my Ombraz Armless Sunglasses. I’ve got sensitive eyes and a penchant for losing things—these dandies solve both of those problems. They stay tethered to my neck or head, even when I’m underwater or upside down, and offer fully polarized eye protection. Next is my Knives of Alaska folding knife, which is big enough for most camp tasks and still fits in a pocket. I also always keep a bandana handy, because it’s the single most versatile tool a backpacker can carry (serving as a headband, handkerchief, surface cleaner, hot mitt, face mask, etc.).

If you follow Backpacker’s Editor’s Gear Picks, you’ll recognize my Nocs Zero Tube Monocular, which is one of my favorite backpacking tools. For scoping routes, spotting wildlife, or just enhancing the details of a view, it’s an incredible companion. My no-frills Petzl headlamp is getting old, but still serves me well when I get caught on the trail after dark.

Then I usually keep tissues for when I get sniffly, a pen and paper for taking notes, my ID and money, the sunscreen and chapstick I apply on the go, and, of course, a lighter (preferably one with a recognizable graphic so people are less likely to “accidentally” snatch it).

Not pictured: My dog, a compass, and my Coros Pace 4 Pro watch.

I’m on a never-ending quest to see how many essential items I can cram into a waist pack, but one thing I usually leave at home during non-working hours is my smartphone; I’ve found that the more I disconnect, the happier I am. Instead, I’m generally packing an AT&T Cingular Flex 2 flip phone, which cost me all of $15 and, besides texting and calling, can display rudimentary hiking maps with the O.map app. I supplement it with a button compass, which is enough for me to rough out directions, and my Life Camera S168, a tiny digital camera capable of taking better photos and videos than my Walmart phone.

A cheap space blanket has saved my bacon at least once, and I usually add a lighter wrapped in a twist of duct tape and a travel-size tube of sunscreen. My (sadly discontinued) Leatherman Tread multitool bracelet keeps a TSA- and security-friendly cutting tool and a host of screwdriver heads at hand, and for dayhikes where the possibility of being caught after dark is remote, I toss in my (also sadly discontinued) 40-lumen Black Diamond Ion Keychain Light. My wallet-size first aid kit has antibiotic ointment and a couple of adhesive bandages in kid-friendly patterns for the inevitable skinned knees and elbows that happen on family hikes.

I carry a waterproof notepad for jotting things down. My pen of choice is a Pilot Precise Varsity disposable fountain pen; it’s probably not the lightest scribbler out there, but it’s fun to write with. I usually bring cheap sunglasses so I don’t stress when I break them—these are from last year’s Outside Days in Denver. My choice of snacks is cheap, too: fruit snacks, granola bars, or whatever I most recently bought in bulk for my kids. And the toothbrush? I’ve just found my quality of life is way higher if I can brush my teeth whenever I want.

Most days, I walk out my front door and hit my local trails with very little in my pockets save for my iPhone and one or two dog poop bags (whatever brand was on sale last time I ran out). If I’m carrying any snacks, gummy candy is the first thing I reach for, and Nerds Gummy Clusters have never let me down. On long, difficult efforts, I like Honey Stinger Organic Energy Chews. My Garmin Instinct Solar watch is always on my wrist to track mileage or elevation gain, and of course, if I’m going far, I’ll pack my inReach to contact help in an emergency. Whether I’m hitting the trail or exploring a new city, my Nalgene is along for the ride, too.

Not pictured: My Kula cloth, avalanche transceiver for winter adventures, collapsible dog bowl, and some Leukotape wrapped around my sunscreen stick.

#8218. Lindsey Vonn Is Headed for Her 9th Surgery. She’s Still Thinking About Skiing.

Lndsey Vonn inspects the slope before the second official training for the women's downhill event at the Tofane Alpine Skiing Centre during Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games (Photo: Stefano Rellandini/AFP via Getty Images)

Lindsey Vonn is just days away from her ninth surgery in as many months, and the three-time Olympic medalist is still thinking about skiing.

On November 9, Vonn, 42, is heading into what’s slated to be the final surgery on her left leg following her severe crash during the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics in February. In an exclusive interview with Forbes, the alpine skier detailed her upcoming surgery.

“The plan is to remove all of the hardware, finally fix the ACL, and hopefully that’s my last surgery,” she told Forbes.

In February 2026, Vonn started the Olympic downhill race despite rupturing the ACL in her left knee just days earlier. After taking an aggressive line through the first few turns, Vonn clipped a gate just 13.4 seconds into her run, pushing her off course at the Tofane Alpine Skiing area.

The impact sent her spinning through the air before she crashed onto the icy surface, ending her race. Vonn was eventually airlifted to a hospital and diagnosed with complex fractures of the two bones in her lower left leg. Doctors put three plates and up to 20 screws in her leg, but couldn’t fix her ACL until her bones healed properly, she told Parade.

In the weeks following her initial surgery, Vonn shared that her injuries were so severe that she had to undergo an emergency fasciotomy, a procedure used to treat acute compartment syndrome. This potentially life-threatening condition occurs when pressure builds up around muscle groups, restricting blood flow or damaging muscles, tendons, and fascia. Colorado-based surgeon Dr. Tomas Hackett performed the complicated operation that saved her left leg from being amputated.

In a video shared to Instagram, the ski champion is sailing on a hydrofoil, writing that the event “was a big step in my recovery that made me incredibly happy. It may not have been snow but … it was one step closer to skiing.”

“I know I won’t be doing this, or much else, for quite some time after this next surgery, but I know I’ll get back to it,” she continued. “Eventually, I will.”

She said she expects to be on crutches for about four weeks and still has at least six months of rehabilitation in the works.

In 2010, Vonn became the first American woman to win Olympic gold in downhill skiing. Wherever she winds up, whether it’s slopeside or downhill, Vonn will always be our favorite comeback story.

#8217. 20 Steals From Backcountry’s Early Black Friday Sale

I love Black Friday. I also hate Black Friday. Sure, you can snag unbelievable bargains on outdoor gear on what’s become the national holiday of capitalism, but it’s also easy to get lost in the digital vortex. There are just so many sales to choose from, and often those sales are limited to a brief window. Decision paralysis and exhaustion ensue—even if you haven’t loaded up on tryptophan-laced turkey.

That said, I’m happy to report that Backcountry’s Early Black Friday sale starts today, November 6th. While the online outfitter will add heaps of gear to the sale as Black Friday approaches, the early sale gives bargain hunters weeks to shop.

Even better? Right now, Backcountry is offering up to 20% off full-price items and an extra 10 to 20% off clearance, from high-end brands like The North Face, Blundstone, Dakine, Black Diamond, and more. No code necessary, just add your wish list gear and the discount shows up in your cart when you’re signed in to your (free) Summit Club Membership. And if you’re a Summit+ Member, you get even more savings, like an extra $50 cash back on certain deals.

This is pretty cool. I write about the best gear sales every month for Outside, and this discount code gives shoppers a rare opportunity to scoop up current gear (not last season’s inventory) at a double-digit discount. To celebrate, I rounded up 20 picks from Backcountry’s Early Black Friday Sale, all of which I’ve personally tested or am currently putting on the chopping block here in Tahoe.

Long story short: keep reading for my top picks or check out the sale in its entirety here.

Three decades after its debut, The North Face dug into the archives and dropped an alpine-ready version of the iconic Nuptse Jacket (available in both men’s and women’s styles). Generously stuffed with 800-fill goose down (Backcountry’s current product description says 700-fill, but The North Face claims higher-grade 800-fill down here), the Summit Nuptse puffy is as warm as they come. I love the boxy cut and classic color-blocked colorways—style elements that are at home in mountain towns and metros alike. In my opinion, this puffy is overkill on the slopes, but I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend it as a winter camping basecamp parka or a belay puffy. That said, you can also deploy it as a daily winter essential, whether you’re partaking in parking lot après at your local ski resort or on a frigid dog walk.

This pairing of the Smith Method Pro MIPS helmet and the Squad MAG goggle has everything I’m looking for in a helmet-and-goggle combo. The helmet offers solid protection thanks to a MIPS liner and in-mold construction, while the grid-style ear pads are comfortable and removable to boot. I love the low-profile silhouette of the helmet, the built-in ventilation, and the quick-and-easy magnetic buckle. It’s also light enough for me to bring on backcountry tours. The Method Pro’s flat brim fits seamlessly with the Squad MAG, a stylish cylindrical goggle that features Smith’s streamlined lens interchangeability system and top-of-the-line ChromaPop contrast-enhancing lens tech. Separately, I’m a big fan of these Smith options, but together, they’re a dynamic duo that can seriously amp up your on-hill enjoyment.

I’ve never had a pair of Smartwool base layers that I haven’t liked—and that’s saying something, as I’ve tested enough of the brand’s thermal merino offerings over the last 15 years to have a fresh set of long johns for every day of the week. One of the alluring aspects of merino wool, however, is the natural fiber’s antimicrobial and anti-odor properties, so if you’re traveling, camping, or only have one set, you can wear these Smartwool pieces multiple days in a row without inciting the ire of your ski buddies. These base layers are crafted from 100% merino wool, and the mid-heavyweight fabric is toasty and ready for sub-zero days on the slopes.

I just got my hands on this Norrona Lofoten Gore-Tex Pro kit last week, and I took it out during the first snowfall of the season here in Tahoe. It withstood fat, sopping flakes with no problem—unsurprising considering that it’s crafted with Gore-Tex Pro, what many (myself included) consider to be the best-in-class membrane for skiing and snowboarding. I was surprised, however, by how much I dug the style (the two-tone red is unabashedly fly), and I love how the pant and jacket zip together for extra defense on the deepest of days. I can’t offer anything beyond these first impressions right now, but if you’re in the market for premium outerwear—and want to save some money while you’re at it—this Scandinavian alpine armor merits a closer look.

While I appreciate the breathability of a softshell kit for touring, I love to chase powder and shred through storm cycles. I also call the moisture-prone Sierra home. As such, I often gravitate toward a less breathable but more waterproof hardshell. Enter Norrona’s More outerwear—a featherweight option that skintrack regulars will appreciate.

The Gore-Tex weatherproofing is on point when winter storm warnings roll in, while the 40D face fabric and a no-frills feature set keep weight low. It’s not the most durable jacket in my closet, but it’s one of the most capable in its weight class and one I reach for on backyard adventures and international trips alike. The low-slung bib is a highlight of the kit, too: the cut is high enough to keep powder from soaking your base layers, but low enough that you won’t overheat as much while touring.

Gram-counting backpackers won’t even consider this Therm-a-Rest NeoLoft Sleeping Pad. But if you prioritize comfort over pack weight, the 4.6-inch-thick NeoLoft is worth considering, especially if you split time between moderate backpacking missions and car camping adventures. My favorite feature is the curvature of the side rails, which keep you from falling off the comfy, supportive, well-insulated sleeping pad onto cold, hard ground.

The tried-and-true Wawona tent series has long been a favorite of Outside staff, but the new Universal 3-person version is an entirely fresh addition to the lineup. Essentially, it’s designed using “universal design” principles, which seek to improve outdoor accessibility and inclusivity. Noteworthy additions on that front include a massive, floor-to-ceiling vestibule that can fit two wheelchairs and a leash attachment for service dogs. This tent is truly universal, though, as any campers will appreciate the vertical space, durable materials, and painless setup.

Equal parts fire pit, grill, and campground centerpiece, Snow Peak’s Takibi will change the way you camp more than any other piece of gear in this guide. Forged from stainless steel, the Japanese-made fire pit is built to last. While the heirloom-quality build isn’t lightweight, intentional design makes folding, transporting, and storing it relatively chill. The raised, removable grill is a welcome tool if you’re looking to get into open-fire cooking—one best paired with wagyu steaks, fresh-caught trout, sizzling prawns, and other such delicacies. And Snow Peak makes veritable mountains of accessories, so you can customize your Takibi setup to your camp cooking needs.

I love DB’s Snow Roller Pro for a few reasons. First off, an internal “ribcage” protects contents in transit. The versatile roller handles both skis and boards thanks to an adjustable length that fits 203-centimeter skis and chubby, volume-shifted snowboards. The wheels are beefy, and the handle connects to the DB 90L Hugger Roller Bag for near-effortless one-handed steering. But as someone with limited gear storage at home, my favorite feature is that the Snow Roller Pro rolls up into a compact, easy-to-stash bundle when you’re not using it. All told, it’s a welcome addition to any powder-chaser’s arsenal, and a great gift for anyone you tolerate enough to invite on a ski trip.

This rolling Black Hole Wheeled Duffel features the same tester-beloved armored fabric, pocket configuration, and heavy-duty lash points. However, it’s much more expensive, but you get a ton of utility for the extra outlay, with oversized wheels and a telescoping handle for easy maneuvering in international airports and crowded subway stations. This is my go-to for powder pilgrimages to Japan, British Columbia, you name it.

#8216. After an Accident Left Her Paralyzed, Brittany Chadbourne Found a Way to Keep Climbing

“I'm the giant asterisk at the end of ‘climbing is dangerous.'" —Brittany Chadbourne (Photo: Maya Silver)

For some climbers, campusing—climbing with only your upper body—is a training strategy. For Utah climber Brittany Chadbourne, it’s her only choice.

I met Chadbourne in early October at Momentum Millcreek, one of the gyms she regularly visits in the Salt Lake Valley. She pulled onto a V3 boulder problem angled at least 45 degrees, working her way to the top and back down in about a minute. Then she eased herself into her wheelchair, hardly out of breath.

Bouldering carries particular risks for Chadbourne. Because she can’t control how she lands, a fall could cause additional injuries, including damage to the rods in her spine. These days, she saves harder climbing for ropes and sticks to boulder problems she knows she can safely descend. Afterward, I belayed the 28-year-old on a 5.11c. Her powerful shoulders, arms, and back carried her up the route without the use of her legs or lower abs.

Four years ago, a routesetting accident left Chadbourne paralyzed from the belly button down, so she had to find a new way to practice the sport she loves. “I’ve always wanted to be in Climbing Magazine,” Chadbourne told me. “But I thought it would be for something way cooler than a V2 boulder. I’m still proud that I’m continuing with it and being positive, or at least as positive as I can be.”

Chadbourne discovered climbing while in school at Weber State University in Ogden, Utah, and really got into it in 2020. But before she started climbing, while growing up in northern Utah, she was a gymnast who had heard plenty of stories about gymnasts breaking their necks and becoming paralyzed.

“It was something that I always feared and tried to avoid,” Chadbourne says of paralysis.

On November 22, 2022, that fear became reality.

When Chadbourne began working as a routesetter in September of that year at The Front in Ogden, routesetters used a pull-through system of static lines, an alpine butterfly knot, and quickdraw anchors to access the wall. Chadbourne says the setup made her nervous from the start. She worried the knot could slip through the quickdraw carabiners. And the system differed from the one she’d used while routesetting at Weber State University.

“I was pretty new to all of it. So I was just like, ‘If this is what you guys have been using, obviously it’s safe. I’m sure it’s fine.’ Obviously, it wasn’t fine.”

Not long after she started, Chadbourne and The Front have stated that another routesetter reattached the wrong side of the rope when they were lowering and fell from the wall. According to both The Front and Chadbourne, the climber wasn’t seriously injured. After the accident, The Front retired the system and hosted trainings to get all routesetters up to speed on the new standards. Eddie Morillas, the gym’s director of routesetting, told Climbing via email that an updated fall-protection plan took effect on October 18, 2022, removing the alpine butterfly setup.

Under the new standard, Morillas explained that routesetters “are only permitted to gain initial access to anchors and remove working lines while on belay or connected to an autobelay unit, where applicable.” He added that Chadbourne attended two training sessions on the new standard before her accident.

According to Chadbourne, the head routesetter that day instructed her to use the alpine butterfly setup. The Front confirmed this, stating in an email to Climbing: “Our understanding is that the routesetter in charge let Brittany use the alpine butterfly system, which went against The Front’s fall protection plan and the training every setter on the team had completed.”

The precise cause of Chadbourne’s fall remains uncertain. Morillas told Climbing that The Front’s investigation found her knots were tied correctly, but that she pulled the rope in the wrong direction, preventing the knot from cinching around the anchor. According to The Front, the knot temporarily caught in the anchor before slipping through as Chadbourne moved up the rope.

Chadbourne says she followed the head routesetter’s instructions when setting up her static line correctly and had a coworker double-check it. Near the top of the wall, as she slid her ascender upward, she felt the rope go slack. She believes the knot slipped through the quickdraws, just as she’d feared.

“I immediately knew that I was falling,” she says. “So I just closed my eyes and fell 30 feet.”

When Chadbourne hit the ground, her left leg took most of the impact. She shattered her tibia and fibula, and suffered a burst fracture of her T12 vertebra and compression fractures at her C7, T5, and T7 vertebrae. The fall left her paralyzed from the belly button down.

Chadbourne says she receives workers’ compensation benefits that cover her medical expenses and equipment, including wheelchairs. She has chosen not to pursue a lawsuit, saying she was already overwhelmed by the aftermath of the accident and didn’t believe legal action would change what had happened.

Initially, Chadbourne felt embarrassed that her accident happened in a gym rather than outdoors. She’d spent years caving, exploring abandoned mines, and climbing outside without serious injury, only to suffer a life-altering fall inside a gym.

But that embarrassment didn’t diminish her desire to climb.

“I pretty much knew immediately that I would go back into climbing,” Chadbourne says. “Even as I was being loaded onto the helicopter to go to the hospital.” She didn’t know a lot about paraclimbing, but she figured there must be people out there climbing without their legs. “Campusing is a thing, so I’m sure somebody’s doing it,” she recalls thinking.

After two months in the hospital and another month adjusting to her new normal at home, Chadbourne’s doctor cleared her to climb. But her first time back on belay was “pretty rough.” She made it about 10 feet off the ground, partially hoisted up by her belayer. At first, she couldn’t climb high enough to experience the fear she’d felt during her fall. But as she grew stronger and began climbing higher, Chadbourne admits some of the fear came back.

Chadbourne still has days when she cries about her injury, sometimes even while climbing.

“Day to day, my life is just as hard now as it was four years ago [when I was first injured],” she adds. “I’m just doing more.” And she is. She’s traveling more, training more, and trying things she once thought were out of reach, including becoming an ambitious competitive climber.

Before the accident, Chadbourne loved technical slab climbing. Now, without the use of her legs or lower abdomen, she competes in the AL1 paraclimbing classification, also known as seated climbing.

In 2024, just two years after her injury, Chadbourne made Team USA. She earned bronze in the women’s AL1 competition at the 2025 Paraclimbing National Championships and silver in 2026.

But she found herself in a small competitive field. With so few women in the AL1 category, Chadbourne often faced just one or two other athletes. She and fellow paraclimber Carlie Cook advocated for mixed-gender AL1 competition, which would allow women and men to compete against each other. In March 2025, the International Federation of Sport Climbing released updated paraclimbing guidelines permitting mixed-gender competition in the category.

Competing against a larger field has made the sport more exciting for Chadbourne. “If it was just women, it would be like three or four of us in the entire world,” she says. “So to be able to compete against 20-plus people is really exciting. And it makes me want to beat the men!”

Now, Chadbourne has her sights set on making a World Cup final one day. She’s also working to bring more athletes with paraplegia, especially women, into the sport. One day, she hopes there will be enough female competitors to support a separate women’s category.

But there’s another stage Chadbourne hopes to compete on someday: the Paralympics.

“When I had heard rumors that [paraclimbing] was going to be in the LA Games, I got really excited,” Chadbourne recalls. But like many paraclimbing categories, AL1 was excluded from climbing’s Paralympic debut at the Los Angeles 2028 Games.

Chadbourne hopes that will change for the 2032 Paralympics in Australia. In the meantime, she’s also training in Nordic skiing and biathlon, with ambitions of making Team USA in both sports.

For Chadbourne, staying busy is one way of coping with the difficult days. “The busier you are, your brain just forgets to be sad,” she says.

“Continual motion builds on itself,” she adds. “I don’t really have any other choice but to just keep on going.”

Chadbourne’s momentum has carried into her work with other climbers. Between competitions and training, she teaches climbing and continues to set routes at Weber State University.

There, she’s become an advocate for safe routesetting and climbing practices, encouraging climbers to ask questions about systems before trusting them.

“I’m the giant asterisk at the end of ‘climbing is dangerous,’” Chadbourne says about teaching college students. “I want to prepare them that this is a possibility, but then I prepare them to avoid it in as many ways as they can.”

The most important lesson Chadbourne underscores is to always speak up if you don’t understand how something works. No matter their experience level, Chadbourne wants all climbers to feel comfortable raising concerns and asking questions.

“I want them to feel like they have a voice.”

#8215. The Best Trail Running Shoes for Fall 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The best trail running shoes boost our confidence on singletrack to scree fields, sand to slick rock. They’re comfortable and nimble and help us run fast or forever, depending on the adventure. As the days grow shorter and colder we’re also looking for shoes that excel under a wide variety of circumstances, like wet leaves, rime ice, and snow. And as the weather deteriorates, we’re also leaning more on road-to-trail models for the days when the roads and paths are calling our names.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across Santa Barbara to Boulder and Nebraska to New Hampshire, our testers Lisa Jhung, Cory Smith, Johnathan Beverly, and Abby Levene provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, speed, traction, cushioning, and their joy of running. The result is Trail Runner Magazine’s best trail shoes for fall 2026. Considering that the “best” shoe can run differently on someone else’s feet, our review is specially curated with a shoe claiming the title of each chosen category it achieves best. For even more models, check out Outside’s guide to best trail running shoes for fall.

Weight: 7.5 ounces (men’s 8.5), 6.2 ounces (women’s 8) Stack Height: 28.5–21.5 mm Drop: 7 mm Sizing: 7-12.5, 13, 14, 15 (men’s), 6-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Responsive and springy + Weightless feeling underfoot + Good ground feel + Excellent traction – Runs small (go half a size up) –Expensive

If the Norda 005 was a car, it would be the Mercedes AMG E63S Wagon. That is to say: it’s quiet performance luxury. IYKYK, as the kids say. Coming in at just 214 grams (7.5 ounces) for a men’s U.S. 8.5, it’s one of the lightest trail running shoes on the market. It’s also made from the highest quality materials: A Biodyneema upper makes it both durable and highly breathable. A slick of Vibram “Megagrip Elite” rubber renders the outsole ultra tacky on the trails while rolling over the roads. And, perhaps most importantly, the midsole is made completely from a proprietary Mouse Arnitel TPEE—a supercritical foam generally only used in small amounts because of the cost—making the shoe featherlight, energetic, and highly durable.

And the simplicity of the design lets the quality shine. As such, it’s a light, fast trail running shoe that can do it all. We’d turn to this shoe for anything from easy days on mixed surfaces, to “fast” trail 100-milers like Western States or Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc. Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene wore one pair of the Norda 005 for the Tour du Mont Blanc, a five-day, 110-mile adventure through the Alps, and she didn’t think about her feet once. There is no higher praise.

The midsole is tuned to be slightly firmer than the superfoam in road racers and thus provides an energetic, bouncy ride that doesn’t trampoline you in wild directions off the trail. While the lack of a plate may disqualify the Norda 005 from being a true trail “super shoe,” don’t mistake semantics for inferiority. We didn’t miss a carbon plate here, and its absence allows for enhanced ground feel and adaptability to varied terrain. The foam and rocker deliver a smooth roll and plenty of precision.

The only real downside to this shoe is the price tag. But sometimes, you get what you pay for. Read our full review of the Norda 005.

Weight: 9.5 oz (men’s), 8.4 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 32–28 mm Drop: 4 mm Sizing: 7-13, 14, 15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Lightweight and nimble – Slippery laces require double-knotting

We’ve tested every version of the Saucony Peregrine since the model’s debut in 2011, and this sixteenth iteration just might be our all-time favorite. The shoe has long been capable of making us feel nimble on rugged terrain, with its great balance of ground feel and cushioning, plus traction on all kinds of trail, wrapped up in a lightweight package. But version 16 takes the Peregrine’s trail capabilities to new levels, and at $150, it’s an easy pick for Best Value.

The upgraded Vibram Megagrip outsole grips rock slabs with aplomb, while the four-millimeter lugs dig into loose dirt and soft ground (though some sandy-trail testers craved even deeper, toothier lugs). The balanced midsole—not too springy, not too mushy, not too thick—delivers a strong connection to the trail while still feeling responsive and shock absorbing, even during wild descents. The flexible, breathable mesh upper with added toe protection kept out trail debris and warded off snags from roots and branches.

The fit of this trail running shoe somehow made a variety of testers feel like it was custom-made for them. It locks down the heel, and the just-roomy-enough toebox allowed toe space to breathe while maintaining control. “The fit is just perfect,” said a tester. “I feel secure and supported from heel to toe, and side to side.”

Weight: 10 oz (men’s), 9 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 33.5 mm–25.5 mm Drop: 8mm Sizing: 7-13, 14 (men’s), 5-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Great traction + Outstanding foothold – Cushioning may feel too firm for some

The Salomon Genesis 2 earned mountain-goat status among our crew, providing outstanding traction over loose dirt and rock. Its supportive Matryx upper—constructed with thin, high-tenacity yarns and durable Kevlar—secures narrow and wide feet alike via Salomon’s quick-pull lacing system. The forefoot offers slightly more room than version 1, enhancing overall comfort without sacrificing agility.

The outsole, made of Salomon’s Contagrip rubber with toothy, 4 mm lugs, provided excellent traction on all surfaces, giving us confidence, even on scrambles over large rocky slabs and slippery descents.

While the EVA-blend midsole runs firm, it offers direct trail feedback. “This shoe makes it fun to pick a line and charge,” noted one tester. “I felt completely present instead of mindlessly rolling over obstacles.”

For technical runners who prefer softer cushioning, we also recommend the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro. (Read our full review of the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro here.)

Weight: 11.7 oz (men’s), 9.5 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 39–31 mm Drop: 8 mm Sizing: 6-15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extremely versatile + Comfortable for all-day wear – Traction could be better

The Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the new model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

The midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

What makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. This shoe’s versatility makes it a great pick as a one-trick pony for the casual runner who doesn’t need a lighter, faster race shoe, and a solid choice for travel.

Weight: 9.5 oz (unisex) Stack Height: 40–34 mm Drop: 6 mm Sizing: 5-12,13 (men’s), 6.5-13.5, 14.5 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag

Brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has launched in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

If you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

When assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

Ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

If the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how quickly and powerfully it rebounds.

The best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, quickly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research shows that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate new releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall update, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to New Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

Freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and says her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

His obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

One of Cory Smith’s go-to routes for testing trail running shoes:

Jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and quickly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every new model as they were released. The parade of shoes continued while he served as shoe editor for Runner’s World, then editor of PodiumRunner, and currently fitness gear editor at Outside. Having now worn nearly every running shoe created in this century—and a fair amount of those dating back to the early models of the ’70s—he’s given up on finding the one best and now relishes the wide variety of excellent options.

Once a 2:46 marathoner regularly doing 50+ mile weeks, recent injuries and his age have reduced his volume and slowed his pace—but he still enjoys an uptempo workout or two each week. Beverly is the author of the book Your Best Stride which explores how each individual’s gait—and thus shoe preference—is unique. He enjoys getting scientists’ take on new shoe trends and trying to describe the nuances of each shoe’s ride.

#8214. Appalachian Trail Threatened by ‘Uncommonly’ Large Wildfire in White Mountains

The Wild River Fire burns in the White Mountain National Forest (Photo: Courtesy USFS)

A wildfire that may be the largest in White Mountains history is currently burning just miles from the Appalachian Trail, and officials say a human may have caused it.

The Wild River Fire started on Tuesday, November 3, in Coos County, New Hampshire, and has grown to 865 acres as of this writing, with just 11 percent contained. While the Appalachian Trail (AT), roughly 10 miles from the blaze, currently remains open, the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) has closed numerous other trails and roads in the area.

Small brush fires and wildfires occur in White Mountains National Forest (WMNF) almost every year, but according to Gorham Fire Chief Philip Cloutier, who spoke with NHPR on Wednesday, a wildfire of this size is unusual. Both extended drought and extremely dry fall conditions have fuelled its speedy growth.

“That’s very uncommon in our area,” Cloutier said. “The largest wildfire that we can remember was just under 100 acres, and that was over 20 years ago.”

Officially, USFS is still investigating the wildfire’s source. Authorities have indicated that they believe it was human-caused, though they have released no further details about the origin.

While the Wild River Fire is burning roughly 10 miles east of the AT, no closures or evacuations have been issued for the trail yet. Still, other trails in the area (some of which connect with the AT) have been closed. Below is the USFS list of trail closures in WMNF.

We will update this article if more closures are announced.

In addition to these closures, Wild River Road is also closed in its entirety.

According to the USFS, the response to the Wild River Fire has been swift, and additional resources, including thje Cherokee Hotshot Crew and a smoke suppression module, have been sent to aid in the fight. The area’s steep, rocky terrain, remote location, and wet conditions have made it particularly challenging for firefighters. A USFS spokesperson told NHPR that firefighters had to cross the Wild River on foot to mount a direct attack.

However, the efforts seem to be paying off. On November 4, the fire swelled to 982 acres. That evening, it was reduced to 865 acres, where it remains currently.

“I am proud of the firefighters who responded quickly and continue to work tirelessly to contain the Wild River Fire,” noted Josh Sjostrom, District Ranger for the White Mountain National Forest’s Androscoggin Ranger District. “We will continue to work with our neighbors and local and state partners to contain this fire.”
